Hot is to cold as up is to ___
Hot and cold are opposites; so are up and down.
Which word does NOT belong? apple, banana, carrot, grape
Apple, banana and grape are fruits; a carrot is a vegetable.
Bird is to nest as bee is to ___
A bird lives in a nest; a bee lives in a hive.
Which word does NOT belong? river, lake, ocean, mountain
River, lake and ocean are bodies of water; a mountain is a landform.
Pen is to write as knife is to ___
A pen is used to write; a knife is used to cut (tool and function).
Author is to book as composer is to ___
An author creates a book; a composer creates a song.

Which word does NOT belong? sprint, jog, stroll, whisper
Sprint, jog and stroll are ways of moving; whisper is a way of speaking.
Drought is to water as famine is to ___
A drought is a shortage of water; a famine is a shortage of food.
Which word is the OPPOSITE of "scarce"?
"Scarce" means hard to find; the opposite is plentiful.
Glove is to hand as sock is to ___
A glove covers a hand; a sock covers a foot.
Which pair has the same relationship as "pebble : boulder"?
A pebble is a small stone and a boulder a large one; a puddle is small water and a lake large water.
All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Which MUST be true?
["All roses are red.","Some roses are red.","No roses are red.","None of these must be true."]
Nothing says the red flowers are roses, so none of the statements must be true.
Which word is closest in meaning to "ephemeral"?
"Ephemeral" means lasting only a short time, i.e. brief.
Candid is to frank as cautious is to ___
"Candid" and "frank" are synonyms; so are "cautious" and "wary".

The teacher said: "Please open your books to page twelve and read the first paragraph quietly."
What should the students do first?
["Close their books","Open their books to page twelve","Talk to a partner","Write a story"]
Key line: "The teacher said: "Please open your books to page twelve and read the first paragraph quietly." So the answer is "Open their books to page twelve".
Sam says: "I'm hungry. I want an apple and a glass of milk."
["An apple and milk","Bread and juice","Pizza","Water only"]
Key line: "I want an apple and a glass of milk." So the answer is "An apple and milk".
Announcement: "The school library will close early today at two o'clock because of a meeting. Please return your books before then."
Why will the library close early?
["It is a holiday","There is a meeting","The books are missing","It is raining"]
Key line: "Announcement: "The school library will close early today at two o'clock because of a meeting." So the answer is "There is a meeting".
Lena tells her friend: "I couldn't come to practice yesterday because my little brother was sick, so I stayed home with him."
["She was tired","She forgot","Her brother was sick","She had a test"]
Key line: "Lena tells her friend: "I couldn't come to practice yesterday because my little brother was sick, so I stayed home with him." So the answer is "Her brother was sick".
The science teacher explains: "Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air. This process is called photosynthesis."
["A way plants make food","A kind of weather","A type of soil","A way animals sleep"]
Key line: "The science teacher explains: "Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air." So the answer is "A way plants make food".
Coach: "We'll meet at the north gate, not the main entrance. The bus leaves at eight, so please don't be late."
["At the main entrance","At the north gate","On the bus","In the gym"]
Key line: "Coach: "We'll meet at the north gate, not the main entrance." So the answer is "At the north gate".
A guide says: "Please stay with the group, and do not touch the exhibits. If you have a question, raise your hand."
What should visitors do if they have a question?
["Touch the exhibit","Leave the group","Raise their hand","Wait outside"]
Key line: "If you have a question, raise your hand." So the answer is "Raise their hand".
Radio: "Tomorrow will start cloudy, but by afternoon the clouds should clear and the temperature will rise to twenty-five degrees."
What will the weather be like tomorrow afternoon?
["Rainy and cold","Clear and warmer","Cloudy all day","Snowy"]
Key line: "Radio: "Tomorrow will start cloudy, but by afternoon the clouds should clear and the temperature will rise to twenty-five degrees." So the answer is "Clear and warmer".
Teacher: "Although the experiment failed, we learned that the metal expands when heated, which is useful information."
["The experiment was perfect","Metal expands when heated","Metal melts at once","Heat is dangerous"]
Key line: "Teacher: "Although the experiment failed, we learned that the metal expands when heated, which is useful information." So the answer is "Metal expands when heated".
Speaker: "Contrary to popular belief, goldfish can remember things for months, not seconds, which is why they can be trained to recognize feeding times."
What is the speaker's main point?
["Goldfish have poor memories","Goldfish can remember for months","Goldfish dislike feeding","Goldfish cannot be trained"]

Key line: "Speaker: "Contrary to popular belief, goldfish can remember things for months, not seconds, which is why they can be trained to recognize feeding times." So the answer is "Goldfish can remember for months".
Tom has a red ball. He plays with it at the park every day after school.
Where does Tom play with his ball?
["At school","At the park","At home","At the beach"]
Key line: "He plays with it at the park every day after school." So the answer is "At the park".
Rosa planted seeds in a small pot. She watered them every morning. After two weeks, tiny green leaves appeared.
["The pot broke","Green leaves appeared","Rosa stopped watering","The seeds disappeared"]
Key line: "After two weeks, tiny green leaves appeared." So the answer is "Green leaves appeared".
The class went to the zoo. They saw lions, monkeys, and a very tall giraffe. Everyone liked the monkeys best.
Which animal did everyone like best?
Key line: "They saw lions, monkeys, and a very tall giraffe." So the answer is "Monkeys".
Recycling means turning old things into new things. When we recycle paper, fewer trees are cut down, and less energy is used.
What is one benefit of recycling paper?
["It makes more trash","Fewer trees are cut down","It costs more energy","It makes paper heavier"]
Key line: "When we recycle paper, fewer trees are cut down, and less energy is used." So the answer is "Fewer trees are cut down".
Because the river flooded last spring, the villagers built a wall of stones along its bank. Since then, the houses have stayed dry.
Why did the villagers build the wall?
["To make a road","To stop the river flooding their homes","To catch fish","To start a market"]
Key line: "Because the river flooded last spring, the villagers built a wall of stones along its bank." So the answer is "To stop the river flooding their homes".
Volcanoes form where hot melted rock, called magma, rises through cracks in the Earth's crust. When pressure builds up, the magma can erupt as lava.
What causes a volcano to erupt?
["Heavy rain","Pressure from rising magma","Strong wind","Ocean waves"]
Key line: "When pressure builds up, the magma can erupt as lava." So the answer is "Pressure from rising magma".
The word "transparent" means that light can pass through something so you can see clearly. Glass windows are usually transparent.
Which object is most likely transparent?
["A wooden door","A glass window","A brick wall","A metal box"]
Key line: "Glass windows are usually transparent." So the answer is "A glass window".
Although the festival was small when it began, word of mouth gradually drew visitors from neighbouring towns, and within a decade it had become the region's most anticipated event.
What can be inferred about the festival?
["It stopped after ten years","It grew because people told others","It was always large","It only had local visitors"]

Key line: "Although the festival was small when it began, word of mouth gradually drew visitors from neighbouring towns, and within a decade it had become the region's most anticipated event." So the answer is "It grew because people told others".

Some people think students should wear uniforms; others disagree. Write a paragraph giving your opinion with at least two reasons.
Introduce yourself. Say your name, your age, and two things you like to do. (Record for about 30 seconds.)

When the town planted trees along Maple Street, many residents complained about the cost. Ten years later, the shade lowered summer temperatures by several degrees, and neighbours began gathering under the branches each evening. The mayor admitted that the trees had paid for themselves in ways no budget could measure.
What is the mayor's attitude toward the trees by the end of the passage?
He admits they paid for themselves.

The mayor admitted that the trees had paid for themselves in ways no budget could measure.
Which sentence best states a theme of the passage?

According to the passage, what happened ten years later?

Scientists studying coral reefs have noticed that reefs near busy harbours often recover more slowly after storms. The researchers suspect that pollution weakens the coral, but they caution that more data is needed before the cause can be confirmed.
Which word best describes the researchers' conclusion?
"Suspect" and "more data is needed" signal caution.

Scientists studying coral reefs have noticed that reefs near busy harbours often recover more slowly after storms. The researchers suspect that pollution weakens the coral, but they caution that more data is needed before the cause can be confirmed.
What does "caution" mean as used in the passage?

What is the passage mainly about?

The wind is given a human action.
Choose the correct word: "They ___ going to the zoo."
Which sentence begins with a capital letter and ends correctly?
["we like pizza.","We like pizza.","We like pizza","we Like pizza?"]
Choose the correct plural: one child, two ___
Which word completes the sentence? "She ran ___ than her brother."
Which sentence is in the past perfect tense?
["I eat lunch.","I had eaten lunch before she arrived.","I will eat lunch.","I am eating lunch."]
Choose the correct possessive: "The ___ toys were everywhere."
Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?
["She nearly drove her kids to school every day.","She drove her kids to school every day.","Every day, she drove her kids to school.","She drove her kids to school daily."]
"Nearly" should modify "every day" or be placed differently.
Which is the best transition: "The experiment failed. ___, the team learned something useful."
Day is to night as summer is to ___
Day and night are opposites; so are summer and winter.
Which word does NOT belong? dog, cat, horse, chair
Dog, cat and horse are animals; a chair is furniture.
Eye is to see as ear is to ___
The eye is used to see; the ear is used to hear.
Which word means the same as "huge"?
Chapter is to book as scene is to ___
A chapter is a part of a book; a scene is a part of a play.
Which word is the OPPOSITE of "generous"?
"Generous" means giving; the opposite is selfish.
Which word does NOT belong? triangle, square, circle, cube
Triangle, square and circle are flat (2-D); a cube is solid (3-D).
Thermometer is to temperature as ruler is to ___
A thermometer measures temperature; a ruler measures length.
All birds have feathers. A penguin is a bird. Which MUST be true?
["A penguin has feathers.","A penguin can fly.","All feathered animals are birds.","Penguins live in cold places only."]
Penguins are birds and all birds have feathers, so penguins have feathers.
Which word is closest in meaning to "ambiguous"?
"Ambiguous" means open to more than one meaning, i.e. unclear.
Prudent is to reckless as frugal is to ___
"Prudent" is the opposite of "reckless"; "frugal" is the opposite of "wasteful".
Anna says: "My birthday is on Saturday. I'm having a party at my house."
["At school","At her house","At the park","At a restaurant"]
Key line: "I'm having a party at my house." So the answer is "At her house".
Teacher: "Tomorrow is picture day. Please wear your school shirt and bring your homework."
Key line: "Please wear your school shirt and bring your homework." So the answer is "Their school shirt".
Dad: "We're out of milk, so I'm going to the store. Do you need anything?"
Why is Dad going to the store?
["To buy milk","To meet a friend","To return a book","To get gas"]
Key line: "Dad: "We're out of milk, so I'm going to the store." So the answer is "To buy milk".
Principal: "The assembly will begin at ten, but students from Room 4 should arrive early to help set up chairs."
Key line: "Principal: "The assembly will begin at ten, but students from Room 4 should arrive early to help set up chairs." So the answer is "Students from Room 4".
Ranger: "Because the trail is muddy after the rain, we will take the lower path, which is longer but safer."
Why will the group take the lower path?
["It is shorter","It is safer","It has a view","It is closed"]
Key line: "Ranger: "Because the trail is muddy after the rain, we will take the lower path, which is longer but safer." So the answer is "It is safer".
Lecturer: "Although electric cars produce no exhaust, their overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated."
["Electric cars are always clean","Benefits depend on the electricity source","Exhaust is harmless","Electric cars are expensive"]

Key line: "Lecturer: "Although electric cars produce no exhaust, their overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated." So the answer is "Benefits depend on the electricity source".
Mia has a cat named Pepper. Pepper likes to sleep on the sofa and drink milk.
What does Pepper like to drink?
Key line: "Pepper likes to sleep on the sofa and drink milk." So the answer is "Milk".
On Monday, the class started a garden. They planted beans, carrots, and corn. Each student has a job.
What did the class start on Monday?
Key line: "On Monday, the class started a garden." So the answer is "A garden".
The library offers free programs during the summer. Children can join a reading club, and older students can volunteer as helpers.
Key line: "Children can join a reading club, and older students can volunteer as helpers." So the answer is "Older students".
Rain forests are home to millions of species. Many of these plants and animals cannot live anywhere else on Earth.
["They are cold","They shelter species found nowhere else","They have no animals","They are small"]
Key line: "Rain forests are home to millions of species." So the answer is "They shelter species found nowhere else".
The inventor tested hundreds of materials before finding one strong enough. "Every failure," she said, "taught me what not to do."
What does the inventor's statement show?
["She gave up easily","She learned from failures","She disliked testing","She worked alone"]
Key line: "Every failure," So the answer is "She learned from failures".
Economists note that when a product becomes scarce, its price typically rises unless demand falls at the same time.
What usually happens to the price of a scarce product?
["It falls","It rises","It stays the same","It disappears"]
Key line: "Economists note that when a product becomes scarce, its price typically rises unless demand falls at the same time." So the answer is "It rises".
Describe what you do on a typical weekend. Use at least five sentences and words like "first", "then", and "finally".
Talk about your favorite food. What is it, how is it made, and why do you like it? (Record for about 45 seconds.)

A plant cannot walk away from the spot where it grows, yet its seeds often end up far from home. Why does this matter? If every seed fell straight down, the young plants would crowd around their parent. They would have to compete for sunlight, water, and space in the soil. So plants have found clever ways to send their seeds on long trips.

Some seeds ride the wind. A dandelion seed hangs from a tiny tuft of soft threads that works like a parachute, so a light breeze can carry it across a whole field. Maple seeds have a flat wing on one side. When they drop, they spin like little helicopters and drift away from the tree.

Other seeds travel by water. A coconut has a thick, hollow husk that lets it float. It can bob on the ocean for weeks before it washes up on a faraway beach, where it may sprout into a new palm tree.

Animals are helpful travel partners, too. Burdock seeds are covered in tiny hooks that catch on a passing dog's fur or a hiker's socks. The seeds get carried a long way before they finally fall off. Birds eat berries and later drop the seeds in new places.

Some plants do not wait for help at all. When the pods of certain plants dry out, they suddenly twist and burst open, and the seeds shoot out like popcorn jumping from a hot pan.

Wind, water, animals, or a sudden pop: each of these methods helps a seed find room to grow.
["the reasons palm trees grow near beaches","how birds choose which berries to eat","the ways plants send their seeds to new places","why dandelions grow best in open fields"]
The first paragraph says plants "have found clever ways to send their seeds on long trips," and the rest of the passage describes those ways.

Have you ever noticed that the Moon seems to change shape from night to night? One week it looks like a thin silver smile, and a week or so later it is a bright, round circle. But the Moon itself never changes shape at all; it is always a ball of rock. What changes is how much of its sunny side we are able to see.

The Moon does not make its own light. Like a mirror, it reflects light that comes from the Sun. At every moment, half of the Moon is lit by sunlight, while the other half remains dark. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half. These different views are called phases.

When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its bright side faces away from us, so we see almost nothing. This is called a new moon. Over the next two weeks, a little more of the lit side comes into view each night. First we see a thin sliver called a crescent, then we see half of the Moon's face, and later we see almost all of it. At last, when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, we see the whole bright side. This is called a full moon.

After the full moon, the pattern runs backward. The lit part shrinks night by night until the new moon comes back, and the whole cycle takes about twenty-nine and a half days.

Long ago, people used this steady, repeating pattern to keep track of time. In fact, the English word "month" comes from an old word for "moon." So the next time you look up at night, remember that you are looking at a calendar in the sky.

Today, almost every pencil has a pink eraser on its end. But for a long time, people who made mistakes with pencils had a messy problem. To remove a pencil mark, they rubbed it with a ball of damp bread. The bread picked up the gray marks, but it also left crumbs everywhere. Worse, the bread could grow moldy if it sat too long.

In the 1700s, explorers brought a strange material to Europe from South America. It came from the sticky sap of certain trees. A popular story says that in 1770, an English engineer reached for his bread to fix a mistake. By accident, he grabbed a piece of this tree material instead. To his surprise, it erased the mark very well! Around the same time, a scientist noticed the same thing. Because the material could rub out pencil marks, he called it "rubber." That is how rubber got its name.

Early rubber erasers had problems, though. In hot weather they turned soft and gooey. In cold weather they became hard and cracked. Then, in the 1840s, inventors learned to heat rubber with a yellow mineral called sulfur. This made the rubber strong and bendy in any weather.

Finally, in 1858, an American inventor had a simple idea. He attached an eraser right onto the end of a pencil. Now a writer never had to hunt for an eraser again.

The next time you fix a mistake, think of all the steps it took to make that little eraser.

Every fall, gray squirrels get very busy. They gather acorns and other nuts and bury them in the ground. A single squirrel may hide thousands of nuts in one season. Instead of keeping them all in one pile, it digs a separate small hole for almost every nut. Scientists call this scatter hoarding.

Why spread the nuts out? If a squirrel kept all its food in one place, a hungry thief could steal everything at once. With nuts hidden in many spots, a thief can find only a few.

Scientists have watched squirrels closely to learn how they find their nuts again in winter. Squirrels have a strong sense of smell, which helps them sniff out buried food. But smell is not the whole story. Studies show that squirrels also remember where they dug. They seem to use trees, rocks, and other landmarks like a map.

Squirrels can also be sneaky. In some studies, scientists saw that when a squirrel knew another animal was watching, it would dig a hole and pretend to drop in a nut. Then it would cover the empty hole and carry the real nut somewhere else. The watcher would be tricked into searching an empty spot.

Even the smartest squirrel does not find every nut. Some stay buried all winter. In spring, these forgotten nuts may sprout into new trees. In this way, busy squirrels help plant the forests they live in.

Mina pressed her hands around the lump of wet clay and pushed the pedal with her foot, and the potter's wheel began to hum and spin. "Gently," said Grandpa Joon from the stool beside her. "Let the clay find its center."

Mina did not feel gentle at all. She had watched Grandpa make bowls all summer, and he made it look as easy as stirring soup. She wanted her own bowl to be finished before her parents arrived to pick her up, so she pressed harder. The clay wobbled for a moment, then flopped over sideways like a tired puppy.

"Ugh, it's ruined!" Mina groaned.

Grandpa did not laugh; instead, he scooped up the clay, patted it into a smooth ball, and set it back in the middle of the wheel. "Do you know how many bowls I ruined when I was learning?" he asked. "More than there are stars over the lake."

Mina looked at him in surprise, because she had always imagined that Grandpa was simply born knowing how to do this.

She tried again, and this time she kept her elbows steady against her knees and let the spinning wheel do most of the work. She thought about the clay instead of the clock, and slowly the lump rose into a short, thick cup, although one side was a little lower than the other.

"It's crooked," she said with a sigh.

"It's yours," Grandpa answered with a smile. "And tomorrow it will be a little less crooked."

When her parents finally arrived, Mina was still sitting at the wheel, her hands gray with clay, and for once she did not ask to go home early.

["It is best to finish every job as fast as possible.","A crooked cup is not worth keeping.","Learning a new skill takes patience and practice.","Only people who are born with talent can make art."]

In the early 1800s, the cliffs near the small English seaside town of Lyme Regis were crumbling. Storms and waves regularly tore away chunks of rock, and with them came strange shapes: coiled shells, bony spines, and teeth set in stone. Most visitors saw curiosities. Mary Anning saw a living.

Anning was born in 1799 into a poor family. Her father, a cabinetmaker, collected fossils on the beach and sold them to tourists, and he taught his children to do the same. When he died in 1810, the family was left deep in debt, and selling fossils became a matter of survival rather than a hobby. The work was risky. The best finds appeared after storms, exactly when landslides were most likely, and Anning herself once barely escaped a falling section of cliff.

Her first major discovery came when she was about twelve. After her brother found an unusual skull, Mary spent months carefully digging out the rest of the skeleton. It belonged to a creature that looked partly like a fish and partly like a lizard. Scientists later named it Ichthyosaurus, meaning "fish lizard." In 1823 she uncovered the first nearly complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a sea reptile with a tiny head, a very long neck, and four paddle-like flippers. The find was so odd that one famous expert at first suspected it was a fake. After careful study, he admitted that he had been wrong.

Anning was more than a skilled digger. She taught herself anatomy, cut open modern fish to compare them with fossils, and noticed details that others missed. She recognized, for example, that certain stones found inside skeletons were actually fossilized droppings, which revealed what ancient animals had eaten.

Despite these achievements, Anning was largely shut out of the scientific world. Women were not allowed to join the leading geological society of her day, and the wealthy men who bought her specimens often published descriptions of them without mentioning her name. She struggled with money for much of her life.

Recognition came slowly. Near the end of her life, members of the geological society collected money to support her, and after her death in 1847, its president honored her in a public speech. Today, historians count her among the founders of paleontology, the study of ancient life. Her story is proof that important science can begin on a windswept beach with a hammer and a sharp eye.

Around the year 1700, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori was working in Florence, Italy, for a wealthy family that loved music. The most popular keyboard instrument of the day was the harpsichord. When a player pressed one of its keys, a small quill inside plucked a metal string. The harpsichord made a bright, sparkling sound, but it had one major limitation: no matter how hard or how softly a musician pressed the keys, the notes came out at nearly the same volume.

Cristofori set out to solve this problem. Instead of plucking the strings, his new instrument struck them with small hammers covered in leather. A gentle touch on a key sent the hammer moving slowly, producing a quiet note; a firm touch sent it flying, producing a loud one. For the first time, a keyboard player could make the music swell and fade simply by changing the pressure of the fingers.

Building such an instrument was far trickier than it sounds. If a hammer stayed pressed against a string, it would stop the vibration and kill the sound at once. Cristofori designed a clever device, now called an escapement, that let each hammer strike its string and then instantly fall back, allowing the note to ring. He also added dampers, small pads that settled onto the strings to silence them when the player let go of a key.

Cristofori called his invention a "harpsichord with soft and loud." In Italian, the words for soft and loud are piano and forte, so the instrument became known as the pianoforte, a name later shortened to piano.

Surprisingly, the invention did not catch on right away. Early pianos were fairly quiet, and many musicians preferred the familiar harpsichord. Over the next century, however, builders in Germany, Austria, and England improved the design. They made the frames sturdier, the strings thicker, and the hammers heavier, and they eventually covered the hammers with felt for a warmer tone. Composers began writing music that took advantage of the piano's range, with sudden contrasts between whispering and thundering passages.

By the 1800s, the piano had pushed the harpsichord aside and become the centerpiece of concert halls and family parlors alike. Every time a pianist plays a note softly, he or she is using the idea Cristofori had more than three hundred years ago.

A glacier may look like a frozen, motionless mountain of ice, but it is actually a slow-moving river. Understanding how glaciers form and travel helps explain the shapes of many landscapes around the world, including places where no ice remains today.

Glaciers begin with snow. In very cold regions, such as high mountains or lands near the poles, more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, new layers pile up. The weight of the upper layers presses down on the older snow beneath, squeezing out the air between the flakes. Gradually, the fluffy snow turns into grainy, packed material and finally into dense, bluish ice. This process can take many decades.

Once the ice becomes thick enough, it begins to move under its own weight. Gravity pulls it downhill, and the enormous pressure at the bottom allows the ice to bend and flow slowly, almost like extremely thick honey. Most glaciers creep only a few centimeters to a few meters a day, though some occasionally surge forward much faster.

As a glacier moves, it reshapes the land beneath it. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the ice act like sandpaper, scraping and polishing the bedrock. Over thousands of years, a glacier can widen a narrow, V-shaped river valley into a broad valley shaped like the letter U. Long scratches left on exposed rock show the direction in which the ice once traveled.

Glaciers also carry material great distances. When the ice finally melts, it drops everything it was carrying. Long ridges of mixed rock and soil, called moraines, mark the places where a glacier's edge once stood. Sometimes a single enormous boulder is left sitting alone in a field, far from any rock of the same type. Such boulders, known as erratics, puzzled early scientists until they realized that ice had carried them there.

Today, glaciers cover about a tenth of Earth's land. Scientists watch them carefully, because changes in their size reveal changes in climate. By studying U-shaped valleys, moraines, and erratics, researchers can also map where glaciers spread during past ice ages, reading the story of ancient ice in landscapes that are now green and warm.

The passage moves from how glaciers form (second paragraph) to how they move (third) to how they reshape land and leave evidence (fourth through sixth).

Glaciers begin with snow. In very cold regions, such as high mountains or lands near the poles, more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, new layers pile up. The weight of the upper layers presses down on the older snow beneath, squeezing out the air between the flakes. Gradually, the fluffy snow turns into grainy, packed material and finally into dense, bluish ice. This process can take many decades.

Once the ice becomes thick enough, it begins to move under its own weight. Gravity pulls it downhill, and the enormous pressure at the bottom allows the ice to bend and flow slowly, almost like extremely thick honey. Most glaciers creep only a few centimeters to a few meters a day, though some occasionally surge forward much faster.

As a glacier moves, it reshapes the land beneath it. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the ice act like sandpaper, scraping and polishing the bedrock. Over thousands of years, a glacier can widen a narrow, V-shaped river valley into a broad valley shaped like the letter U. Long scratches left on exposed rock show the direction in which the ice once traveled.

Glaciers also carry material great distances. When the ice finally melts, it drops everything it was carrying. Long ridges of mixed rock and soil, called moraines, mark the places where a glacier's edge once stood. Sometimes a single enormous boulder is left sitting alone in a field, far from any rock of the same type. Such boulders, known as erratics, puzzled early scientists until they realized that ice had carried them there.

Today, glaciers cover about a tenth of Earth's land. Scientists watch them carefully, because changes in their size reveal changes in climate. By studying U-shaped valleys, moraines, and erratics, researchers can also map where glaciers spread during past ice ages, reading the story of ancient ice in landscapes that are now green and warm.

Look at a map of the eastern United States, and you may notice something curious. A string of cities, among them Trenton, Richmond, and Augusta, lies along an invisible line that runs roughly parallel to the Atlantic coast. These cities were not placed there by accident. They grew up along what geographers call the fall line, and their story shows how geography can shape economic life.

The fall line marks the boundary between two different kinds of land. To the west lie the hard, ancient rocks of the hilly Piedmont region. To the east lies the coastal plain, made of softer layers of sand and clay. Over millions of years, rivers flowing toward the ocean wore away the soft rock of the plain more quickly than the hard rock upstream. As a result, wherever a river crosses from one region to the other, it tumbles over waterfalls and rapids.

For early travelers, these falls were a barrier. Boats could sail upriver from the coast, but they could go no farther once they reached the rapids. Cargo had to be unloaded and carried around the falls or loaded onto wagons heading inland. Places where goods must change from one kind of transport to another often become busy trading centers, because the work of unloading, storing, buying, and selling creates jobs. Warehouses, inns, and markets sprang up at the falls, and small settlements became towns.

The falls offered a second advantage: power. Before electricity, rushing water was one of the most valuable sources of energy available. Water wheels built beside the rapids turned millstones to grind grain into flour and later powered machines that sawed lumber and spun cotton into thread. The same feature that blocked boats could run factories.

Over time, the growth fed on itself. As businesses gathered, workers arrived; as workers arrived, more shops, schools, and roads were built. Even after railroads and highways made river travel less important, many fall line cities kept growing, because they were already established centers of trade and industry.

The fall line reminds us that the locations of cities are rarely random. Physical features such as rivers, harbors, and mountain passes create opportunities, and people tend to settle where those opportunities are greatest.

Leo had lived in Harborview for exactly nine days, and he still could not find his way anywhere without getting hopelessly turned around. His old town had been small enough to cross on a bicycle in fifteen minutes, with streets arranged in a tidy grid. Harborview, by contrast, sprawled along the bay in a tangle of hills and narrow lanes, and every corner seemed to lead somewhere he had not expected.

On the tenth morning, determined to fight back, he packed a sketchbook, a pencil, and a bottle of water and set out to create his own map of the neighborhood.

At first, the work was extremely frustrating, because almost nothing he drew matched what he actually saw. He drew the street outside his apartment far too wide and had to erase it completely. The bakery he thought he had passed twice turned out to be two different bakeries on two different corners. By noon, his paper was smudged and wrinkled, and his map looked less like a town than a plate of spaghetti.

He was sitting on a bench, glaring at the page, when an elderly woman carrying a basket of oranges settled down beside him. She glanced at his sketch with obvious interest. "Ah," she said, "you've discovered the trouble with Harborview. The streets were laid out by goats."

Leo laughed in spite of himself, and the woman introduced herself as Mrs. Okafor and explained that she had lived on Juniper Hill for forty years. Then, pointing to his drawing, she said, "You have Lantern Street running the wrong way; it curves toward the water, not away from it. Everything in this town bends toward the harbor, like flowers turning toward the sun."

That single observation changed everything. Once Leo understood that the streets curved toward the bay, the confusing puzzle gradually began to make sense. He spent the afternoon walking, checking, and redrawing, and by evening he had produced a map that actually worked. He had also included details that no ordinary map would show: the stairway decorated with painted tiles, the bench where Mrs. Okafor rested each morning, and the corner where a gray cat dozed in the window of a secondhand bookstore.

That night, Leo pinned the finished map above his desk. He realized that it was not merely a guide to Harborview's streets but also a record of the first day the unfamiliar town had started to feel like his.

When a honeybee forager discovers a rich patch of flowers, she faces a communication problem that would challenge any engineer. How can she inform her nestmates, inside a dark hive, where to find food that may be several kilometers away? The answer, decoded by the Austrian biologist Karl von Frisch in the mid-twentieth century, is one of the most remarkable examples of symbolic communication in the animal kingdom.

Von Frisch observed that returning foragers often performed a peculiar routine on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. A bee would run forward in a straight line while vigorously shaking her abdomen, then circle back to her starting point and repeat the run, alternating between left and right loops. He spent years on patient experiments, training marked bees to visit feeding stations at carefully measured locations and then watching them dance. In this way, von Frisch determined that the "waggle dance" encoded two pieces of information. The angle of the straight run, measured relative to vertical, corresponded to the angle between the food source and the sun's position. The duration of the waggle portion indicated distance: the longer the waggle, the farther away the flowers.

The discovery was startling because it implied that bees could translate a direction in the open landscape into an abstract representation on a wall, and that other bees could translate it back. Not everyone was persuaded. In the 1960s, a group of researchers argued that recruits located food primarily by following floral odors carried on the dancer's body, and that the dance itself might convey little useful information. Their experiments showed that scent did play a role, and for a time the debate grew heated.

Resolving the controversy required technology that von Frisch never had. Researchers eventually built small robotic bees that could perform programmed dances in a hive. Some recruits flew toward the locations the robot indicated, even though the robot carried no scent from those sites. Most decisively, a team in the early 2000s attached tiny radar transponders to newly recruited bees and tracked their flights. Recruits that had been moved to an unfamiliar release point flew in the direction, and for roughly the distance, that the dance had specified, demonstrating that they were relying on the dance's information rather than simply searching for familiar smells.

Today, most biologists regard the waggle dance as a genuine symbolic signal, though one supplemented by odor and other cues once recruits approach their target. The episode also offers a lesson about how science proceeds. Von Frisch's interpretation was correct in its essentials, yet the skeptics were not merely obstinate; their challenge exposed the importance of scent and forced researchers to devise more rigorous tests. Von Frisch shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973. Yet the full confirmation of his insight depended in part on the persistence of those who doubted it.

For centuries, sailors could find their latitude, or position north or south, by measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon. Longitude, their position east or west, was a far more stubborn problem. Because Earth rotates fifteen degrees every hour, a navigator who knew both the exact time at a home port and the local time aboard ship could calculate longitude from the difference. Local time was comparatively easy to determine by observing the sun at noon. The difficulty lay in preserving the home port's time across thousands of kilometers of ocean.

In principle, a reliable clock would solve the problem. In practice, the finest clocks of the early eighteenth century depended on swinging pendulums, which were useless on a pitching deck. Variations in temperature caused metal components to expand and contract, altering the clock's rate, and humidity thickened the lubricants inside. An error of only a few minutes could place a ship many kilometers from where its crew believed it to be, an uncertainty that contributed to costly shipwrecks.

In 1714, the British government offered a substantial prize for a practical method of determining longitude at sea. Many prominent scientists assumed the solution would emerge from astronomy, perhaps by using the predictable movement of the moon against the background stars as a kind of celestial clock. John Harrison, a largely self-taught carpenter and clockmaker from the north of England, pursued a mechanical answer instead.

Harrison devoted more than four decades to the challenge. His first three timekeepers were large, intricate machines. They included ingenious innovations, such as linked metal bars that compensated for temperature changes and bearings that reduced the need for oil. Yet each fell short of his own exacting standards. His breakthrough came with a fourth design that abandoned the bulky approach altogether: a timepiece only somewhat larger than a pocket watch. On a voyage to the Caribbean in the early 1760s, it reportedly lost only a few seconds over many weeks at sea.

Even this triumph did not bring immediate reward. The officials responsible for the prize, some of whom favored the astronomical method, questioned whether Harrison's results could be replicated, demanded additional trials, and insisted that he fully disclose his design. Only after years of negotiation, and when he was in his eighties, did Harrison receive payments approaching the full amount.

Harrison's persistence nonetheless transformed navigation. Within several decades, copies of his design, known as marine chronometers, were becoming standard equipment on long voyages, and navigators often used astronomical and mechanical methods together to verify each other. The story suggests that a problem regarded as the province of theorists may sometimes yield to the patient work of a skilled craftsman.

An error of only a few minutes could place a ship many kilometers from where its crew believed it to be, an uncertainty that contributed to costly shipwrecks.

Beneath the floor of nearly every forest lies a vast, hidden partnership. The roots of most plants are entwined with the threads of fungi. Together they form associations called mycorrhizae, from the Greek words for "fungus" and "root." The fungal threads, called hyphae, are far thinner than even the finest roots. This allows them to penetrate tiny pores in the soil and absorb water and mineral nutrients, such as phosphorus, that roots alone would struggle to reach. In exchange, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis. Neither partner is merely a passenger; each provides something the other cannot easily obtain on its own.

This exchange is ancient. Fossil evidence suggests that fungi were associated with some of the earliest land plants more than four hundred million years ago. Many botanists believe that such partnerships helped plants colonize barren continents in the first place. Today, the great majority of plant species form such relationships. Experiments show that many grow poorly when their fungal partners are removed.

In recent decades, researchers have investigated a more surprising possibility. Because a single fungus can connect to the roots of several plants, and a single plant can host several fungi, forests may be laced with underground networks linking trees of different ages and even different species. Using chemical tracers, some studies have detected the movement of carbon from one tree to another through these connections. Such findings inspired the popular nickname "the wood wide web" and the appealing notion that mature "mother trees" deliberately nourish their seedlings.

Other scientists urge caution. They note that many of the field studies were small. It is also difficult to rule out alternative routes by which carbon could travel through soil, and the amounts transferred were sometimes too small to matter much to a tree's survival. Moreover, describing trees as devoted parents may project human motives onto organisms whose interactions could be explained by simpler processes, such as fungi distributing resources according to their own needs. A recent review of the evidence concluded that, while mycorrhizal networks clearly exist, several widely repeated claims about their role in forest communication and sharing rest on limited data.

This debate does not diminish the importance of mycorrhizae. The basic exchange of nutrients for sugars is firmly established and essential to most ecosystems on land. Instead, it illustrates a recurring tension in science between a compelling story and the slower work of verification. The underground world remains difficult to observe directly, and the most accurate description of forest networks may ultimately prove less romantic, but no less fascinating, than the popular version.

Many of the most celebrated wall paintings of the Italian Renaissance were created using a demanding technique known as buon fresco, or "true fresco." Unlike an artist working on canvas, who can revise a composition over weeks or months, the fresco painter worked against a chemical deadline, and the discipline this imposed shaped both the methods and the appearance of the art.

The process began with the preparation of the wall. Workers applied several layers of plaster made from lime, sand, and water, each finer than the last. The final layer, called the intonaco, was spread only over an area that the painter expected to complete in a single session. While this layer was still damp, the artist brushed on pigments mixed with nothing but water. As the plaster dried, a chemical reaction with carbon dioxide in the air transformed the lime into a hard, crystalline form of calcium carbonate. This reaction locked the particles of pigment into the surface of the wall itself. The color did not merely rest on top of the plaster; it became part of it.

This chemistry gave true fresco its remarkable durability, but it also left little room for error. Once the plaster had set, typically within a day, the paint could no longer bond with it. A serious mistake required chiseling away the section and starting over with fresh plaster. Consequently, painters divided large compositions into sections called giornate, an Italian word derived from "day," and carefully planned the sequence in which they would be painted. The seams between these daily patches often followed the outlines of figures or architectural details, where they would be least noticeable. Modern conservators, examining frescoes under angled light, can still trace these joins and thereby reconstruct the order, and sometimes the pace, of an artist's work.

Not every pigment could survive the chemically harsh environment of wet lime, so fresco painters relied on a limited palette composed largely of earth-based colors. Certain brilliant blues and other sensitive pigments had to be applied afterward on dry plaster, a method called fresco secco. These additions, attached with glue or egg rather than bound chemically into the wall, were far less permanent; in many surviving works they have flaked away, leaving areas that appear strangely faded compared with the robust colors surrounding them.

The constraints of fresco thus left their mark on the finished paintings. The necessity of working quickly encouraged confident, economical brushwork and meticulous advance planning, often with full-scale drawings transferred to the wall before painting began. Far from merely limiting artists, the technique's demands helped produce works whose colors have endured for five centuries.

At five o'clock in the morning, the marsh was the color of weak tea, and Ruth was convinced that volunteering for the spring bird survey had been the most serious miscalculation of her sixteen years. Her cousin Dev, who had persuaded her to come, was already crouched at the edge of the boardwalk with a notebook balanced on his knee, his binoculars raised toward a stand of reeds that, as far as Ruth could determine, contained nothing whatsoever.

"Listen," he whispered.

Ruth listened obediently, cataloguing each sound in turn: the steady hum of insects, the distant grumble of a delivery truck on the highway, and the unpleasant squelch of her own sneakers, which had proven considerably less waterproof than their packaging had advertised. Nothing she heard resembled a bird.

Dev made a small mark in his notebook and murmured, "Marsh wren, two of them, actually, answering each other from opposite ends of the reeds."

She was prepared to accuse him of inventing it, but then, as though the reeds had decided to settle the argument, a rattling, bubbling song spilled out of them, followed almost instantly by a reply from farther away. Ruth realized, with mild irritation, that she had been hearing the sound for several minutes and had simply filed it away with the insects.

For the next two hours, Dev taught her to separate the morning into its individual threads. The liquid three-note phrase belonged to a red-winged blackbird; the dry, insistent chip came from a sparrow that refused to reveal itself; the thin whistle overhead was a hawk circling patiently above the water. Gradually, the marsh, which had seemed empty and monotonous, became crowded and argumentative, as though she had wandered into a room where everyone had been conversing all along and she was only now beginning to understand the language.

What surprised her most was not the number of birds but the transformation in her own attention. Ordinarily, Ruth moved through the world at the speed of her phone, glancing, evaluating, and moving on without a second thought. Here, a single unremarkable patch of cattails rewarded ten minutes of stillness with a flicker of movement, a flash of yellow, a bird that would have remained invisible to anyone in a hurry.

When the survey concluded, Dev tallied the results: forty-one species. Ruth had personally identified six, and she privately suspected that at least two of those had been fortunate guesses rather than genuine recognitions. Nevertheless, as they walked back toward the parking lot, she caught herself pausing at a song from the hedgerow, head tilted, attempting to name it before Dev could.

"Same time next week?" he asked, not entirely concealing his grin.

Ruth pretended to deliberate, frowning theatrically at the condition of her sneakers. "Maybe," she said, which they both understood perfectly well to mean yes.

["Patient, careful attention can reveal a richness that hurried observers miss.","Marshes are too noisy to be good places for birds.","Volunteering is usually a waste of time for teenagers.","Competition between cousins makes any activity more enjoyable."]
Ruth is most surprised by "the transformation in her own attention" and notes a bird "would have remained invisible to anyone in a hurry."

Every morning, Marisol climbed the narrow stairs to her grandfather's workshop, where dozens of clocks ticked out of step with one another. As a small child she had found the noise maddening, but now she barely heard it. Her grandfather, bent over a brass gear no larger than a coin, never looked up when she entered. "Hand me the tweezers," he would say, and she would, and that was their entire conversation until noon. Yet she had come to understand that this silence was not coldness. It was the way he welcomed her: by assuming she belonged there. When a customer once asked why such a quiet girl bothered to visit, her grandfather answered without lifting his eyes. "She is the only one who knows when to stay still," he said. Marisol pretended to polish a clock face, but her cheeks burned with pride.

["A girl's growing appreciation of her grandfather's quiet way of showing acceptance","A customer's complaint about a clock repair","A child's frustration with a noisy workplace","The history of clockmaking in a small town"]

Octopuses are masters of disguise, but the mechanism behind their transformations is stranger than most people realize. Beneath an octopus's skin lie thousands of tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each surrounded by muscles. When the animal wants to change color, its brain signals the muscles to stretch the sacs open or squeeze them shut, altering the pattern across its body within a fraction of a second. Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colorblind; their eyes contain only one type of light-sensing cell. Researchers therefore puzzle over how the animal matches its background so well. Before the Erie Canal opened in 1825, shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City cost about one hundred dollars and took weeks of jolting travel by wagon. The canal, a 363-mile waterway dug largely by hand, cut that cost to roughly ten dollars and shortened the trip considerably. Farmers in the Midwest suddenly found that their grain could reach eastern markets profitably, and they planted more. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew rapidly along the route, and New York City surpassed rival ports to become the nation's busiest. Not everyone benefited, however. Farmers in New England, facing cheaper western produce, struggled to compete, and many abandoned their land for factory jobs or for the West itself. The canal thus illustrates how a single improvement in transportation can reshape the economy, creating winners and losers at the same time.

Translators are often described as invisible, and the best are said to be those whose work readers never notice. Yet this ideal is more contested than it appears. A translator who renders a novel into smooth, natural English may erase the strangeness that made the original distinctive; the foreign rhythms, unfamiliar idioms, and odd turns of phrase are, after all, part of what the author intended. Some contemporary translators therefore deliberately preserve awkwardness, trusting readers to tolerate friction in exchange for authenticity. Critics reply that a translation no one can comfortably read has failed its audience as surely as one that distorts the original. The disagreement is unlikely to be settled, because it reflects a genuine tension between two loyalties: fidelity to the author and service to the reader. Every translator, in effect, must choose where to stand between them.

When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a "waggle dance" to share the news. The bee shuffles in a figure-eight pattern, vibrating its abdomen during the straight middle section. The angle of this waggle run, measured against the vertical wall of the comb, tells the other bees which direction to fly relative to the sun. The length of the run indicates distance: the longer the waggle, the farther away the food. Observers in dark hives have confirmed that the bees follow these instructions with surprising accuracy, even when the sun is hidden behind clouds. Scientists consider the dance remarkable because few animals other than humans communicate information about things that are not present.

Seventeenth-century Dutch painters turned away from the grand religious and mythological scenes that had dominated European art. Instead, a rising merchant class wanted pictures of their own world: a woman pouring milk, a tavern crowded with card players, a quiet street after rain. Such works were modest in scale, since they were meant to hang in ordinary homes rather than cathedrals. Yet their apparent simplicity is deceptive. Painters labored over the fall of light on a copper pot or the texture of a linen cloth, convinced that attention to the everyday could reveal something enduring. Some scholars read hidden moral lessons into these scenes, such as warnings against idleness or excess. Others argue that the paintings celebrate ordinary life for its own sake. Probably both views contain some truth, for the artists seldom explained themselves.
According to the passage, why were these paintings modest in scale?
["Churches forbade large canvases.","Painters lacked skill.","Paint was scarce.","They were meant to hang in ordinary homes."]
The passage says they were meant for ordinary homes rather than cathedrals.

Leo did not want to spend his summer vacation pulling weeds. His mother had signed him up to volunteer at the community garden on Maple Street, and he was not happy about it. "All of my friends are swimming at the neighborhood pool," he grumbled as they walked down the sunny block together.

At the garden, an elderly woman named Mrs. Alvarez waved them over. She wore a wide straw hat, and there was dirt on both of her knees. "You must be Leo," she said with a friendly smile. "I have been waiting all week for a strong helper, and this little plot belongs to you now."

Leo stared at a small square of dry, lumpy soil that did not look like much at all. Mrs. Alvarez handed him a packet of tomato seeds and a tiny shovel. She demonstrated how to dig shallow holes, drop in the seeds, and pat the dirt down gently with his palm. "Water them every single morning," she instructed. "Plants are patient, but they are never forgetful."

For two long weeks, absolutely nothing happened. Leo watered the bare soil each day and felt ridiculous. Then one morning, he noticed tiny green sprouts poking up through the dirt. He knelt down carefully and counted twelve of them! He raced across the garden to tell Mrs. Alvarez, and she laughed and clapped her hands.

By the middle of July, the tomato plants were taller than his waist. However, one morning Leo discovered that something had chewed the leaves and nibbled two green tomatoes. He also noticed small paw prints in the mud. "Rabbits," Mrs. Alvarez said, shaking her head. Leo felt his face get hot, because all of his hard work seemed ruined.

That afternoon, Leo did not hurry home early. Instead, he located some old wire and wooden stakes behind the tool shed. He spent three hours constructing a low fence around his plot. His fingers got scratched, but he refused to stop until every gap was closed.

The fence worked perfectly. In August, Leo picked his first ripe tomato, which was warm from the sun and bright red. He carried a heavy basket to Mrs. Alvarez and offered her the biggest one.

"Next summer," Leo announced, "may I grow peppers too?"
Which sentence best states a theme of the story?

["Older people always know more than young people.","Wild animals should never be allowed near a garden.","It is better to spend the summer with friends at the pool.","Patience and hard work can turn something small into something rewarding."]
Leo waits two weeks for sprouts, fixes the rabbit problem by building a fence, and is finally rewarded with ripe tomatoes. The story shows that patience and hard work pay off.

Leo did not want to spend his summer vacation pulling weeds. His mother had signed him up to volunteer at the community garden on Maple Street, and he was not happy about it. "All of my friends are swimming at the neighborhood pool," he grumbled as they walked down the sunny block together.

At the garden, an elderly woman named Mrs. Alvarez waved them over. She wore a wide straw hat, and there was dirt on both of her knees. "You must be Leo," she said with a friendly smile. "I have been waiting all week for a strong helper, and this little plot belongs to you now."

Leo stared at a small square of dry, lumpy soil that did not look like much at all. Mrs. Alvarez handed him a packet of tomato seeds and a tiny shovel. She demonstrated how to dig shallow holes, drop in the seeds, and pat the dirt down gently with his palm. "Water them every single morning," she instructed. "Plants are patient, but they are never forgetful."

For two long weeks, absolutely nothing happened. Leo watered the bare soil each day and felt ridiculous. Then one morning, he noticed tiny green sprouts poking up through the dirt. He knelt down carefully and counted twelve of them! He raced across the garden to tell Mrs. Alvarez, and she laughed and clapped her hands.

By the middle of July, the tomato plants were taller than his waist. However, one morning Leo discovered that something had chewed the leaves and nibbled two green tomatoes. Long ago in ancient Greece, a young woman named Arachne lived in a small village near the sea. Her family was poor, but Arachne had a special talent. She could weave cloth more beautifully than anyone in the land. Her pictures in thread showed rivers that seemed to ripple and birds that looked ready to fly away.

People came from faraway towns just to watch her work. "Surely the goddess Athena taught you this skill," they often said. Athena was the goddess of wisdom and weaving. The people of the village believed every great weaver owed her thanks.

Arachne would toss her head proudly. "Nobody taught me anything," she boasted. "My skill belongs to me alone. In fact, I am a better weaver than Athena herself. If she disagrees, let her come and try to beat me."

High on Mount Olympus, Athena heard these arrogant words. She dressed herself as a bent old woman and walked into the village. She gently warned Arachne, "Be careful, child. Ask the goddess to forgive you before it is too late." Arachne only laughed at the stranger and said her challenge again.

Suddenly the old woman vanished, and Athena stood there, tall and shining. The people dropped to their knees, but Arachne did not say she was sorry. Instead, she set up her loom, and the contest began.

Athena wove a grand scene of the gods sitting on their thrones. Arachne wove a picture that made fun of the gods and showed their mistakes. Her threads were so fine and her colors so bright that even Athena could not find a single flaw. Still, the goddess was furious that a human would mock the gods so boldly.

Athena touched Arachne lightly on the forehead. At once, Arachne began to shrink. Her arms and legs grew thin, and soon she had eight of them. Her body became small and round. Arachne had been changed into the very first spider.

"You love to weave," Athena said, "so you and your children will weave forever." From that day on, Arachne spun thin, silky webs in the corners of houses and between the branches of trees.

The people of ancient Greece told this story to remind others that talent is a gift. Even the most skillful person should stay humble.
What lesson does this myth teach?
["Spiders are helpful animals that should be protected.","Strangers should never be trusted.","People should practice every day to improve a skill.","Even very talented people should stay humble."]
The last paragraph says the story reminds people that talent is a gift and that even the most skillful person should stay humble.

In the spring of 1848, eleven-year-old Hannah Brooks left her home in Missouri. Her family had sold their farm, packed everything into a covered wagon, and joined a wagon train heading west on the Oregon Trail. Her father dreamed of rich farmland in Oregon, more than two thousand miles away.

The journey was harder than Hannah had imagined. Each day, the wagons rolled slowly across the endless prairie. Hannah walked beside the wagon for hours because the oxen were already pulling a heavy load. At night, she gathered dried buffalo chips for the cooking fire, since there were almost no trees to burn.

After six weeks, the wagon train reached a wide, muddy river. The water was brown and fast after the spring rains. The wagon master studied the river for a long time. "We cannot wait for the water to go down," he announced. "Snow will close the mountain passes if we arrive too late."

Hannah's little brother, Thomas, grabbed her hand. He was only six, and his lip was trembling. "What if the wagon tips over?" he whispered. Hannah was frightened too, and her stomach felt tight. However, she did not want Thomas to see her fear.

"Papa has crossed rivers before," she told him calmly. "We will hold on tight and sing our counting song. By the time we reach one hundred, we will be on the other side."

The men raised the wagon boxes onto blocks of wood so the water would not soak their supplies. Then Papa cracked the whip, and the oxen stepped into the cold current. The wagon rocked and creaked. Water splashed over the sides, and a sack of flour floated away. Hannah held Thomas tightly and kept counting out loud, even when her voice shook.

At last, the oxen climbed onto the far bank. The family was soaked, and they had lost some flour, but everyone was safe. Mama hugged both children and looked at Hannah with surprise. "You were so brave," she said softly.

That night, Hannah wrote in her small journal by the light of the campfire. "Today I learned that being brave does not mean you are not scared," she wrote. "It means you keep going anyway."
Why does the wagon master decide NOT to wait for the river to go down?
["Snow could close the mountain passes if they arrive too late.","Another wagon train is waiting behind them.","The families have run out of flour.","The oxen are too tired to keep walking."]
The wagon master says, "Snow will close the mountain passes if we arrive too late." That is the cause of his decision.

When you flip a light switch, the room fills with light right away. It may seem like magic, but it is really science. The light turns on because electricity is moving along a path called a circuit.

Electricity is a form of energy. It is made of tiny bits called electrons that move from place to place. But electrons cannot move just anywhere. They need a complete path that forms a loop. That loop is a circuit.

A simple circuit has three main parts. First, it needs a source of energy, such as a battery. Second, it needs wires to carry the current. Third, it needs something that uses the energy, like a light bulb or a small motor. All of these parts must be joined in an unbroken loop. Then electrons can flow from the battery, through the wire and the bulb, and back to the battery again.

There are two kinds of circuits you should know about. In a closed circuit, the path is complete. The current can flow, so the bulb glows. In an open circuit, there is a gap somewhere in the path. Because the loop is broken, the electrons stop moving and the bulb goes dark. A switch is just a tool that opens and closes a circuit. When you turn a switch off, you make a gap on purpose.

Not every material lets current pass through it easily. Materials that let it flow are called conductors. Most metals, such as copper and steel, are good conductors. That is why the wires inside your walls are usually made of copper. Materials that block the flow are called insulators. Rubber, plastic, glass, and wood are common insulators. Power cords are covered with plastic or rubber. This coat keeps the current inside the wire, so it does not shock the person who is holding the cord.

Knowing about circuits helps people stay safe. Water from a river or a sink can carry current, so you should never touch a switch or plug with wet hands. You should also never poke anything into an outlet. Electricity is useful, but it can be dangerous when it goes where it should not go.

The next time you turn on a lamp, think about the hidden loop that makes it work.
What is the main idea of the passage?

["Batteries are the only source of energy for light bulbs.","Copper is the most useful metal in the world.","Light switches were invented to save energy in homes.","Electricity flows through a complete loop called a circuit, and knowing how circuits work helps people stay safe."]
The whole passage explains what a circuit is, its parts, open and closed circuits, conductors and insulators, and safety.

When you flip a light switch, the room fills with light right away. It may seem like magic, but it is really science. The light turns on because electricity is moving along a path called a circuit.

Electricity is a form of energy. It is made of tiny bits called electrons that move from place to place. But electrons cannot move just anywhere. They need a complete path that forms a loop. That loop is a circuit.

A simple circuit has three main parts. First, it needs a source of energy, such as a battery. Second, it needs wires to carry the current. Third, it needs something that uses the energy, like a light bulb or a small motor. All of these parts must be joined in an unbroken loop. Then electrons can flow from the battery, through the wire and the bulb, and back to the battery again.

There are two kinds of circuits you should know about. In a closed circuit, the path is complete. The current can flow, so the bulb glows. In an open circuit, there is a gap somewhere in the path. Because the loop is broken, the electrons stop moving and the bulb goes dark. A switch is just a tool that opens and closes a circuit. When you turn a switch off, you make a gap on purpose.

That is why the wires inside your walls are usually made of copper. Materials that block the flow are called insulators. Rubber, plastic, glass, and wood are common insulators. Two hundred years ago, moving goods across New York State was slow and costly. Farmers in the West grew plenty of wheat and corn, but getting their crops to cities on the East Coast was a big problem. Roads were rough and muddy. Wagons pulled by horses could carry only small loads, and a trip could take weeks.

DeWitt Clinton, who later became governor of New York, had a bold idea. He wanted to dig a canal, or a man-made river, across the state. It would connect the Hudson River near Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Boats could then travel all the way from the Great Lakes to New York City by water.

Many people laughed at the plan. The canal would need to stretch about 363 miles through forests, swamps, and hills. Some people called it "Clinton's Ditch" and said it would never work. Still, Clinton did not give up, and digging began on July 4, 1817.

Building the canal was very hard work. Thousands of workers used shovels, picks, and horses to dig the long ditch. Many of the workers were new arrivals from Ireland. They cleared trees, pulled out stumps, and moved tons of dirt and rock. In some places, the land rose or fell too steeply for boats. To solve this problem, workers built locks. A lock is like a water elevator that raises or lowers a boat from one level to the next.

In 1825, after eight years of work, the Erie Canal was finally finished. Boats were pulled along the water by mules that walked on a path beside the canal. The trip that once took weeks by wagon now took about ten days. The cost of shipping goods dropped to about one tenth of what it had been.

The canal changed the country in many ways. Towns such as Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo grew quickly along its banks. New York City became the busiest port in the United States. Settlers also used the canal to travel west, which helped new states grow.

Today, trains and trucks carry most goods. However, people still ride boats on parts of the Erie Canal for fun and remember the "ditch" that changed America.

Garrett Morgan was born in 1877 in Paris, Kentucky. His parents had once been enslaved, and his family worked hard to make a living. Garrett went to school only until about the sixth grade. But he never stopped learning. He loved to find out how machines worked. He would take them apart and put them back together.

As a teenager, Garrett moved north to Ohio to look for work. He settled in the city of Cleveland and got a job fixing sewing machines. He became so skilled that he soon opened his own repair shop. Later, he started other businesses as well, such as a shop that made clothing.

Garrett was always looking for ways to solve problems. He noticed that firefighters often got sick from breathing thick smoke. So he designed a safety hood that covered a person's head. A long tube hung down near the floor, where the air was cleaner. With this hood, a person could breathe more safely in a room full of smoke. Garrett got a patent for his invention in 1914.

Two years later, his hood was put to a real test. In 1916, a blast trapped workers in a tunnel under Lake Erie. The tunnel filled with deadly gas, and rescuers could not get inside. Garrett and his brother rushed to the scene with his safety hoods. They went down into the tunnel. They helped carry several men out to safety. Because of their bravery, more fire departments became interested in his hood.

Garrett also cared about safety on the roads. In the early 1900s, cars, horses, bikes, and people all shared busy streets. Many early traffic signals had only two signs, "Stop" and "Go." They switched with no warning, so crashes were common. One day Garrett saw a bad crash. He decided to make a better signal. His design added a third position that stopped traffic in all directions for a moment. This gave drivers time to slow down before the signal changed. He got a patent for it in 1923. Later, he sold the rights to a large company.

Garrett Morgan died in 1963. Today, his ideas live on in the masks that protect rescue workers. They also live on in the traffic lights that warn drivers before they must stop at a busy corner.
What is the author's main purpose in writing this passage?
["to tell about an inventor whose ideas helped keep people safe","to persuade readers to become firefighters","to describe what life was like in Kentucky","to explain how to repair a sewing machine"]
The passage tells the life of Garrett Morgan and focuses on his safety hood and traffic signal, which protected people.

Observe means to watch closely. Binoculars are used for watching.

"After the baby fell asleep, the house was as quiet as a mouse."

What does this simile tell you about the house?
["It was very quiet.","It was very small.","It had mice in it.","It was very messy."]
"As quiet as a mouse" compares the house to a mouse, which is known for being quiet. The house was very quiet.

During the experiment, please RECORD the temperature in your notebook every hour.

What does RECORD mean in this sentence?
"Record" has several meanings. Because you record it "in your notebook," here it means to write down.
The prefix PRE- in "preview" and "preheat" means
pre- means "before." To preheat an oven is to heat it before you bake.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The girl ___ won the spelling bee is in my class.
Use the relative pronoun "who" to refer to a person who does the action.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

This is the park ___ we had our class picnic.
Use the relative adverb "where" to refer to a place.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

I met a boy ___ dog can do five tricks.
"Whose" shows that the dog belongs to the boy.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Do you remember the day ___ it snowed in April?
Use the relative adverb "when" to refer to a time, such as a day.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Nobody knows the reason ___ the lights went out.
Use the relative adverb "why" after "the reason."

Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

Right now, my sister ___ her homework at the kitchen table.
"Right now" shows the action is happening at this moment, so use the present progressive "is doing."

Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

We ___ dinner when the phone suddenly rang.
The past progressive "were eating" shows an action that was going on in the past when something else happened.

Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

At this time tomorrow, I ___ on an airplane to Seoul.
"At this time tomorrow" points to an action that will be going on in the future, so use the future progressive "will be flying."

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

It is a school rule: you ___ wear a helmet when you ride your bike to school.
"It is a school rule" shows that wearing a helmet is required, so the modal "must" is correct.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Take your umbrella. It ___ rain later, but I am not sure.
"I am not sure" shows that rain is only possible, so use "might."

Choose the words in the correct order.

We adopted a ___ puppy.
["white little cute","little cute white","cute little white","cute white little"]
Adjectives usually go in this order: opinion (cute), size (little), color (white).

Choose the words in the correct order.

My grandmother has a ___ table in her kitchen.
["beautiful old wooden","beautiful wooden old","wooden old beautiful","old wooden beautiful"]
The order is opinion (beautiful), age (old), material (wooden).

Choose the words in the correct order.

Dad bought me a ___ sweater for the winter.
["red wool new","new red wool","wool new red","red new wool"]
The order is age (new), color (red), material (wool).

Which group of words is the prepositional phrase in this sentence?

The cat slept under the warm blanket.
["The cat","slept under","The cat slept","under the warm blanket"]
A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition (under) and ends with a noun (blanket): "under the warm blanket."
Which of these is a complete sentence?
["After the movie ended.","Running down the long hallway.","The bus was late this morning.","Because the bus was late."]
"The bus was late this morning" has a subject (the bus) and a verb (was) and expresses a complete thought. The others are fragments.
Which of these is a run-on sentence?
["The sun came out. We went to the beach.","When the sun came out, we went to the beach.","The sun came out we went to the beach.","The sun came out, so we went to the beach."]
"The sun came out we went to the beach" joins two complete sentences with no punctuation or conjunction, so it is a run-on.

I was hungry I ate a sandwich.
["I was hungry so, I ate a sandwich.","I was hungry, so I ate a sandwich.","I was hungry I ate, a sandwich.","I was, hungry I ate a sandwich."]
Add a comma and the conjunction "so" between the two complete thoughts.

If you are going to the store, I want to come ___.

"Their" shows that the backpacks belong to the students.

The little bird flapped ___ wings and flew away.
