Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

["Last July, my family visited the Grand Canyon in Arizona.","Last july, my family visited the Grand Canyon in arizona.","Last July, my Family visited the grand Canyon in Arizona.","last July, my family visited the grand canyon in Arizona."]
The first word, the month (July), the place name (Grand Canyon), and the state (Arizona) are capitalized. "Family" is a common noun.
Which book title is capitalized correctly?
["The Secret of the Old Mill","The secret of the old mill","the Secret Of The Old Mill","The Secret Of the old Mill"]
In a title, capitalize the first word and important words. Short words like "of" and "the" in the middle stay lowercase.
["\"Let's go to the park,\" said Mia.","\"Let's go to the park\" said Mia.","Let's go to the park, \"said Mia.\"","\"Let's go to the park.\" said Mia."]
When a quotation comes before the speaker tag, put a comma inside the closing quotation mark.
["Mom asked \"Did you finish your chores?\"","Mom asked, \"Did you finish your chores?\"","Mom asked, Did you finish your chores?","Mom asked, \"Did you finish your chores\"?"]
Put a comma after "asked," and put the question mark inside the closing quotation mark.

["\"When we get home said Dad, we will make pancakes.\"","\"When we get home,\" said Dad \"we will make pancakes.\"","\"When we get home\", said Dad, \"we will make pancakes\".","\"When we get home,\" said Dad, \"we will make pancakes.\""]
When a quotation is split, put a comma inside the first closing quotation mark and a comma after the speaker tag. The period goes inside the final quotation mark.
Which sentence uses a comma correctly?

["I wanted, to play outside but it started to rain.","I wanted to play outside but, it started to rain.","I wanted to play, outside but it started to rain.","I wanted to play outside, but it started to rain."]
Put a comma before a coordinating conjunction (but) that joins two complete sentences.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The store was already closed, ___ we went back home.
"So" shows the result: because the store was closed, we went home.

Where should a comma be added?

Lily studied hard for the test and she got every answer right.
"Lily studied hard for the test" and "she got every answer right" are complete sentences joined by "and," so a comma goes before "and," right after "test."
Which sentence uses the past progressive tense?
["The dogs will bark all night.","The dogs barked all night.","The dogs bark every night.","The dogs were barking all night."]
The past progressive uses "was" or "were" plus a verb ending in -ing: "were barking."

Rosa had wanted to paint the library mural since the first day of fifth grade, so when Ms. Patel announced that two students would design it together, Rosa raised her hand so quickly that her elbow cracked.

Her partner turned out to be Ethan Brooks, a quiet boy who decorated every scrap of paper with dragons. Rosa preferred to draw flowers, tropical birds, and the colorful outdoor market where her grandmother sold mangoes.

At their first meeting, Ethan unrolled an enormous sketch of a green dragon curling across the entire page and breathing fire over a castle. "This goes in the middle," he declared. "It's going to be incredible."

Rosa frowned. "It's a library, not a battlefield, and the kindergarteners will be terrified."

"Little kids love dragons," Ethan snapped. "Your flowers are boring."

The word stung like a bee. Rosa grabbed her pencil case and stood up, determined to march straight to Ms. Patel and ask for a new partner. Then she remembered something her grandmother always said: a closed fist cannot shake hands.

She sat back down. "Okay," she said slowly. "Tell me why the dragon matters so much to you."

Ethan looked surprised, and he picked nervously at the corner of his sketch. "My dad reads me dragon stories every night," he admitted. "They're the reason I actually enjoy reading."

Rosa considered that before she pulled out her own drawing. "My grandmother taught me to read using the signs at the market," she explained. "That's why every flower here has a word written beside it."

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Then Ethan pointed at her page. "What if the dragon is flying over your market, and instead of fire, he's breathing out letters and words?"

Rosa felt a smile tug at her mouth. "And the words could transform into flowers when they land."

They worked through lunch for the rest of the week, with Ethan painting the shimmering scales while Rosa painted the market stalls and the swirling words. They still disagreed about colors, but now their arguments ended in laughter instead of slammed doors.

On the afternoon the mural was finished, a first grader stood in front of it for ten minutes, sounding out every word the dragon had breathed. Rosa and Ethan watched from the doorway, and neither of them said "I told you so." There was nothing left to win.
Which sentence best states a theme of the story?

["The best way to keep a friendship is to win every argument.","Younger students should always be the ones who choose the art in a library.","Listening to someone else's reasons can turn a conflict into something better for everyone.","Talented artists do their best work when they are allowed to work alone."]

Rosa almost quits, but when she asks Ethan why the dragon matters, they discover a shared love of reading and create a mural better than either plan. The story never says artists should work alone, never lets young students choose, and the ending says there was 'nothing left to win.'

Hannah Pratt was eleven years old in the spring of 1769, and she disliked the spinning wheel more than any other chore. It squeaked, the wool tangled, and her thread always came out lumpy. Her older sister, Abigail, could spin a smooth strand while humming a hymn, but Hannah could barely spin while holding her breath.

"Why can't we just buy cloth from the shop the way we used to?" Hannah grumbled one morning.

Mother set down her basket. "Because that cloth comes from England, and the British government has placed new taxes on many goods it sends to the colonies. Your father and the other men in town have promised not to purchase British goods until the taxes are removed. If we want new clothes, we must make them ourselves."

Hannah knew about the taxes, since everyone in town discussed them. Still, it seemed unfair that a king across the ocean could decide how she spent her mornings.

That afternoon, Abigail rushed in with news. "The minister's wife is organizing a spinning bee on Saturday," she announced. "Girls from all over town will spin together on the green to demonstrate that we can make our own cloth."

Hannah's stomach dropped. Spinning in front of the entire town would be far worse than spinning alone, because everyone would notice her lumpy thread.

For the next three evenings, Abigail sat beside her near the fire. She showed Hannah how to keep her foot steady on the pedal and how to let the wool slip gently through her fingers instead of squeezing it. Gradually, the lumps grew smaller and the thread grew smoother.

On Saturday, the green was crowded with wheels, and their steady whirring sounded like a hive full of bees. Hannah finally understood the name. Neighbors brought bread and cider, and an elderly farmer in a patched coat wandered from wheel to wheel, nodding with approval.

When he reached Hannah, she froze. He picked up the end of her thread and rolled it between his fingers. "Not perfect," he said, "but strong. Every strand helps, young lady."

By sunset, her arms ached, and Hannah's thread still had a few bumps. Yet when she looked across the green at the long rows of wheels, she felt something unexpected: pride. The squeaky wheel was no longer just a chore; it was her way of standing up for her community.
What is the main reason the town holds the spinning bee?

["to raise money so the town can pay the new British taxes","to choose which girl is the best spinner in town","to teach young girls how to bake bread and make cider","to show that the colonists can make their own cloth instead of buying British goods"]
Abigail says the girls 'will spin together on the green to demonstrate that we can make our own cloth.' This connects to the town's promise not to buy British goods while the taxes remain.

Hannah Pratt was eleven years old in the spring of 1769, and she disliked the spinning wheel more than any other chore. It squeaked, the wool tangled, and her thread always came out lumpy. Her older sister, Abigail, could spin a smooth strand while humming a hymn, but Hannah could barely spin while holding her breath.

"Why can't we just buy cloth from the shop the way we used to?" Hannah grumbled one morning.

Mother set down her basket. "Because that cloth comes from England, and the British government has placed new taxes on many goods it sends to the colonies. Hannah knew about the taxes, since everyone in town discussed them. Still, it seemed unfair that a king across the ocean could decide how she spent her mornings.

On Habitat Seven, the only green things for a million miles grew inside the greenhouse dome. Twelve-year-old Kai Mendoza had volunteered there every morning since his family moved to the moon, and he loved the earthy smell of damp soil, which was the only thing that reminded him of home.

So when the emergency alarm began to wail during breakfast, Kai dropped his spoon and raced down the corridor.

Inside the dome, the air felt thin and frigid. Rows of bean plants were drooping like exhausted soldiers, and a small maintenance robot named Pip rolled toward him with its blue light blinking rapidly.

"Heater failure in Section B," Pip announced. "Temperature is falling. Plants will freeze in approximately forty minutes."

"Where's Dr. Osei?" Kai asked.

"Dr. Osei is outside repairing the solar panels. She will not return for two hours."

Kai's heart pounded like a drum. He was not permitted to touch the heater, and the rule was printed in enormous red letters across the control panel: AUTHORIZED ADULTS ONLY.

He pressed the radio button. "Dr. Osei, the greenhouse heater is broken! What should I do?"

Only static answered, because the solar panels were located on the far side of the crater, out of range.

Kai studied the drooping plants. Those beans were not merely plants; they were dinner for forty people next month. He considered breaking the rule, and then he considered another possibility.

"Pip," he said, "the plants need heat, not necessarily the heater. What else in here produces heat?"

Pip's light flickered while it searched its files. "Grow lamps produce heat. Section A lamps are currently off for the night cycle."

Kai grinned, because switching on grow lamps was one of his regular daily responsibilities. Together, he and Pip dragged the tall lamp stands from Section A into Section B and switched them on, and warm orange light spilled across the leaves.

Kai watched the thermometer anxiously. For ten long minutes, the number barely moved, but then it crept upward one degree, then two.

When Dr. Osei finally hurried through the airlock, she discovered Kai asleep against a lamp stand, with Pip parked beside him like a loyal dog. Every bean plant was standing tall.

She read the computer log, then knelt beside him. "You followed the rule and rescued the crop," she said quietly. "That is harder than accomplishing only one of those things."
What is the main problem Kai faces in the story?

["He must repair the solar panels before Dr. Osei returns.","He must save the freezing plants without breaking the rule about the heater.","He must find Pip, who has rolled away during the alarm.","He must convince his family to move back to Earth."]
The heater fails and the plants will freeze in forty minutes, but only adults may touch the heater and Dr. Osei cannot be reached. Kai has to protect the crop while still following the rule.

Pour a spoonful of sugar into a glass of warm water and stir. In a few seconds, the white grains seem to vanish. The water looks exactly as clear as it did before. Has the sugar disappeared? Scientists would say no, and they can prove it.

Everything around you is made of matter. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Your desk, the air you breathe, and the water in your glass are all matter. Matter is built from particles that are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.

When sugar dissolves, its particles spread out evenly among the water particles. The sugar is still there, but the pieces are now too tiny and too scattered for your eyes to notice. A mixture like this, in which one substance spreads evenly through another, is called a solution.

One simple test shows that the sugar is still present. Take a small sip. The water now tastes sweet, so the sugar has not gone anywhere. Another test uses a scale. Weigh a cup of water and a spoonful of sugar separately, and add the two numbers. Next, stir the sugar into the water and weigh the mixture. The total weight stays the same. Even though the sugar can no longer be seen, every particle is still counted.

Scientists call this idea conservation of matter. It means that when substances mix, melt, freeze, or dissolve, the total amount of matter stays the same. Particles can move around and change position, but they do not simply vanish.

You can even get the sugar back. If you leave the sugar water in a sunny window for several days, the water will slowly evaporate into the air. As the water leaves, the sugar particles crowd closer together. Eventually, small crystals form on the bottom of the glass. The sugar was there the whole time, waiting.

Not every substance dissolves, however. Stir sand into water, and the grains will sink to the bottom. Sand and water make a mixture, but not a solution, because the sand does not spread out evenly.

So the next time something seems to disappear, think like a scientist. Ask yourself where its particles went. Chances are, the matter is still nearby, just hidden from view.
What is the main idea of the passage?

["Sand is heavier than sugar, so it sinks to the bottom of a glass.","Sugar is the only substance that can dissolve in water.","When a substance dissolves or changes, its matter does not disappear.","Scientists use microscopes to find particles of sugar."]
The whole passage explains that dissolved sugar is still present and that the total amount of matter stays the same. This idea is called conservation of matter.

In December of 1777, the American Revolution was not going well for the Continental Army. British soldiers had captured Philadelphia, the largest city in the colonies. General George Washington needed a safe place for his tired troops to spend the winter. He chose Valley Forge, a windy area of hills about twenty miles from the city.

When the army marched in on December 19, about twelve thousand soldiers arrived. Many had no shoes. Some left bloody footprints in the snow. Their first job was to build shelter. Working in small groups, the men cut down trees and built wooden huts. Each hut was about fourteen feet long and held twelve soldiers. Within a few weeks, a small city of logs stood on the frozen hills.

The huts kept out the wind, but they could not solve every problem. Food and clothing were hard to find. Farmers often preferred to sell their crops to the British, who paid in silver coins instead of paper money. On some days, soldiers ate only firecake, a plain mix of flour and water baked on hot stones. Even worse, diseases spread quickly through the crowded camp. About two thousand soldiers died that winter, mostly from illness rather than cold.

Then, in February of 1778, help arrived in an unusual form. A Prussian officer named Baron Friedrich von Steuben came to camp. He spoke very little English, yet he knew a great deal about training an army. Steuben began drilling a small group of soldiers. He taught them to march in step, to load their muskets quickly, and to charge together. Those soldiers then taught others. Before long, the whole army was practicing the same skills.

The change was remarkable. The soldiers who had stumbled into Valley Forge in December marched out in June as a stronger, more confident army. Only days later, they fought the British at the Battle of Monmouth in New Jersey. The fight ended without a clear winner, but the Americans held their ground against well-trained British troops.

In December of 1777, the American Revolution was not going well for the Continental Army. British soldiers had captured Philadelphia, the largest city in the colonies. General George Washington needed a safe place for his tired troops to spend the winter. He chose Valley Forge, a windy area of hills about twenty miles from the city.

When the army marched in on December 19, about twelve thousand soldiers arrived. Many had no shoes. Some left bloody footprints in the snow. Their first job was to build shelter. Within a few weeks, a small city of logs stood on the frozen hills.

Picture a schoolyard where students pull carrots from the ground, chase butterflies between rows of sunflowers, and taste a tomato still warm from the sun. I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this. A school garden costs very little, and it teaches lessons that no textbook can.

First, gardens make science come alive. In class, students read that plants need water, air, and light to grow. In a garden, they see it happen. When students forget to water their bean plants for a week, they watch the leaves droop and turn yellow. That lesson sticks far better than a page in a book. Gardens also show how living things depend on one another. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, and worms loosen the soil so roots can spread.

Second, gardens help children eat better. Many kids refuse to touch vegetables at dinner. Yet something surprising happens when they grow the vegetables themselves. Teachers across the country report that students who plant and harvest lettuce are much more willing to eat a salad. Pride, it seems, is a powerful seasoning.

Third, gardens teach responsibility and teamwork. A garden cannot be finished in one afternoon. Someone must water it, pull weeds, and protect it from hungry rabbits. Students learn to make schedules, share jobs, and keep promises to one another. If one group slacks off, everyone can see the result.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough space or money for gardens. This concern is understandable, but it is not a good reason to give up. A garden does not need to be large. A few wooden boxes along a sunny wall can grow herbs, peppers, and strawberries. Many local hardware stores and garden clubs are happy to donate seeds, soil, and tools. Parents and grandparents often volunteer their time, too.

Others worry that gardening takes time away from reading and math. In fact, gardens can strengthen those subjects. Students measure how tall their plants grow, keep journals about what they observe, and calculate how many seeds fit in each row.

A school garden is more than a patch of dirt. It is a classroom without walls. Let's give every child the chance to dig in.

["Every elementary school should have a garden because it teaches valuable lessons.","Students should grow all the food served in school lunches.","Only schools with large yards should have gardens.","Schools should replace science textbooks with gardening tools."]
In the first paragraph the author writes, 'I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this,' and the rest of the article gives reasons to support that claim.

The words INSPECT, SPECTATOR, and SPECTACLES all share the root SPECT. What does SPECT most likely mean?
To inspect is to look closely, a spectator watches an event, and spectacles help people see. The Latin root spect means 'to look.'
What does the prefix in MISUNDERSTAND mean?
The prefix mis- means 'wrongly' or 'badly.' To misunderstand is to understand something wrongly.
Which phrase best explains the meaning of DEPENDABLE?
["without any help","full of worry","able to be trusted","in a slow way"]
The suffix -able means 'able to be.' Dependable means able to be depended on, or trusted.
The Greek root GRAPH appears in AUTOGRAPH, PARAGRAPH, and PHOTOGRAPH. What does GRAPH mean?

An autograph is a person's own written name, a paragraph is a section of writing, and a photograph is 'drawn' with light. Graph means 'write or draw.' (Auto means 'self,' phon means 'sound,' and tele means 'far.')
TRANSPORT, PORTABLE, and EXPORT share the Latin root PORT. What does PORT mean?
To transport is to carry across, something portable can be carried, and exports are goods carried out of a country. Port means 'carry.'
Which word is a SYNONYM for ENORMOUS?
Enormous means extremely large, so huge is a synonym. Tiny is an antonym.
Which word is a SYNONYM for RELUCTANT?
A reluctant person does not want to do something. Unwilling has the same meaning; eager is the opposite.
Which word is an ANTONYM for FRAGILE?
Fragile means easily broken. Sturdy means strong and hard to break, so it is the opposite. Delicate and breakable are synonyms.
Which word is an ANTONYM for ANCIENT?
Ancient means very old, from long ago. Modern means new or of the present time, so it is the opposite.
Read the sentence: "The desert is so ARID that it may not rain there for months." What does ARID mean?
The clue 'it may not rain there for months' shows that arid means very dry.
Read the sentence: "After running the long race, Marcus was so EXHAUSTED that he fell asleep on the bus." What does EXHAUSTED mean?
Running a long race and then falling asleep are clues that exhausted means extremely tired.
Read the sentence: "Before the experiment, Lena wrote her HYPOTHESIS: 'I think the plant in the sunny window will grow taller.'" What is a HYPOTHESIS?
["a list of supplies","a final result","a prediction that can be tested","a drawing of a plant"]
Lena writes 'I think...' before the experiment begins. A hypothesis is a prediction, or educated guess, that an experiment can test.

["We could hear the WIND whistling through the trees.","The WIND blew the leaves across the yard.","A cold WIND came down from the mountains.","Please WIND the yarn into a tight ball."]
Only 'WIND the yarn into a ball' uses wind as a verb meaning to turn or twist. In the other sentences, wind is a noun meaning moving air.

["in attendance; not absent","to hand over formally","a gift for a birthday","the time happening now"]
Here present is a verb: the principal will give, or hand over, the trophy in a formal way. The other choices are different meanings of the same spelling.

["a loud sound","turned around something","a small hill","an injury"]
A nurse cleans and bandages an injury, so wound means an injury in this sentence. 'Turned around something' is the meaning of wound (rhymes with sound), the past tense of wind.

["crack a frozen pond","end a game early","cool down a hot room","help people feel relaxed when they first meet"]
The idiom 'break the ice' means to do something that helps people feel comfortable when they first meet.
"I have a spelling test tomorrow, so I need to HIT THE BOOKS tonight." What does HIT THE BOOKS mean?
["buy new books","go to the library","study hard","throw books on the floor"]
The idiom 'hit the books' means to study. The clue is the spelling test the next day.

The idiom 'a piece of cake' means something is very easy to do.
What is the meaning of the proverb DON'T COUNT YOUR CHICKENS BEFORE THEY HATCH?

["Don't depend on something good happening until it really happens.","Always take good care of animals on a farm.","Count carefully so that you do not make mistakes.","Be patient while you wait for spring to come."]
Eggs might not all hatch, so counting chickens early is a mistake. The proverb warns not to rely on a result before it actually happens.
What does the saying THE EARLY BIRD CATCHES THE WORM mean?
["People who start early have a better chance of success.","It is unwise to wake up before sunrise.","Birds are hungriest early in the morning.","People should share what they find with others."]
The bird that wakes up first gets the worm. The saying means that people who act early get an advantage.
What does the adage ACTIONS SPEAK LOUDER THAN WORDS mean?

["People who talk a lot are usually very active.","What you do shows more about you than what you say.","It is better to stay quiet than to give an opinion.","You should always speak in a loud voice."]
The adage means that a person's actions prove what they really think or feel better than their words do.
Complete the analogy. HOT is to COLD as TALL is to ______.
Hot and cold are opposites. The opposite of tall is short. High and large have meanings similar to tall, not opposite.
Complete the analogy. PETAL is to FLOWER as PAGE is to ______.
A petal is one part of a flower, and a page is one part of a book. This is a part-to-whole relationship.
Complete the analogy. AUTHOR is to NOVEL as COMPOSER is to ______.
An author creates a novel, and a composer creates a symphony. The relationship is creator to the thing created.
Your teacher asks you to ANALYZE a poem. What should you do?

To analyze means to examine something closely by looking at its parts and how they work together.

A summary briefly states the main ideas and key events without all the small details or your opinions.

["hide something from others","make sure something is true","forget about something","change something completely"]
Repeating a test helps a scientist make sure the results are correct. Confirm means to show or make sure that something is true.

The prefix pre- means 'before.' To preheat the oven is to heat it before putting the food in.

Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"______ my brother ______ my sister likes spinach, so we never cook it."
'We never cook it' shows that no one likes spinach. 'Neither' must be paired with 'nor.'

Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"Mia is ______ a talented singer ______ a skilled dancer."
["not only / or","either / but also","neither / and","not only / but also"]
'Not only' is always paired with 'but also.' The sentence means Mia is good at both singing and dancing.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Neither the students nor the teacher ______ ready for the surprise fire drill."
With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. 'Teacher' is singular, so the verb is 'was.'

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Either the twins or their mother ______ going to pick us up after practice."
With 'either...or,' the verb agrees with the closer subject. 'Mother' is singular, so the verb is 'is.'

Which word in the sentence is an interjection?
"Wow, that rainbow has so many bright colors!"
An interjection is a word that expresses strong feeling or surprise. 'Wow' shows surprise and is set apart by a comma.
Which sentence correctly punctuates the interjection?
["Ouch. that pan is hot.","Ouch, That pan is hot.","Ouch! That pan is hot.","Ouch that pan is hot."]
A strong interjection can be followed by an exclamation point, and the next sentence begins with a capital letter. The other choices are missing punctuation or use capital letters incorrectly.
Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an introductory phrase?

["After the long hike we, rested beside the stream.","After the long hike, we rested beside the stream.","After the long, hike we rested beside the stream.","After, the long hike we rested beside the stream."]
The introductory phrase is 'After the long hike.' The comma belongs right after the whole phrase, before the main clause 'we rested beside the stream.'
["Yes I would love, to come to your party.","Yes, I would love to come to your party.","Yes I, would love to come to your party.","Yes I would love to come, to your party."]
A comma is used to set off the word 'yes' or 'no' at the beginning of a sentence.
Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a tag question?
["You finished your science project, didn't you?","You finished, your science project didn't you?","You finished your science, project didn't you?","You finished your science project didn't, you?"]
A tag question such as 'didn't you?' at the end of a sentence is set off with a comma.
Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off a person being spoken to?

["Thank you Ms. Rivera for helping us with the play.","Thank you, Ms. Rivera for helping us with the play.","Thank you, Ms. Rivera, for helping us with the play.","Thank you Ms., Rivera for helping us with the play."]
When a name in direct address comes in the middle of a sentence, commas go both before and after it.
["Is that your, backpack Sam?","Is that your backpack Sam?","Is that, your backpack Sam?","Is that your backpack, Sam?"]
Sam is being spoken to directly, so his name is set off from the rest of the sentence with a comma.
Which sentence correctly punctuates the title of a song?

["Our class sang This Land Is Your Land at the assembly.","Our class sang \"This Land\" Is Your Land at the assembly.","Our class sang \"This Land Is Your Land\" at the assembly.","Our class \"sang This Land Is Your Land\" at the assembly."]
Titles of short works such as songs, poems, and short stories are placed in quotation marks. The quotation marks must surround the whole title and only the title.
When you write the title of a BOOK by hand, what should you do?
["write it in all capital letters","put it in parentheses","underline it","put it in quotation marks"]
Titles of long works, such as books and movies, are italicized when typed and underlined when written by hand.
Which of these titles should be placed in quotation marks instead of being underlined or italicized?
["a short poem in a poetry collection","a long novel","a monthly magazine","a full-length movie"]
Short works, such as a single poem, go in quotation marks. Long works, such as novels, movies, and magazines, are underlined or italicized.

Which word in the sentence is a preposition?
"The kite drifted above the tall trees."
A preposition shows the relationship between a noun and another word. 'Above' shows where the kite drifted in relation to the trees.

Choose the preposition that correctly completes the sentence.
"Ava is very interested ______ learning about volcanoes."
In standard English, we say someone is 'interested in' something.

Choose the preposition that correctly completes the sentence.
"The library is ______ the bakery and the post office."
'Between' is used to show a position in the middle of two things: the bakery and the post office. 'Among' is used for three or more.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"The box of crayons ______ on the top shelf."
The subject is 'box,' which is singular. 'Of crayons' is a prepositional phrase and does not change the subject, so the verb is 'is.'

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Each of the players ______ a new jersey for the championship game."
'Each' is singular, even when it is followed by 'of the players.' So the singular verb 'has' is correct.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"The news about the storm ______ worrying everyone in town."
'News' ends in -s but is a singular noun. The singular verb 'is' agrees with it.

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Grandpa took Leo and ______ to the aquarium on Saturday."
The pronoun is an object of the verb 'took.' Try it alone: 'Grandpa took me,' not 'Grandpa took I.' So 'me' is correct.

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"______ and Ella built the robot for the science club."
The pronoun is part of the subject of the sentence. Try it alone: 'She built the robot,' not 'Her built the robot.' So 'She' is correct.

Every weekday morning at 7:15, Mrs. Alvarez settled onto the green bench beside the bus stop on Fulton Street. She never actually rode the bus; she simply sat with her hands folded on her cane and observed the commuters hurrying past without speaking.

Jonah noticed her only because he had no alternative. The bench was the only place to sit while he waited for the school bus, and she always occupied the left half of it. For the first two weeks of sixth grade, he stood instead, earbuds in, staring at the corner where the bus would appear.

On a gloomy Tuesday in October, the rain came down hard and sideways, and Jonah, who had forgotten his jacket, was trying to decide whether to sprint home when an enormous black umbrella tilted over his head.

"Sit," Mrs. Alvarez said. It was not a question.

He sat. The umbrella was large enough to shelter both of them, and it smelled faintly of cedar, like the inside of an old closet. Eventually she pointed her cane at a man in a gray suit who was jogging anxiously toward the train station.

"That one is late every Tuesday because his daughter has swim practice, and he drops her off first," she said.

Jonah stared at her and asked how she could possibly know that.

"I pay attention," she replied. "People will tell you their entire life stories if you watch them patiently enough."

Afterward, Jonah stopped wearing his earbuds at the bus stop. Mrs. Alvarez taught him to notice the baker who whistled the same three notes every morning and the girl with the cello case who always counted her steps. Jonah began inventing stories about each of them, and Mrs. Alvarez corrected him whenever he got the facts wrong.

In December, the bench remained empty for three days in a row. On the fourth day, Jonah knocked on the door of the yellow house where he had seen her go inside. Her nephew explained that she had fallen and was recovering in the hospital.

The next morning, Jonah sat on the left half of the bench and watched the man in the gray suit, the whistling baker, and the girl with the cello. That afternoon he wrote down everything he had observed, folded the paper twice, and carried it to the hospital so she would not miss a thing.
Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?

["Bad weather can ruin even the most carefully planned day.","Young people should always respect the rules set by older adults.","People who live alone usually prefer to keep to themselves.","Paying close attention to others can lead to unexpected and meaningful friendships."]
Jonah ignores the people around him until Mrs. Alvarez teaches him to watch closely; that habit grows into a caring friendship. The other choices are not developed by the story.

The summer I turned eleven, my father announced that I would not be getting a new bicycle; instead, I would be repairing the old one.

The old one was a rusty red mountain bike that had belonged to my cousin, then to my older brother, and finally to me. Its chain squealed like an angry bird, and the back brake worked only when it felt like cooperating. I had been begging for a shiny new bike since April. My father listened patiently to every argument I made, nodded thoughtfully, and then handed me a wrench.

"A bike is just a puzzle," he said, "and you are perfectly capable of solving a puzzle."

I did not want to solve a puzzle; I wanted to ride. Since I had no other choice, however, I spent the first week of July sitting on the scorching driveway with a library book about bicycle repair open beside me. The diagrams looked simple, but the actual bicycle was far more complicated.

On the first day, I removed the back wheel and could not figure out how to reattach it. On the third day, I lost a tiny spring under the porch and spent an hour searching for it with a flashlight. On the fifth day, I tightened the brake cable so hard that the wheel refused to turn at all, and I collapsed onto the concrete and cried, partly from frustration and partly from the heat.

My father came outside and sat beside me, but he did not pick up the wrench. Instead, he asked me what I had learned so far. I listed everything that had gone wrong. He laughed and said, "That's not a list of mistakes. That's a list of things you know now."

By the end of July, the chain was silent and both brakes worked perfectly. The first time I coasted down Maple Hill, with the wind roaring in my ears, I felt as if I had built the bicycle myself from nothing.

I am an adult now, and I have owned many bicycles since then, but not one of them has mattered as much as that rusty red one. Whenever something in my life breaks, I still hear my father's voice reminding me that it is just a puzzle, and I still believe him.
What is the central idea of this narrative?

["Riding down a steep hill is the most exciting part of owning a bike.","Working through repeated mistakes taught the narrator patience and confidence that lasted into adulthood.","Library books are the best way to learn how to repair a bicycle.","The narrator's father was too strict to buy his child a new bicycle."]
The narrator struggles, learns from each failure, succeeds, and still uses the lesson as an adult. The other choices are minor details or unsupported opinions.

The summer I turned eleven, my father announced that I would not be getting a new bicycle; instead, I would be repairing the old one.

The old one was a rusty red mountain bike that had belonged to my cousin, then to my older brother, and finally to me. Its chain squealed like an angry bird, and the back brake worked only when it felt like cooperating. I had been begging for a shiny new bike since April. My father listened patiently to every argument I made, nodded thoughtfully, and then handed me a wrench.

"A bike is just a puzzle," he said, "and you are perfectly capable of solving a puzzle."

I did not want to solve a puzzle; I wanted to ride. Since I had no other choice, however, I spent the first week of July sitting on the scorching driveway with a library book about bicycle repair open beside me. The diagrams looked simple, but the actual bicycle was far more complicated.

On the first day, I removed the back wheel and could not figure out how to reattach it. On the third day, I lost a tiny spring under the porch and spent an hour searching for it with a flashlight. Every April, Theo and his older sister June constructed a kite together. They reused the same wooden frame every year, repaired with tape, and decorated it with whatever paper they could find. One year it was faded road maps, and another year it was the colorful comics from the Sunday newspaper. This year, June had covered it with pages from her old school notebooks, so the kite was crowded with her loopy handwriting and half-finished math problems.

"Last one," she said quietly, tying on the tail. In August she would be leaving for college, three states away.

Theo did not answer; he pretended to be extremely busy untangling the string.

They climbed to the top of Carver Hill, where the wind always blew steadily from the west. June ran first, as she always did, and the kite leaped into the air, wobbled uncertainly, and then climbed until it was a small bright square against the clouds. Theo watched the string grow tight as it hummed in the wind, a thin line connecting the hill to the sky.

After a while, June held the spool out to him and said, "You take it."

"But you always fly it," Theo protested.

"Not anymore," she said gently, nudging his elbow with encouragement.

He accepted the spool. The kite pulled harder than he expected, tugging at his arms as if it wanted to travel somewhere he could not follow, and for a moment he was afraid he would lose it. Then he discovered the rhythm, releasing a little string when the wind gusted and reeling it back when the wind calmed. If he held the string too tightly, it might snap, but if he held it too loosely, the kite would fall.

"See?" June remarked approvingly. "It's not about holding on as hard as you can."

In late August, the house felt unbearably quiet. One windy evening, Theo carried the kite up Carver Hill by himself, launched it on the second try, and let it climb higher than it had ever gone before. June's handwriting was too far away to read now, but he could feel the steady tug through the string, faint and patient, like someone on the other end saying hello.
In the story, the kite string most likely symbolizes

["the danger of playing outside on a windy day.","the bond between Theo and June that remains even when they are far apart.","the rules that Theo's parents expect him to follow.","the schoolwork June left unfinished before college."]
The string connects Theo to the kite (covered in June's handwriting); at the end its "tug" feels "like someone on the other end saying hello," showing a connection that survives distance.

More than five thousand years ago, some of the world's first cities grew up in a region called Mesopotamia. The name comes from Greek words meaning "the land between the rivers." The two rivers were the Tigris and the Euphrates, which flow through what is now Iraq. Although the region got little rain, the rivers made life there possible.

Each spring, melting snow in the northern mountains caused the rivers to flood. The floodwaters spread rich, dark soil across the land. However, the floods were hard to predict. Some years they came too late to help the crops, and other years they were strong enough to wash away whole villages. To control the water, farmers dug canals and built walls of earth called levees. This system of irrigation carried river water to fields that would otherwise have been too dry to farm.

Irrigation changed everything. Farmers could now grow more barley and wheat than their families needed. This extra food, called a surplus, meant that not everyone had to be a farmer. Some people became potters, weavers, metalworkers, or traders. Others became priests or leaders. As villages grew larger, they turned into city-states such as Ur and Uruk. Each city-state had its own ruler and its own temple, often a tall stepped tower called a ziggurat.

With so much trade and so many goods, people needed a way to keep track of who owned what. The Sumerians, who lived in southern Mesopotamia, solved this problem by creating one of the earliest known writing systems. At first, they pressed simple pictures into wet clay to record sheep or bags of grain. Over time, the pictures changed into wedge-shaped marks made with a cut reed. Today, this writing is called cuneiform, from a Latin word meaning "wedge."

Learning cuneiform was hard, so only a small group of people, called scribes, could read and write. Students trained for years in special schools. In time, scribes used cuneiform for much more than counting grain. They recorded laws, prayers, letters, and even long stories, such as the adventures of a king named Gilgamesh.

The achievements of Mesopotamia did not vanish when its cities fell. Ideas about writing, laws, and city life spread to other peoples and helped shape the civilizations that followed.

On a hot summer afternoon, the sky can change surprisingly fast, and a clear blue morning may turn into a dark, rumbling storm by dinnertime. To understand why, you need to know how heat and water work together in the air.

Every thunderstorm needs three ingredients: moisture, unstable air, and something to lift that air upward. Moisture usually evaporates from oceans, lakes, or damp ground. On sunny days, the sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air just above it. Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises, much like a hot-air balloon. If the air higher up is much cooler, the rising air keeps going. Scientists call this condition unstable.

As the warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much water vapor as warm air, so some of the vapor condenses into tiny droplets. Billions of these droplets form a puffy cumulus cloud. If the updraft, or rising current of air, stays strong, the cloud keeps growing taller. In a large storm, it can tower more than ten miles high, and its top may spread out in a flat shape. This giant storm cloud is called a cumulonimbus.

Inside the cloud, droplets collide and gradually grow heavier until they become too heavy for the updraft to hold up, and they fall as rain or hail. The falling rain drags cool air down with it, creating a downdraft. When people feel a sudden cold gust just before a storm arrives, they are feeling this downdraft.

Lightning forms as bits of ice crash into each other inside the cloud, building up electric charges. When the charges grow strong enough, a giant spark leaps between the cloud and the ground or between parts of the cloud. Lightning heats the air around it to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is hotter than the surface of the sun. The heated air expands so suddenly that it makes a booming sound wave. That sound is thunder.

Because light travels much faster than sound, you see lightning before you hear thunder. Weather experts offer a simple rule: if you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Go indoors immediately and remain there until thirty minutes after the last rumble.

The passage explains the whole process of storm formation step by step. The lightning temperature is a detail, and the other choices are not supported.

On a hot summer afternoon, the sky can change surprisingly fast, and a clear blue morning may turn into a dark, rumbling storm by dinnertime. To understand why, you need to know how heat and water work together in the air.

Every thunderstorm needs three ingredients: moisture, unstable air, and something to lift that air upward. Moisture usually evaporates from oceans, lakes, or damp ground. On sunny days, the sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air just above it. Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises, much like a hot-air balloon. If the air higher up is much cooler, the rising air keeps going. Scientists call this condition unstable.

As the warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much water vapor as warm air, so some of the vapor condenses into tiny droplets. Billions of these droplets form a puffy cumulus cloud. If the updraft, or rising current of air, stays strong, the cloud keeps growing taller. In a large storm, it can tower more than ten miles high, and its top may spread out in a flat shape. This giant storm cloud is called a cumulonimbus.

Inside the cloud, droplets collide and gradually grow heavier until they become too heavy for the updraft to hold up, and they fall as rain or hail. The falling rain drags cool air down with it, creating a downdraft. When people feel a sudden cold gust just before a storm arrives, they are feeling this downdraft.

Ask a group of sixth graders to name their favorite class, and you will hear answers like art, science, or gym. You will probably not hear "cooking," because most middle schools no longer offer it. That is a mistake. Every middle school should require students to take a basic cooking class.

First, cooking teaches skills that students will use for the rest of their lives. Not everyone will grow up to solve equations for a living, but everyone needs to eat. Students who learn to make simple, healthy meals are less likely to depend on fast food when they are older. Health researchers have found that people who cook at home more often tend to eat more vegetables and less sugar than people who rarely cook.

Second, a kitchen is a hands-on classroom for other subjects. Doubling a recipe requires multiplying fractions. Baking bread shows how yeast, a living organism, produces gas that makes dough rise. At one middle school, teachers reported that students in a cooking elective became better at measuring in math class. Following a recipe also strengthens reading skills, since skipping a single direction can ruin an entire dish.

Third, cooking builds confidence and teamwork, two qualities that matter in every subject. In a kitchen, every person has a job, and the meal succeeds only if everyone does their part. My younger brother refused to eat anything green until he made his own vegetable soup at a summer cooking camp. Now he asks for broccoli.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough money or time to add another class. They point out that kitchens are expensive and that the school day is already full. These concerns are reasonable, but they can be solved. A cooking class does not need a fancy kitchen; portable burners and basic tools can cost less than a classroom set of new textbooks. Schools could also combine cooking lessons with existing science or health classes instead of adding extra hours.

Cooking is not just about food. It is about health, learning, and independence. If we want students to be ready for real life, we should hand them a whisk along with their pencils.

Two independent clauses can be joined with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (", and"). The second choice creates a comma splice, and the others misplace commas.
Which sentence correctly fixes this comma splice? Kai loves soccer, he practices every day.
["Kai loves soccer he practices every day.","Kai loves soccer, he practices, every day.","Kai loves soccer; he practices every day.","Kai, loves soccer, he practices every day."]
A semicolon can correctly join two closely related independent clauses. The other choices are still run-ons or comma splices.
Choose the verb that keeps the tense consistent: Yesterday, Lina walked to the library and ___ three books about volcanoes.
"Yesterday" and "walked" are past tense, so the second verb should also be past tense: "borrowed."
Which sentence contains an inappropriate shift in verb tense?

["Marcus opened the box and found a tiny kitten inside.","Marcus opens the box and finds a tiny kitten inside.","Marcus opened the box and finds a tiny kitten inside.","Marcus will open the box and find a tiny kitten inside."]
The sentence shifts from past ("opened") to present ("finds") without a reason. The others keep one tense.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: By the time we arrived at the theater, the movie ___.
["is starting","had already started","will have started","already starts"]
The movie started before another past event (arriving), so the past perfect "had already started" is correct.
Which sentence contains a MISPLACED MODIFIER?

["The boy wore his pajamas while he fed the goldfish.","The boy, wearing his pajamas, fed the goldfish.","Wearing his pajamas, the boy fed the goldfish.","The boy fed the goldfish wearing his pajamas."]
Placing "wearing his pajamas" next to "goldfish" makes it sound as if the fish is wearing pajamas.
Which is the best revision of this sentence? Running for the bus, my backpack fell open.

["My backpack, running for the bus, fell open.","My backpack fell open, running for the bus.","Running for the bus, the backpack fell open on me.","As I was running for the bus, my backpack fell open."]
The original sentence says the backpack was running. Only the revision with the clause "As I was running" makes clear that the speaker was running.
Choose the answer that keeps the sentence parallel: On Saturdays, Ella likes hiking, swimming, and ___.
The items in the series are all -ing forms (gerunds), so "reading" keeps the structure parallel.
Which sentence has correct PARALLEL STRUCTURE?

["The recipe tells you to chop the onions, stir the sauce, and the pasta should be baked.","The recipe tells you chopping the onions, to stir the sauce, and baking the pasta.","The recipe tells you to chop the onions, stir the sauce, and bake the pasta.","The recipe tells you to chop the onions, stirring the sauce, and bake the pasta."]
All three actions use the same verb form (chop, stir, bake). The other choices mix forms.
Which choice combines these two sentences most effectively? The volcano erupted. Ash covered the nearby village.

["The volcano erupted, ash covered the nearby village.","Erupting, the nearby village was covered with ash by the volcano.","The volcano erupted and ash, covered the nearby village.","When the volcano erupted, ash covered the nearby village."]
Adding "When" turns the first sentence into a dependent clause, creating a correct complex sentence. The others create a comma splice, a misplaced comma, or a dangling modifier.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The teacher praised Rosa and ___ for our clear presentation.
The pronoun is an object of "praised," so the objective case "me" is correct: "The teacher praised me."

Jun had lived on Maple Street for only two weeks, and he did not know anyone in his new neighborhood yet. Every afternoon, he sat on the front steps and watched the cars go by while he thought about his old friends and his old school.

Next door lived an older woman named Mrs. Ortiz, who spent every afternoon working in her backyard garden. One afternoon she waved at Jun over the fence. "I could use some help," she called. "My tomato plants are thirsty, and my back is tired."

Jun shrugged, but he walked over to her yard anyway. Mrs. Ortiz handed him a green watering can and showed him how to pour the water slowly at the bottom of each plant. "Roots drink better when you are gentle," she explained.

The plants were tall, but the tomatoes were still small, hard, and green. "When will they be ready?" Jun asked.

"Not today," Mrs. Ortiz answered with a gentle smile, "but good things take time."

After that, Jun came over every afternoon. He pulled weeds and tied the long stems to wooden sticks so they would not bend. Some days were very hot, and he wanted to quit, but he kept coming back because he liked to hear Mrs. Ortiz tell stories about the garden she had as a girl.

Slowly, the tomatoes grew bigger, and then one morning, Jun noticed a flash of red and ran to the fence. "Mrs. Ortiz! The first one is ripe!" They picked it together, and it tasted sweet and delicious.

Soon there were too many tomatoes for one person to eat. Mrs. Ortiz filled a basket with tomatoes and gave it to Jun. "Share these with your class," she said. "You helped grow them."

The next day, Jun carried the basket to school, and his teacher let him tell the class about the garden. A girl named Lily raised her hand. "Can you show me how to grow tomatoes?" she asked. "I want to plant some too."

Jun grinned. "Sure," he said, "but you have to be patient. Good things take time."

That afternoon, Jun did not sit alone on the steps, because he and Lily walked to the garden next door together. Jun thought about how lonely he had felt just a few weeks before. Now he had a garden, a teacher next door, and a brand-new friend.
What is the main lesson of this story?

["It is better to stay home than to go to a new school.","Being patient and helping others can lead to good things, like new friends.","Tomatoes are the easiest plants to grow in a garden.","You should never talk to your neighbors."]
Jun is patient in the garden and helps Mrs. Ortiz, and this leads to sharing tomatoes and making a new friend, Lily.

Long ago, a tired traveler walked into a small village at the end of a cold day. He carried only a walking stick, a big iron pot, and a smooth gray stone, and he was very hungry.

The traveler knocked on the first door he saw. "Could you spare a little food?" he asked. The woman inside shook her head. "The harvest was poor this year," she said. "We barely have enough food from our fields for ourselves." At every house, the answer was the same, because the worried villagers had hidden their food away.

The traveler did not get angry. Instead, he calmly set his pot in the middle of the village square. He filled it with water from the well, built a small fire under it, and then dropped the gray stone into the pot.

A curious boy came closer. "What are you making?" he asked.

"Stone soup," the traveler answered. "It is the best soup in the world. Still, it would taste even better with one carrot."

The boy ran home, came back with a carrot, and dropped it into the pot. Soon other villagers gathered around to watch. "Stone soup is tasty," the traveler said as he stirred. "But a few potatoes would make it perfect."

An old farmer remembered the potatoes in his cellar. He brought a whole sack. A baker brought onions, a young girl brought a handful of beans, and someone else added salt and herbs. Each person gave just a little, but the pot grew fuller and fuller.

At last, the soup was ready, and its delicious smell filled the whole square. The villagers brought bowls and spoons and sat down together. For the first time in months, they laughed and told stories while they ate. Everyone had enough, and there was even some left over.

When the meal was over, the traveler fished the stone out of the pot. He wiped it clean and carefully put it back in his pocket.

"Wait!" called the boy. "How will we make stone soup without your magic stone?"

The traveler smiled. "The stone was never magic," he said. "The soup was made from what all of you shared."

The next morning, the traveler walked on down the road. But the villagers never forgot the lesson. From then on, they shared what they had, and no one in the village went hungry again.
What is the lesson of this folktale?
["When everyone shares a little, there can be enough for all.","Travelers should always carry their own food.","A magic stone can make delicious food.","It is wise to hide food when times are hard."]
Each villager added a small amount, and together they made a meal for everyone. The traveler says the soup came from what they shared.

Maya and her little brother, Theo, had waited all summer for this hike. Their aunt Rosa was a park ranger, and she had promised to take them to the top of Eagle Ridge. From the lookout, she said, you could see three lakes and a river shining like a silver ribbon.

They started early in the morning, and Aunt Rosa gave each of them a small backpack with water, a snack, and a whistle. She also gave Maya a compass. "Remember," she said, "the trail markers are blue. If you ever stop seeing blue, stop walking. And if you get lost, stay where you are."

For the first hour, the sky was clear and bright. Theo counted chipmunks, and Maya carefully checked the compass every time the trail turned. Then, near the top, the air grew cool, and a thick gray fog rolled over the ridge like a soft blanket. Soon Maya could barely see the trees beside the path.

"Aunt Rosa?" Theo called. His voice sounded small. Aunt Rosa had stopped to tie her boot a few steps behind them, and now the fog hid her completely.

Maya's heart was beating fast, but she remembered the safety rules. "Stay right next to me," she told Theo. She took out her whistle and blew it three times. Three short blasts meant "Come find us."

Have you ever seen a frog leap into a pond? That frog did not always look the way it does now. Like all animals, frogs go through a life cycle. A life cycle is the set of changes a living thing goes through as it grows. A frog's life cycle has four main stages: egg, tadpole, froglet, and adult frog.

The life cycle begins in the water. In spring, a female frog lays hundreds of eggs in a pond. The eggs are tiny black dots wrapped in clear jelly. The jelly protects the eggs and helps them stick together in a clump. Many hungry fish and birds eat frog eggs, so a frog lays a lot of them. That way, at least some will survive.

After about one to three weeks, tadpoles hatch from the eggs. A tadpole looks more like a little fish than a frog. It has a long tail for swimming and gills for breathing underwater. Tadpoles spend most of their time eating tiny plants called algae. They grow quickly.

Over the next few weeks, the tadpole begins to change in amazing ways. First, back legs start to grow. Then front legs appear. Inside its body, the tadpole grows lungs so it will be able to breathe air. Its tail gets shorter and shorter. At this stage, the young animal is called a froglet. A froglet can leave the water for short periods of time.

Finally, the tail disappears, and the froglet becomes an adult frog. For many frogs, this whole process takes three or four months. Some kinds take longer. Adult frogs have strong back legs for jumping and long sticky tongues for catching insects. They can live both in water and on land. Animals that spend part of their lives in water and part on land are called amphibians.

When the adult frog is ready, it returns to the water to lay eggs of its own. Then the life cycle starts all over again.

Scientists study frogs closely because frogs can tell us a lot about the health of a place. Frogs have thin skin that soaks up water. If a pond becomes dirty, frogs are often the first animals to get sick. A pond full of healthy frogs is usually a healthy pond.
What is the main idea of this passage?
["Tadpoles and fish are the same kind of animal.","Frogs lay their eggs on dry land.","A frog goes through several stages of change as it grows.","Frogs are the fastest swimmers in a pond."]
The passage explains each stage of the frog life cycle: egg, tadpole, froglet, and adult.

Look up at the sky. Do you see any clouds? Clouds may look like fluffy cotton, but they are really made of billions of tiny drops of water or tiny bits of ice. Each drop is so small and light that it floats in the air.

How do clouds form? It all starts with the sun. The sun warms water in oceans, lakes, and even puddles. Some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. You cannot see it, but it is all around you. This change is called evaporation. The warm water vapor rises high into the sky, where the air is much colder. The cold air cools the vapor, and it changes back into tiny drops of water. This change is called condensation. When billions of these drops crowd together, they form a cloud.

Clouds come in different shapes, and each shape has a name. Cumulus clouds are big, white, and puffy. They often look like piles of cotton balls. On a sunny day, cumulus clouds usually mean nice weather. But if they grow very tall and dark, a thunderstorm might be on the way.

Stratus clouds are flat and gray. They spread across the sky like a blanket and can hide the sun all day. Stratus clouds often bring light rain. Fog is really a stratus cloud that forms close to the ground.

Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy. They float very high in the sky, where it is so cold that they are made of ice instead of water drops. Cirrus clouds often look like white feathers. They can be a sign that the weather will change in a day or two.

So why does rain fall from clouds? Inside a cloud, the tiny drops bump into each other and join together. Little by little, they grow bigger and heavier. When the drops become too heavy to float, they fall to the ground as rain. If the air is cold enough, they fall as snow instead.

Weather scientists study clouds to help them tell what the weather will be. You can be a weather watcher, too. The next time you go outside, look up. The clouds may be telling you what kind of day is coming.
What is the main idea of this passage?

["Fog is the most dangerous kind of weather.","The sun makes clouds disappear every afternoon.","Clouds form from water in the air, and their shapes can help us know the weather.","Only weather scientists can learn about clouds."]
The passage explains how clouds form and describes three kinds of clouds and the weather each can bring.

Roads were rough and muddy, and wagons moved very slowly. It could take weeks to send a load of wheat from the farms in the West to New York City. It cost a lot of money, too.

A man named DeWitt Clinton had an idea. He wanted to build a canal across the state of New York. A canal is a waterway that people dig across land so that boats can travel on it. Clinton's canal would join Lake Erie in the west to the Hudson River in the east. Then boats could carry goods all the way from the Great Lakes to New York City.

Many people thought the plan was foolish. They made fun of it and called it "Clinton's Ditch." The canal would need to be 363 miles long! Still, Clinton did not give up. In 1817, after he became governor of New York, workers began to dig.

The work was very hard. Thousands of workers dug with shovels and picks. Horses helped them move dirt and rock. The land had hills and valleys, so the workers built locks. A lock is like a water elevator. It raises or lowers a boat so that it can move to a higher or lower part of the canal.

In 1825, after eight years of work, the Erie Canal was finally done. Flat boats called barges floated on the water. Mules and horses walked on a path beside the canal and pulled the barges with long ropes.

The canal changed the country. Shipping goods became much faster and much cheaper. Farmers could sell their crops in faraway cities. Towns along the canal, such as Buffalo and Rochester, grew into busy cities. New York City became one of the most important ports in the world.

Today, trucks and trains carry most goods, but the Erie Canal is still open. Now people ride in small boats or bike along the old path to enjoy the view. The canal that people once called a foolish ditch helped a young nation grow.

AB + BA = (10×A + B) + (10×B + A) = 11×(A + B) = 121이므로 A + B = 11입니다. A − B = 3이므로 A = 7, B = 4입니다. 따라서 AB = 74입니다. (확인: 74 + 47 = 121)

ABC − CBA = 99×(A − C) = 396이므로 A − C = 4입니다. A + C = 18 − 6 = 12이므로 A = 8, C = 4입니다. 따라서 ABC = 864입니다. (확인: 864 − 468 = 396)
1부터 100까지의 자연수 중에서 3의 배수도 아니고 4의 배수도 아닌 수는 모두 몇 개입니까?
3의 배수는 33개, 4의 배수는 25개, 3과 4의 공배수(12의 배수)는 8개입니다. 3 또는 4의 배수는 33 + 25 − 8 = 50개이므로, 둘 다 아닌 수는 100 − 50 = 50개입니다.
어떤 자연수로 50을 나누어도 나머지가 2이고, 74를 나누어도 나머지가 2입니다. 이런 자연수 중에서 가장 큰 수는 얼마입니까?
어떤 수는 50 − 2 = 48과 74 − 2 = 72를 모두 나누어떨어지게 하는 수, 즉 48과 72의 공약수입니다. 가장 큰 공약수는 24이고, 24는 나머지 2보다 크므로 조건에 맞습니다.
다음 중 가장 큰 수는 어느 것입니까?
3/7 < □/14 < 5/6 을 만족하는 자연수 □는 모두 몇 개입니까?
1부터 50까지의 자연수를 모두 썼습니다. 쓴 숫자들을 모두 더하면 얼마입니까? (예: 12는 1 + 2로 더합니다.)
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + … + 39 의 값은 얼마입니까? (1부터 39까지의 홀수를 모두 더합니다.)
2를 50번 곱한 수의 일의 자리 숫자는 무엇입니까?
2를 곱할 때 일의 자리는 2, 4, 8, 6이 4개씩 반복됩니다. 50 ÷ 4 = 12 … 2이므로 반복의 2번째인 4입니다.
어떤 수를 6으로 나누었더니 몫이 13, 나머지가 5였습니다. 이 수를 8로 나누면 나머지는 얼마입니까?
숫자 카드 3, 0, 7, 5, 1을 한 번씩 모두 사용하여 다섯 자리 수를 만들려고 합니다. 만들 수 있는 수 중에서 50000에 가장 가까운 수는 무엇입니까?
50000보다 크면서 가장 가까운 수는 5 다음에 남은 숫자 0, 1, 3, 7을 작은 순서로 놓은 50137(차 137)입니다. 50000보다 작으면서 가장 가까운 수는 37510(차 12490)입니다. 따라서 50137이 가장 가깝습니다.
1부터 50까지의 자연수 중에서 약수의 개수가 홀수인 수는 모두 몇 개입니까?
약수는 보통 짝(예: 12 = 1×12 = 2×6 = 3×4)을 이루므로 개수가 짝수이지만, 같은 수를 두 번 곱한 수(제곱수)는 짝이 하나 겹쳐 홀수가 됩니다. 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49로 7개입니다.
시계가 3시 30분을 가리킬 때, 짧은바늘과 긴바늘이 이루는 작은 쪽의 각은 몇 도입니까?
긴바늘은 6을 가리키므로 12에서 180°입니다. 짧은바늘은 3에서 30분 동안 15°(1시간에 30°) 더 가서 90° + 15° = 105° 위치입니다. 180° − 105° = 75°입니다.
삼각형 ABC에서 각 A의 크기는 50°입니다. 각 B를 똑같이 둘로 나누는 선과 각 C를 똑같이 둘로 나누는 선이 점 P에서 만날 때, 각 BPC는 몇 도입니까?
각 B + 각 C = 180° − 50° = 130°이므로 그 절반의 합은 65°입니다. 삼각형 PBC에서 각 BPC = 180° − 65° = 115°입니다.
정팔각형의 한 각의 크기는 몇 도입니까?
팔각형은 한 꼭짓점에서 대각선을 그으면 삼각형 6개로 나뉘므로 각의 합은 180° × 6 = 1080°입니다. 정팔각형의 한 각은 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°입니다.
팔각형에 그을 수 있는 대각선은 모두 몇 개입니까?
한 꼭짓점에서 자기 자신과 이웃한 두 꼭짓점을 뺀 5개의 꼭짓점으로 대각선을 그을 수 있습니다. 8 × 5 = 40인데 각 대각선이 두 번씩 세어졌으므로 40 ÷ 2 = 20개입니다.
그림은 정사각형 6개를 붙여 만든 도형입니다. 그림에서 찾을 수 있는 크고 작은 사각형(정사각형과 직사각형 모두)은 모두 몇 개입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 180" width="260" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><line x1="10" y1="10" x2="10" y2="170" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="90" y1="10" x2="90" y2="170" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="170" y1="10" x2="170" y2="170" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="250" y1="10" x2="250" y2="170" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="10" x2="250" y2="10" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="90" x2="250" y2="90" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="170" x2="250" y2="170" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/></svg>
세로선 4개 중 2개, 가로선 3개 중 2개를 고르면 사각형 하나가 정해집니다. (4개 중 2개 고르기 6가지) × (3개 중 2개 고르기 3가지) = 18개입니다.
그림은 가로, 세로 3칸씩인 정사각형 모양입니다. 그림에서 찾을 수 있는 크고 작은 정사각형은 모두 몇 개입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 230 230" width="230" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><line x1="10" y1="10" x2="10" y2="220" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="80" y1="10" x2="80" y2="220" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="150" y1="10" x2="150" y2="220" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="220" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="10" x2="220" y2="10" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="80" x2="220" y2="80" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="150" x2="220" y2="150" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="10" y1="220" x2="220" y2="220" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/></svg>
그림과 같이 삼각형의 위쪽 꼭짓점에서 밑변 위의 세 점으로 선분을 그었습니다. 그림에서 찾을 수 있는 크고 작은 삼각형은 모두 몇 개입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 200" width="340" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><polygon points="170,15 20,185 320,185" fill="none" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="170" y1="15" x2="95" y2="185" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="170" y1="15" x2="170" y2="185" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="170" y1="15" x2="245" y2="185" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/></svg>
모든 삼각형은 위쪽 꼭짓점을 포함하고 밑변 위의 점 2개를 고르면 정해집니다. 밑변 위의 점은 양 끝을 포함해 5개이므로 5개 중 2개를 고르는 방법은 4+3+2+1 = 10가지, 즉 10개입니다.
어떤 도형을 시계 방향으로 90°만큼 5번 돌렸습니다. 이 결과는 처음 도형을 어떻게 움직인 것과 같습니까?
["시계 반대 방향으로 90°만큼 돌린 것","180°만큼 돌린 것","시계 방향으로 90°만큼 돌린 것","움직이지 않은 것(처음과 같음)"]
시계 방향으로 90°씩 5번 돌리면 450°입니다. 360°는 한 바퀴이므로 450° − 360° = 90°, 즉 시계 방향으로 90°만큼 돌린 것과 같습니다.
어떤 도형을 오른쪽으로 뒤집은 다음, 다시 아래쪽으로 뒤집었습니다. 이 결과는 처음 도형을 어떻게 움직인 것과 같습니까?
["시계 방향으로 90°만큼 돌린 것","움직이지 않은 것(처음과 같음)","시계 반대 방향으로 90°만큼 돌린 것","180°만큼 돌린 것"]
오른쪽으로 뒤집으면 왼쪽과 오른쪽이 바뀌고, 아래쪽으로 뒤집으면 위와 아래가 바뀝니다. 좌우와 상하가 모두 바뀐 모양은 180°만큼 돌린 모양과 같습니다.
가로 12cm, 세로 8cm인 직사각형의 오른쪽 위 귀퉁이에서 가로 4cm, 세로 3cm인 직사각형을 잘라 내어 그림과 같은 도형을 만들었습니다. 이 도형의 둘레는 몇 cm입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-24 0 364 250" width="340" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><polygon points="30,20 217,20 217,95 310,95 310,220 30,220" fill="#eee" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><polyline points="217,20 310,20 310,95" fill="none" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6,5"/><text x="170" y="242" text-anchor="middle">12cm</text><text x="18" y="125" text-anchor="end" font-size="14">8cm</text><text x="263" y="15" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">4cm</text><text x="318" y="62" font-size="14">3cm</text></svg>
잘라 낸 부분의 두 변(4cm, 3cm)을 바깥쪽으로 옮기면 처음 직사각형의 둘레와 같아집니다. (12 + 8) × 2 = 40cm입니다.
네 변의 길이가 모두 자연수(cm)이고 둘레가 24cm인 직사각형(정사각형 포함) 중에서 넓이가 가장 큰 것의 넓이는 몇 cm²입니까?
그림과 같은 전개도를 접어 정육면체를 만들었습니다. 면 "나"와 마주 보는 면은 어느 것입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 200" width="260" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><rect x="70" y="10" width="60" height="60" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="100" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">가</text><rect x="10" y="70" width="60" height="60" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="40" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">나</text><rect x="70" y="70" width="60" height="60" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="100" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">다</text><rect x="130" y="70" width="60" height="60" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="160" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">라</text><rect x="190" y="70" width="60" height="60" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="220" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">마</text><rect x="70" y="130" width="60" height="60" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="100" y="167" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20">바</text></svg>
가운데 한 줄로 이어진 네 면 "나, 다, 라, 마"는 정육면체의 옆면을 한 바퀴 둘러싸므로 한 칸 건너 있는 면끼리 마주 봅니다. 따라서 "나"와 "라", "다"와 "마"가 마주 보고, 위·아래에 붙은 "가"와 "바"가 마주 봅니다.
오각형의 다섯 각 중 네 각의 크기가 100°, 110°, 120°, 95°일 때, 나머지 한 각의 크기는 몇 도입니까?
다음 도형 중에서 대칭축(접었을 때 완전히 겹치게 하는 직선)의 개수가 가장 많은 것은 어느 것입니까?
대칭축의 개수는 정삼각형 3개, 정사각형이 아닌 직사각형 2개, 정오각형 5개, 정육각형 6개입니다. 가장 많은 것은 정육각형입니다.

다음과 같은 규칙으로 수를 늘어놓았습니다. 20번째 수는 얼마입니까?
3, 7, 11, 15, 19, …
성냥개비로 정사각형을 옆으로 한 줄로 이어 붙여 만듭니다. 정사각형 1개는 성냥개비 4개, 2개는 7개, 3개는 10개가 필요합니다. 정사각형 10개를 만들려면 성냥개비가 몇 개 필요합니까?
처음 1개에 성냥개비 4개, 그 뒤로 정사각형 하나를 붙일 때마다 3개씩 더 필요합니다. 4 + 3 × 9 = 31개입니다.
바둑돌을 삼각형 모양으로 1개, 3개, 6개, 10개, …와 같이 늘어놓습니다. 7번째 모양에 놓이는 바둑돌은 몇 개입니까?
★, ◆, ●, ★, ◆, ●, …와 같은 순서로 모양을 계속 늘어놓을 때, 50번째에 놓이는 모양은 무엇입니까?
민수, 지호, 서연이가 빨간색, 파란색, 노란색 모자를 하나씩 썼습니다(세 사람의 모자 색은 모두 다릅니다). 민수는 빨간색 모자를 쓰지 않았고, 지호는 빨간색 모자도 파란색 모자도 쓰지 않았습니다. 서연이가 쓴 모자는 무슨 색입니까?
지호는 빨간색도 파란색도 아니므로 노란색입니다. 민수는 빨간색이 아니고 노란색은 지호가 썼으므로 파란색입니다. 남은 빨간색이 서연이의 모자입니다.

A, B, C 세 사람 중 한 사람이 꽃병을 깼습니다. 세 사람의 말 중 참말은 하나뿐입니다.
A: "B가 깼어."
B: "나는 안 깼어."
C: "나는 안 깼어."
꽃병을 깬 사람은 누구입니까?
A가 깼다면 B, C의 말이 참이라 참말이 2개입니다. B가 깼다면 A, C의 말이 참이라 2개입니다. C가 깼다면 A 거짓, B 참, C 거짓으로 참말이 하나뿐입니다. 따라서 C입니다.
윗옷 3벌, 바지 4벌, 신발 2켤레가 있습니다. 윗옷, 바지, 신발을 하나씩 골라 입는 방법은 모두 몇 가지입니까?
윗옷 3가지 각각에 바지 4가지, 그 각각에 신발 2가지를 고를 수 있으므로 3 × 4 × 2 = 24가지입니다.
숫자 카드 1, 2, 3, 4 중에서 2장을 골라 두 자리 수를 만들 때, 만들 수 있는 짝수는 모두 몇 개입니까?
일의 자리가 2이면 십의 자리는 1, 3, 4 중 하나(3개), 일의 자리가 4이면 십의 자리는 1, 2, 3 중 하나(3개)입니다. 3 + 3 = 6개입니다.
계단 5칸을 한 번에 1칸 또는 2칸씩 올라가려고 합니다. 맨 위까지 올라가는 방법은 모두 몇 가지입니까?
1칸까지 1가지, 2칸까지 2가지이고, 어떤 칸까지의 방법 수는 바로 아래 두 칸까지의 방법 수의 합입니다. 3칸 3가지, 4칸 5가지, 5칸 8가지입니다.
상자 안에 빨간 공, 파란 공, 노란 공이 각각 10개씩 들어 있습니다. 눈을 감고 공을 꺼낼 때, 같은 색 공을 반드시 2개 이상 꺼내려면 적어도 몇 개를 꺼내야 합니까?
운이 나쁘면 3개를 꺼낼 때 세 가지 색이 하나씩 나올 수 있습니다. 4개를 꺼내면 색은 3가지뿐이므로 반드시 같은 색이 2개 이상 나옵니다.
학생 30명이 있는 반에서 태어난 달이 같은 학생은 적어도 몇 명 이상 반드시 있습니까?
12달에 2명씩 고르게 나누어도 24명뿐이므로 30명이면 어떤 달에는 반드시 3명 이상이 있습니다. 30 = 12 × 2 + 6이므로 3명이 확실히 보장되고, 12 × 3 = 36 > 30이므로 4명은 보장되지 않습니다.
자연수를 1부터 차례로 한 줄에 7개씩 씁니다. 첫째 줄은 1~7, 둘째 줄은 8~14, …입니다. 100은 몇째 줄의 몇째 칸에 있습니까?
작은 정사각형 타일로 가로, 세로 각각 n개씩인 큰 정사각형을 만들고, 가장 바깥쪽 테두리에 있는 타일만 빨간색으로 칠합니다. n = 3이면 빨간 타일은 8개, n = 4이면 12개입니다. n = 10일 때 빨간 타일은 몇 개입니까?
지우는 수학 시험을 4번 보았는데 평균이 85점입니다. 5번째 시험을 보고 5번의 평균을 87점으로 만들려면 5번째 시험에서 몇 점을 받아야 합니까?
어떤 수에 3을 곱하고 7을 뺀 다음 2로 나누었더니 13이 되었습니다. 어떤 수는 얼마입니까?
하은이는 가지고 있던 사탕의 절반을 동생에게 주고, 남은 사탕 중 3개를 먹었습니다. 그다음 남은 사탕의 절반을 친구에게 주었더니 5개가 남았습니다. 하은이가 처음에 가지고 있던 사탕은 몇 개입니까?
거꾸로 풉니다. 친구에게 주기 전: 5 × 2 = 10개, 3개 먹기 전: 10 + 3 = 13개, 동생에게 주기 전: 13 × 2 = 26개입니다.
1분에 60m씩 걷는 사람이 2.4km를 걸으려면 몇 분이 걸립니까?
오전 9시 45분에 출발한 기차가 3시간 50분 동안 달려 도착했습니다. 도착한 시각은 언제입니까?
어느 해 3월 1일은 화요일입니다. 같은 해 3월 31일은 무슨 요일입니까?
숫자 카드 2, 5, 7, 8, 0을 한 번씩 모두 사용하여 (세 자리 수) − (두 자리 수)를 만들려고 합니다. 계산 결과가 가장 클 때의 값은 얼마입니까?
세 자리 수는 가장 크게 875, 남은 카드 0, 2로 만든 가장 작은 두 자리 수는 20입니다. 875 − 20 = 855입니다. (870 − 25 = 845 등은 더 작습니다.)
길이가 100m인 길의 한쪽에 처음부터 끝까지 5m 간격으로 나무를 심으려고 합니다. 길의 처음과 끝에도 나무를 심는다면 나무는 모두 몇 그루 필요합니까?
간격의 수는 100 ÷ 5 = 20개입니다. 처음과 끝 모두 심으면 나무 수는 간격 수보다 1 많으므로 21그루입니다.
통나무 하나를 4도막으로 자르는 데 9분이 걸렸습니다. 같은 빠르기로 같은 통나무를 7도막으로 자르는 데는 몇 분이 걸립니까? (한 번 자르는 데 걸리는 시간은 항상 같습니다.)
4도막으로 자르려면 3번 잘라야 하므로 한 번에 9 ÷ 3 = 3분입니다. 7도막은 6번 잘라야 하므로 3 × 6 = 18분입니다.
레모네이드를 만들 때 레몬즙 1컵마다 물 4컵을 섞습니다. 같은 맛의 레모네이드를 2L 만들려면 레몬즙은 몇 mL가 필요합니까?
올해 아버지의 나이는 42세, 아들의 나이는 12세입니다. 몇 년 후에 아버지의 나이가 아들 나이의 2배가 됩니까?
두 사람의 나이 차이는 항상 30세입니다. 아버지가 아들의 2배일 때 아들 나이는 나이 차이와 같은 30세입니다. 30 − 12 = 18년 후입니다. (확인: 60 = 2 × 30)
닭과 토끼가 모두 15마리 있고, 다리 수를 세어 보니 46개였습니다. 토끼는 몇 마리입니까?
15마리가 모두 닭이라면 다리는 30개입니다. 토끼 한 마리는 닭보다 다리가 2개 많으므로 (46 − 30) ÷ 2 = 8마리가 토끼입니다. (확인: 닭 7 × 2 + 토끼 8 × 4 = 14 + 32 = 46)
사과 3개의 무게는 배 2개의 무게와 같고, 배 3개의 무게는 멜론 1개의 무게와 같습니다. 멜론 2개의 무게는 사과 몇 개의 무게와 같습니까? (같은 과일끼리는 무게가 같습니다.)
멜론 2개 = 배 6개입니다. 배 2개 = 사과 3개이므로 배 6개 = 사과 9개입니다.
500원짜리 동전과 100원짜리 동전이 합하여 12개 있고, 금액은 모두 3600원입니다. 500원짜리 동전은 몇 개입니까?
서로 다른 숫자 A, B, C로 만든 세 자리 수 ABC를 세 번 더했더니 세 자리가 모두 B인 수 BBB가 되었습니다. (ABC + ABC + ABC = BBB) 세 자리 수 ABC는 얼마입니까?
BBB = 111 × B이므로 ABC × 3 = 111 × B, 즉 ABC = 37 × B입니다. 37 × B의 십의 자리가 B인 것을 찾으면 B = 4일 때 148만 맞습니다(185, 259, 296은 십의 자리가 각각 8, 5, 9로 B와 다름). 148 × 3 = 444입니다.
가로 84cm, 세로 60cm인 직사각형 종이를 남는 부분 없이 크기가 같은 정사각형 여러 개로 자르려고 합니다. 정사각형을 가장 크게 자를 때, 정사각형은 모두 몇 개가 됩니까?
정사각형의 한 변은 84와 60의 최대공약수인 12cm입니다. 가로로 84 ÷ 12 = 7개, 세로로 60 ÷ 12 = 5개이므로 7 × 5 = 35개입니다.
2, 3, 4, 5, 6 중 어느 수로 나누어도 나머지가 1인 자연수 중에서 1보다 큰 가장 작은 수는 얼마입니까?
구하는 수에서 1을 빼면 2, 3, 4, 5, 6의 공배수입니다. 최소공배수는 60이므로 구하는 수는 60 + 1 = 61입니다.
한 정류장에서 A버스는 8분마다, B버스는 12분마다 출발합니다. 오전 7시에 두 버스가 동시에 출발했다면, 7시 이후 세 번째로 두 버스가 동시에 출발하는 시각은 언제입니까?
8과 12의 최소공배수는 24이므로 24분마다 동시에 출발합니다. 7시 24분, 7시 48분, 8시 12분이므로 세 번째는 오전 8시 12분입니다.
분모가 24인 진분수 중에서 더 이상 약분되지 않는 기약분수는 모두 몇 개입니까?
분자가 1~23 중 24와 공약수가 1뿐인 수, 즉 2의 배수도 3의 배수도 아닌 수를 찾습니다. 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23으로 8개입니다.
2/5 < 7/□ < 3/4 을 만족하는 자연수 □는 모두 몇 개입니까?
각 괄호를 계산하면 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × … × 9/10입니다. 앞 분수의 분모와 뒤 분수의 분자가 차례로 약분되어 1/10만 남습니다.
각 자리 숫자의 합이 10인 세 자리 수 중에서 가장 큰 수와 가장 작은 수의 차는 얼마입니까?
가장 작은 수는 백의 자리를 1로 하고 남은 9를 일의 자리에 놓은 109, 가장 큰 수는 백의 자리를 9로 하고 나머지 1을 십의 자리에 놓은 910입니다. 910 − 109 = 801입니다.
3을 100번 곱한 수의 일의 자리 숫자는 무엇입니까?
3을 곱할 때 일의 자리는 3, 9, 7, 1이 4개씩 반복됩니다. 100 ÷ 4 = 25로 나누어떨어지므로 반복의 마지막인 1입니다.
5로 나누면 나머지가 3이고, 7로 나누면 나머지가 5인 두 자리 자연수 중에서 가장 작은 수는 얼마입니까?
구하는 수에 2를 더하면 5로도 7로도 나누어떨어지므로 35의 배수입니다. 35 − 2 = 33은 두 자리 수입니다. (확인: 33 = 5 × 6 + 3 = 7 × 4 + 5)
다음 중 계산 결과가 가장 큰 것은 어느 것입니까?
1부터 100까지의 자연수 중에서 약수가 정확히 3개인 수는 모두 몇 개입니까?
네 자리 수 52□4가 3의 배수이면서 4의 배수일 때, □ 안에 들어갈 숫자는 무엇입니까?
4의 배수가 되려면 끝 두 자리 □4가 4의 배수여야 하므로 □는 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 중 하나입니다. 3의 배수가 되려면 5 + 2 + □ + 4 = 11 + □가 3의 배수여야 하므로 □는 1, 4, 7 중 하나입니다. 둘 다 만족하는 것은 4입니다(5244 = 12 × 437).
쌓기나무를 가로 3줄, 세로(앞뒤) 2줄로 놓인 6칸 위에 쌓았습니다. 6칸 모두에 쌓기나무가 1개 이상 있습니다. 앞에서 보면 왼쪽부터 각 세로줄의 가장 높은 층이 2층, 3층, 1층이고, 옆에서 보면 앞줄의 가장 높은 층이 3층, 뒷줄의 가장 높은 층이 2층입니다. 쌓기나무가 가장 많을 때는 몇 개입니까?
