각 칸에는 (그 세로줄의 최고 층)과 (그 앞뒤 줄의 최고 층) 중 작은 수만큼 쌓을 수 있습니다. 앞줄: 2, 3, 1, 뒷줄: 2, 2, 1이므로 최대 2+3+1+2+2+1 = 11개입니다.
쌓기나무를 가로 3줄, 세로(앞뒤) 2줄로 놓인 6칸 위에 쌓았습니다. 6칸 모두에 쌓기나무가 1개 이상 있습니다. 앞에서 보면 왼쪽부터 각 세로줄의 가장 높은 층이 2층, 3층, 1층이고, 옆에서 보면 앞줄의 가장 높은 층이 3층, 뒷줄의 가장 높은 층이 2층입니다. 쌓기나무가 가장 적을 때는 몇 개입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 190" width="330" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><text x="10" y="20" font-size="14">앞에서 본 모양</text><rect x="20" y="110" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="20" y="70" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="60" y="110" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="60" y="70" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="60" y="30" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="100" y="110" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="200" y="20" font-size="14">옆에서 본 모양</text><text x="210" y="178" font-size="13">앞</text><text x="260" y="178" font-size="13">뒤</text><rect x="200" y="110" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="200" y="70" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="200" y="30" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="240" y="110" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="240" y="70" width="40" height="40" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/></svg>
가운데 세로줄의 3층은 뒷줄(최고 2층)에는 놓을 수 없으므로 앞줄 가운데가 3층입니다(앞줄 3층도 해결). 왼쪽 세로줄의 2층과 뒷줄의 2층은 뒷줄 왼쪽 칸 하나를 2층으로 하면 함께 해결됩니다. 나머지 4칸은 1개씩 놓으면 3 + 2 + 1 × 4 = 9개입니다.
별 모양(☆)처럼 한 번에 그린 오각별의 뾰족한 꼭짓점 5개에 있는 각의 크기를 모두 더하면 몇 도입니까?
삼각형의 한 바깥각은 이웃하지 않은 두 안쪽 각의 합과 같습니다. 이를 이용하면 별의 다섯 꼭짓점 각 중 네 개를 모아 한 삼각형 안의 두 각으로 바꿀 수 있어, 다섯 각의 합은 삼각형 한 개의 세 각의 합인 180°가 됩니다. (정오각별이면 한 꼭짓점 각이 36°이므로 36° × 5 = 180°로 확인됩니다.)
마주 보는 면의 눈의 수의 합이 7인 주사위 3개를 바닥 위에 한 줄로 높이 쌓았습니다. 맨 위 주사위의 윗면 눈이 5일 때, 바닥에 닿은 면과 주사위끼리 맞닿아 보이지 않는 면들의 눈의 수를 모두 더하면 얼마입니까?
보이지 않는 면은 맨 아래 주사위의 아랫면·윗면(합 7), 가운데 주사위의 아랫면·윗면(합 7), 맨 위 주사위의 아랫면입니다. 맨 위 주사위의 아랫면은 7 − 5 = 2입니다. 7 + 7 + 2 = 16입니다.
정오각형 ABCDE에서 대각선 AC와 AD를 그었습니다. 각 CAD의 크기는 몇 도입니까?
정오각형의 한 각은 540° ÷ 5 = 108°입니다. 삼각형 ABC는 AB = BC인 이등변삼각형이므로 각 BAC = (180° − 108°) ÷ 2 = 36°이고, 같은 방법으로 각 EAD = 36°입니다. 각 CAD = 108° − 36° − 36° = 36°입니다.
시계가 8시 20분을 가리킬 때, 짧은바늘과 긴바늘이 이루는 작은 쪽의 각은 몇 도입니까?
긴바늘은 4를 가리키므로 12에서 120°입니다. 짧은바늘은 8에서 20분 동안 10° 더 가서 240° + 10° = 250° 위치입니다. 250° − 120° = 130°입니다.
삼각형 ABC와 삼각형 DEF는 서로 합동이고, 꼭짓점 A와 D, B와 E, C와 F가 각각 대응합니다. 각 A가 40°, 각 E가 65°일 때 각 F의 크기는 몇 도입니까?
대응각의 크기는 같으므로 각 D = 각 A = 40°입니다. 삼각형 DEF에서 각 F = 180° − 40° − 65° = 75°입니다.
한 모서리가 3cm인 정육면체의 겉면 전체에 페인트를 칠한 다음, 한 모서리가 1cm인 정육면체 27개로 잘랐습니다. 두 면에만 페인트가 칠해진 작은 정육면체는 몇 개입니까?
두 면만 칠해진 것은 꼭짓점이 아닌 모서리의 가운데에 있는 조각입니다. 정육면체의 모서리는 12개이고 각 모서리마다 1개씩이므로 12개입니다.
다음 중 선대칭도형이면서 동시에 점대칭도형인 것은 어느 것입니까?
정삼각형과 정오각형은 선대칭도형이지만 점대칭도형이 아닙니다. 직사각형도 마름모도 아닌 평행사변형은 점대칭도형이지만 선대칭도형이 아닙니다. 마름모는 두 대각선이 대칭축이고 대각선의 교점이 대칭의 중심이므로 둘 다에 해당합니다.
직육면체의 가로는 세로보다 2cm 길고, 높이는 세로와 같습니다. 이 직육면체의 모든 모서리 길이의 합이 56cm일 때, 가로는 몇 cm입니까?
직육면체에는 가로, 세로, 높이가 각각 4개씩 있으므로 (가로 + 세로 + 높이) × 4 = 56, 가로 + 세로 + 높이 = 14입니다. 세로를 □라 하면 (□ + 2) + □ + □ = 14, □ = 4입니다. 가로는 4 + 2 = 6cm입니다.
한 변이 10cm인 정사각형의 네 변의 가운데 점을 이어 정사각형을 그리고, 그 정사각형의 네 변의 가운데 점을 다시 이어 정사각형을 그렸습니다. 가장 안쪽 정사각형의 넓이는 몇 cm²입니까?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 240 240" width="240" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="16"><rect x="20" y="20" width="200" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="120,20 220,120 120,220 20,120" fill="none" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="70" y="70" width="100" height="100" fill="#ddd" stroke="#000" stroke-width="3"/><text x="120" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">10cm</text></svg>
가운데 점을 이어 만든 정사각형의 넓이는 바깥 정사각형 넓이의 절반입니다(바깥 정사각형을 반으로 접어 생각). 100 → 50 → 25이므로 25cm²입니다.
그림은 가로 4칸, 세로 2칸으로 나누어진 직사각형입니다. 그림에서 찾을 수 있는 크고 작은 사각형(정사각형과 직사각형 모두)은 모두 몇 개입니까?

세로선 5개 중 2개(10가지)와 가로선 3개 중 2개(3가지)를 고르면 사각형 하나가 정해집니다. 10 × 3 = 30개입니다.
어떤 도형을 시계 방향으로 90°만큼 7번 돌린 모양은, 처음 도형을 시계 반대 방향으로 몇 도만큼 한 번 돌린 모양과 같습니까?
시계 방향으로 90° × 7 = 630°이고, 630° − 360° = 270°이므로 시계 방향 270°와 같습니다. 시계 방향 270°는 시계 반대 방향 90°와 같습니다.
5부터 시작하여 7씩 커지는 수를 차례로 늘어놓습니다. (5, 12, 19, 26, …) 이 중에서 200 이하인 수는 모두 몇 개입니까?
각 수는 (순서 × 순서) + 1입니다(1×1+1, 2×2+1, 3×3+1, …). 15번째 수는 15 × 15 + 1 = 226입니다. (이웃한 수의 차가 3, 5, 7, 9, …로 2씩 커지는 것으로도 확인할 수 있습니다.)
성냥개비로 정육각형을 옆으로 한 줄로 이어 붙여 만듭니다(이웃한 정육각형은 한 변을 함께 씁니다). 정육각형 20개를 만들려면 성냥개비가 몇 개 필요합니까?
첫 정육각형에 6개, 하나 더 붙일 때마다 5개씩 더 필요합니다. 6 + 5 × 19 = 101개입니다.
바둑돌을 정사각형 모양으로 1개, 4개, 9개, 16개, …와 같이 늘어놓습니다. 바둑돌 수가 처음으로 200개를 넘는 것은 몇 번째 모양입니까?
n번째 모양의 바둑돌 수는 n × n입니다. 14 × 14 = 196(200 이하), 15 × 15 = 225이므로 15번째입니다.

다음과 같은 규칙으로 분수를 늘어놓았습니다(약분하지 않습니다). 50번째 분수는 무엇입니까?
1/1, 1/2, 2/2, 1/3, 2/3, 3/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, …
분모가 n인 분수가 n개씩 있습니다. 분모 1~9까지의 분수는 1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45개이므로 50번째는 분모가 10인 분수 중 5번째인 5/10입니다.

가윤, 나래, 다솜, 라희는 수영, 축구, 농구, 탁구 중 서로 다른 운동을 한 가지씩 합니다.
① 가윤이는 공을 사용하는 운동을 하지 않습니다.
② 나래는 축구도 탁구도 하지 않습니다.
③ 다솜이는 축구를 하지 않습니다.
라희가 하는 운동은 무엇입니까?
공을 쓰지 않는 운동은 수영뿐이므로 가윤이는 수영입니다. 나래는 축구, 탁구가 아니고 수영도 아니므로 농구입니다. 다솜이는 축구가 아니므로 탁구이고, 라희는 남은 축구입니다.

A, B, C, D 네 사람 중 한 사람이 창문을 깼습니다. 네 사람 중 정확히 한 사람만 거짓말을 했습니다.
A: "C가 깼어."
B: "나는 안 깼어."
C: "D가 깼어."
D: "C는 거짓말을 하고 있어."
창문을 깬 사람은 누구입니까?
C와 D의 말은 정반대이므로 둘 중 정확히 한 명이 거짓말쟁이이고, A와 B는 참말을 합니다. A의 말이 참이므로 C가 깼습니다. 이때 C의 말은 거짓, D의 말은 참이 되어 거짓말한 사람이 C 한 명뿐이므로 조건에 맞습니다.
숫자 카드 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 중에서 3장을 골라 세 자리 수를 만들 때, 만들 수 있는 짝수는 모두 몇 개입니까? (같은 카드를 두 번 쓸 수 없습니다.)
일의 자리가 0이면 백의 자리 4가지, 십의 자리 3가지로 12개. 일의 자리가 2이면 백의 자리는 0과 2를 뺀 3가지, 십의 자리는 남은 3가지로 9개. 일의 자리가 4일 때도 9개. 12 + 9 + 9 = 30개입니다.
가로 4칸, 세로 3칸으로 된 바둑판 모양의 길이 있습니다. 왼쪽 아래 모퉁이에서 오른쪽 위 모퉁이까지 길을 따라 가장 짧은 거리로 가는 방법은 모두 몇 가지입니까?
오른쪽으로 4번, 위쪽으로 3번, 모두 7번 움직입니다. 7번 중 위쪽으로 갈 3번을 고르는 방법은 (7 × 6 × 5) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 35가지입니다.
한 줄로 붙어 있는 4개의 칸을 빨강, 파랑, 노랑 3가지 색으로 칠하려고 합니다. 이웃한 칸은 서로 다른 색으로 칠해야 하고, 같은 색을 여러 번 써도 됩니다. 칠하는 방법은 모두 몇 가지입니까?
첫째 칸은 3가지, 둘째·셋째·넷째 칸은 바로 앞 칸과 다른 2가지씩이므로 3 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 24가지입니다.
1부터 20까지의 자연수 중에서 몇 개를 고를 때, 합이 21인 두 수가 반드시 포함되도록 하려면 적어도 몇 개를 골라야 합니까?
합이 21인 짝은 (1,20), (2,19), …, (10,11)의 10쌍입니다. 각 쌍에서 하나씩 10개를 고르면 합이 21인 두 수가 없을 수 있지만, 11개를 고르면 반드시 어떤 쌍에서 두 수를 모두 고르게 됩니다.
어떤 모임에 있는 사람 중 같은 요일에 태어난 사람이 반드시 4명 이상 있으려면 사람은 적어도 몇 명이어야 합니까?
7개 요일에 3명씩 고르게 나누면 21명까지는 4명 이상인 요일이 없을 수 있습니다. 22명이면 반드시 어떤 요일에 4명 이상이 있습니다. 7 × 3 + 1 = 22명입니다.
8명이 모두 서로 한 번씩 악수를 했습니다. 악수는 모두 몇 번 했습니까?
한 사람은 다른 7명과 악수하므로 8 × 7 = 56인데, 한 번의 악수를 두 사람이 각각 셌으므로 56 ÷ 2 = 28번입니다.

홀수를 다음과 같이 늘어놓았습니다. 10째 줄의 맨 처음 수는 얼마입니까?
1째 줄: 1
2째 줄: 3, 5
3째 줄: 7, 9, 11
4째 줄: 13, 15, 17, 19
…
n째 줄에는 홀수가 n개 있습니다. 9째 줄까지 1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45개이므로 10째 줄의 첫 수는 46번째 홀수, 2 × 46 − 1 = 91입니다.
5명의 평균 키가 140cm입니다. 한 명이 더 들어와서 6명의 평균 키가 142cm가 되었습니다. 새로 들어온 사람의 키는 몇 cm입니까?
어떤 수 4개의 평균을 구하는데, 그중 18을 81로 잘못 보고 계산하여 평균이 42.75가 나왔습니다. 바르게 계산한 평균은 얼마입니까?
잘못 계산한 합은 42.75 × 4 = 171입니다. 81 − 18 = 63만큼 더 크게 계산했으므로 바른 합은 171 − 63 = 108, 바른 평균은 108 ÷ 4 = 27입니다.
어떤 일을 A가 혼자 하면 12일, B가 혼자 하면 6일이 걸립니다. 두 사람이 함께 하면 이 일을 며칠 만에 끝낼 수 있습니까? (두 사람이 하루에 하는 일의 양은 각각 일정합니다.)
하루에 A는 전체의 1/12, B는 1/6 = 2/12를 합니다. 함께 하면 하루에 3/12 = 1/4을 하므로 4일이 걸립니다.
빈 물통을 A관으로 물을 넣으면 10분 만에 가득 차고, 가득 찬 물통의 물을 B관으로 빼면 15분 만에 모두 빠집니다. 빈 물통에 A관과 B관을 동시에 열어 두면 물통이 가득 차는 데 몇 분이 걸립니까?
1분에 A관은 물통의 1/10 = 3/30을 채우고 B관은 1/15 = 2/30을 뺍니다. 1분에 1/30씩 차므로 30분이 걸립니다.
1.8km 떨어진 두 곳에서 지민이와 서준이가 서로를 향해 동시에 출발했습니다. 지민이는 1분에 70m, 서준이는 1분에 50m를 걷습니다. 두 사람은 출발한 지 몇 분 후에 만납니까?
1분에 두 사람 사이의 거리가 70 + 50 = 120m씩 줄어듭니다. 1.8km = 1800m이므로 1800 ÷ 120 = 15분 후에 만납니다.
길이가 200m인 기차가 1초에 25m를 가는 빠르기로 길이 800m인 터널을 지나갑니다. 기차의 맨 앞이 터널에 들어가기 시작해서 기차 전체가 터널을 완전히 빠져나올 때까지 몇 초가 걸립니까?
기차의 맨 앞이 이동해야 하는 거리는 터널 길이 + 기차 길이 = 800 + 200 = 1000m입니다. 1000 ÷ 25 = 40초입니다.
준호는 가진 돈의 3/5으로 책을 사고, 남은 돈의 1/2로 간식을 샀더니 1200원이 남았습니다. 준호가 처음에 가진 돈은 얼마입니까?
간식을 사기 전의 돈은 1200 × 2 = 2400원입니다. 이것은 처음 돈의 1 − 3/5 = 2/5이므로 처음 돈은 2400 ÷ 2 × 5 = 6000원입니다.
어느 반에서 남학생 수는 반 전체 학생 수의 4/7이고, 여학생은 12명입니다. 이 반의 전체 학생은 몇 명입니까?
네 변의 길이가 모두 자연수(cm)이고 둘레가 36cm인 직사각형(정사각형 포함)을 만들려고 합니다. 넓이가 가장 넓을 때와 가장 좁을 때의 넓이의 차는 몇 cm²입니까?
가로 + 세로 = 18cm입니다. 넓이는 9 × 9 = 81cm²일 때 가장 넓고, 1 × 17 = 17cm²일 때 가장 좁습니다. 81 − 17 = 64cm²입니다.
2월이 28일까지 있는 어느 해의 1월 1일이 목요일이었습니다. 같은 해 5월 5일은 무슨 요일입니까?
하루에 4분씩 일정하게 느려지는 시계가 있습니다. 월요일 오전 9시에 이 시계를 정확하게 맞추었습니다. 같은 주 목요일 오전 9시에 이 시계가 가리키는 시각은 언제입니까?
월요일 오전 9시부터 목요일 오전 9시까지는 3일입니다. 4 × 3 = 12분 느려지므로 9시 − 12분 = 오전 8시 48분을 가리킵니다.
1부터 9까지의 수를 한 번씩 써서 3×3 칸에 넣었더니 가로, 세로, 두 대각선 위의 세 수의 합이 모두 15로 같아졌습니다. 가운데 칸의 수가 5이고 왼쪽 위 모서리 칸의 수가 2일 때, 오른쪽 아래 모서리 칸의 수는 무엇입니까?
왼쪽 위, 가운데, 오른쪽 아래는 한 대각선 위에 있으므로 2 + 5 + □ = 15, □ = 8입니다.
모양이 똑같은 동전 9개 중 1개만 가짜이고, 가짜 동전은 진짜보다 가볍습니다. 양팔 저울을 사용하여 가짜 동전을 반드시 찾아내려면 저울을 적어도 몇 번 사용해야 합니까?
9개를 3개씩 세 묶음으로 나누어 두 묶음을 달면 가벼운 묶음(또는 기울지 않으면 남은 묶음)을 찾습니다. 그 3개 중 2개를 달면 가짜를 찾습니다. 2번이면 됩니다. 1번으로는 결과가 3가지뿐이라 9개 중 하나를 항상 가려낼 수 없습니다.
학생들에게 공책을 4권씩 나누어 주면 7권이 남고, 6권씩 나누어 주면 9권이 모자랍니다. 공책은 모두 몇 권입니까?
한 사람당 2권씩 더 주려면 남는 7권과 모자라는 9권을 합한 16권이 더 필요하므로 학생은 16 ÷ 2 = 8명입니다. 공책은 4 × 8 + 7 = 39권입니다. (확인: 6 × 8 − 9 = 39)
사과가 5개 있어요. 3개를 더 받았어요. 사과는 모두 몇 개일까요?
7을 두 수로 가르기 했어요. 7은 3과 □(으)로 가를 수 있어요. □에 알맞은 수는?
수를 비교하면 9 < 11 < 12 < 15 이므로 가장 큰 수는 15예요.
사탕이 9개 있었어요. 4개를 먹었어요. 남은 사탕은 몇 개일까요?
13보다 크고 17보다 작은 수가 아닌 것은 무엇일까요?
수를 순서대로 셀 때 11 바로 다음에 오는 수는?
나무에 새 2마리가 앉아 있었어요. 3마리가 더 날아왔고, 그다음 1마리가 날아갔어요. 나무에 있는 새는 몇 마리일까요?
한 손의 손가락 5개를 모두 펴고, 다른 손은 손가락 2개만 폈어요. 편 손가락은 모두 몇 개일까요?
연필이 8자루, 지우개가 5개 있어요. 연필이 지우개보다 몇 개 더 많을까요?
쿠키 10개를 두 접시에 똑같이 나누어 담았어요. 한 접시에 몇 개씩 담았을까요?
빨간 구슬 4개, 파란 구슬 4개, 노란 구슬 4개가 있어요. 구슬은 모두 몇 개일까요?
어느 쪽으로 굴려도 잘 굴러가는 물건은 무엇일까요?
축구공은 둥근 공 모양이라 어느 쪽으로도 잘 굴러가요. 주사위, 상자, 책은 평평한 면이 있어서 잘 구르지 않아요.
네모(사각형) 모양에는 곧은 선(변)이 몇 개 있을까요?
동물들이 한 줄로 섰어요. 왼쪽부터 토끼, 곰, 고양이, 강아지 순서예요. 곰의 바로 오른쪽에 있는 동물은?
왼쪽부터 토끼, 곰, 고양이, 강아지이므로 곰 바로 오른쪽은 고양이예요.
시계가 가리키는 시각은 몇 시일까요? (짧은바늘은 빨간색, 긴바늘은 파란색이에요.)
시계가 가리키는 시각은 언제일까요? (짧은바늘은 빨간색, 긴바늘은 파란색이에요.)
쌓기나무를 쌓고 위에서 본 모양이에요. 칸에 적힌 수는 그 자리에 쌓은 쌓기나무 개수예요. 쌓기나무는 모두 몇 개일까요?

쌓기나무를 쌓고 위에서 본 모양이에요. 칸에 적힌 수는 그 자리에 쌓은 쌓기나무 개수예요. 쌓기나무는 모두 몇 개일까요?

왼쪽과 오른쪽으로 반을 접었을 때 양쪽이 꼭 겹치는 숫자는 무엇일까요?
숫자 8은 가운데 세로 선으로 접으면 왼쪽과 오른쪽이 똑같이 겹쳐요. 2, 4, 7은 겹치지 않아요.
똑같은 세모 조각 2개를 붙여서 만들 수 없는 모양은 무엇일까요? (세모 조각은 네모 색종이를 대각선으로 반 자른 모양이에요.)
세모 2개로 네모, 큰 세모, 기울어진 네모는 만들 수 있어요. 곧은 선으로만 된 조각으로는 둥근 동그라미를 만들 수 없어요.
친구들이 한 줄로 섰어요. 민지 앞에 2명, 민지 뒤에 3명이 있어요. 줄을 선 친구는 민지까지 모두 몇 명일까요?

나와 친구가 서로 마주 보고 서 있어요. 친구가 자기의 오른손을 들었어요. 내가 볼 때 친구가 든 손은 내 어느 쪽에 있을까요?
마주 보고 서면 방향이 반대가 돼요. 친구의 오른손은 내가 볼 때 내 왼쪽에 있어요.
책장이 3칸이에요. 맨 위 칸에는 인형, 가운데 칸에는 책, 맨 아래 칸에는 공이 있어요. 책 바로 아래 칸에 있는 것은?
책은 가운데 칸에 있고, 그 바로 아래 칸은 맨 아래 칸이에요. 맨 아래 칸에는 공이 있어요.
규칙에 따라 늘어놓았어요. ○ △ ○ △ ○ 다음에 올 모양은?
구슬을 빨강, 빨강, 파랑, 빨강, 빨강, 파랑 … 순서로 꿰었어요. 9번째 구슬은 무슨 색일까요?
달리기를 했어요. 지수는 민호보다 먼저 들어왔고, 민호는 은우보다 먼저 들어왔어요. 1등은 누구일까요?
지수가 민호보다, 민호가 은우보다 먼저 들어왔으니 순서는 지수, 민호, 은우예요. 1등은 지수예요.
한 줄로 섰어요. 하은이는 앞에서 3번째, 뒤에서 2번째예요. 줄을 선 사람은 모두 몇 명일까요?
상자 안에 빨간 공만 들어 있어요. 눈을 감고 공 하나를 꺼냈어요. 꺼낸 공은 무슨 색일까요?
상자에는 빨간 공만 있으니 어떤 공을 꺼내도 빨간색이에요.
곰은 토끼보다 키가 커요. 토끼는 다람쥐보다 키가 커요. 키가 가장 작은 동물은?
키 순서는 곰 > 토끼 > 다람쥐예요. 가장 작은 동물은 다람쥐예요.
두발자전거 1대에는 바퀴가 2개 있어요. 표를 완성하세요. 자전거 1대 → 바퀴 2개, 2대 → 4개, 3대 → □개
"모든 고양이는 꼬리가 있어요. 나비는 고양이예요." 이 말이 맞을 때, 꼭 맞는 말은 무엇일까요?
["나비는 강아지예요.","나비는 꼬리가 없어요.","나비는 꼬리가 있어요.","꼬리가 있는 동물은 모두 고양이예요."]
모든 고양이는 꼬리가 있고 나비는 고양이이므로, 나비도 꼬리가 있어요.
사탕을 2개 먹었더니 5개가 남았어요. 처음에 사탕은 몇 개 있었을까요?
바구니 2개에 사과를 3개씩 담았어요. 사과는 모두 몇 개일까요?
윗옷은 빨간 옷과 파란 옷 2벌, 바지는 긴바지와 반바지 2벌이 있어요. 윗옷 1벌과 바지 1벌을 골라 입는 방법은 모두 몇 가지일까요?
빨간 옷+긴바지, 빨간 옷+반바지, 파란 옷+긴바지, 파란 옷+반바지로 4가지예요.
마당에 닭 2마리와 강아지 1마리가 있어요. 다리는 모두 몇 개일까요?
지우가 계단을 3칸 올라가고, 1칸 내려온 다음, 다시 2칸 올라갔어요. 지우는 처음보다 몇 칸 위에 있을까요?
3칸 올라가고 1칸 내려오면 2칸 위, 다시 2칸 올라가면 4칸 위예요.
나는 7살이고, 형은 나보다 3살 많아요. 2년 뒤에 형은 몇 살일까요?
세 칸에 수를 넣어 합이 10이 되게 하려고 해요. 3, □, 5 에서 □에 알맞은 수는?
길에 나무 4그루를 한 줄로 심었어요. 나무와 나무 사이는 모두 몇 군데일까요?
10원짜리 동전으로 50원을 만들려면 동전이 몇 개 필요할까요?
케이크를 똑같이 4조각으로 잘랐어요. 엄마가 1조각, 내가 1조각을 먹었어요. 남은 조각은 몇 개일까요?
버스에 사람이 타고 있었어요. 정류장에서 3명이 내리고 2명이 탔더니 6명이 되었어요. 처음에 버스에 몇 명이 타고 있었을까요?
거꾸로 생각해요. 2명이 타기 전에는 6 - 2 = 4명, 3명이 내리기 전에는 4 + 3 = 7명이에요.
수 카드 1, 2, 3 중에서 2장을 골라 두 수를 더해요. 나올 수 있는 합은 모두 몇 가지일까요?
사과 1개의 무게는 귤 2개의 무게와 같아요. 사과 2개의 무게는 귤 몇 개의 무게와 같을까요?
개구리가 0에서 출발해서 한 번에 2칸씩 뛰어요. 10에 도착하려면 몇 번 뛰어야 할까요?
수 카드 3, 7, 1 중에서 2장을 골라 두 자리 수를 만들려고 해요. 만들 수 있는 가장 큰 수는?
가장 큰 7을 십의 자리에, 그다음 큰 3을 일의 자리에 놓으면 73이에요.
수 카드 0, 4, 8, 2 중에서 2장을 골라 두 자리 수를 만들려고 해요. 만들 수 있는 가장 작은 수는?
0은 십의 자리에 올 수 없어요. 십의 자리에 가장 작은 2, 일의 자리에 0을 놓으면 20이에요.
10원짜리 동전 4개, 50원짜리 동전 1개, 100원짜리 동전 2개가 있어요. 모두 얼마일까요? (숫자만 쓰세요.)
십 모형 5개와 일 모형 13개가 나타내는 수는 얼마일까요?
일 모형 13개는 십 모형 1개와 일 모형 3개와 같아요. 십 모형 6개, 일 모형 3개이므로 63이에요.
민수는 줄넘기를 48번 했어요. 지아는 민수보다 15번 더 했어요. 지아는 줄넘기를 몇 번 했을까요?
500원짜리 동전 1개와 100원짜리 동전 3개가 있어요. 1000원짜리 장난감을 사려면 얼마가 더 필요할까요?
수 카드 5, 2, 9 중에서 2장을 골라 두 자리 수를 만들어요. 세 번째로 큰 수는 무엇일까요?
만들 수 있는 수를 큰 순서로 쓰면 95, 92, 59, 52, 29, 25예요. 세 번째로 큰 수는 59예요.
십의 자리 숫자는 6이고, 일의 자리 숫자는 십의 자리 숫자보다 3 작은 두 자리 수는?
십의 자리 숫자 6, 일의 자리 숫자 6 - 3 = 3이므로 63이에요.
어떤 수에 10을 3번 더했더니 85가 되었어요. 어떤 수는 얼마일까요?
시계가 가리키는 시각은 언제일까요? (짧은바늘은 빨간색, 긴바늘은 파란색이에요.)
시계가 가리키는 시각에서 2시간 30분이 지나면 몇 시 몇 분일까요? (짧은바늘은 빨간색, 긴바늘은 파란색이에요.)
쌓기나무를 쌓고 위에서 본 모양이에요. 칸에 적힌 수는 그 자리에 쌓은 쌓기나무 개수예요. 쌓기나무는 모두 몇 개일까요?

쌓기나무를 쌓고 위에서 본 모양이에요. 칸에 적힌 수는 그 자리에 쌓은 쌓기나무 개수예요. 네 칸 모두 3층이 되게 하려면 쌓기나무가 몇 개 더 필요할까요?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 140 140" width="140" height="140"><rect x="10" y="10" width="60" height="60" fill="#bbdefb" stroke="#0d47a1" stroke-width="3"/><text x="40" y="49" font-size="26" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111111">2</text><rect x="70" y="10" width="60" height="60" fill="#bbdefb" stroke="#0d47a1" stroke-width="3"/><text x="100" y="49" font-size="26" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111111">2</text><rect x="10" y="70" width="60" height="60" fill="#bbdefb" stroke="#0d47a1" stroke-width="3"/><text x="40" y="109" font-size="26" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111111">1</text><rect x="70" y="70" width="60" height="60" fill="#bbdefb" stroke="#0d47a1" stroke-width="3"/><text x="100" y="109" font-size="26" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle" fill="#111111">3</text></svg>
지금은 2 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 8개예요. 네 칸 모두 3층이면 3 × 4 = 12개이므로 12 - 8 = 4개가 더 필요해요. (칸별로 1 + 1 + 2 + 0 = 4개)
다음과 같이 종이를 접었을 때 두 쪽이 꼭 겹치지 않는 것은 무엇일까요?
["세 변의 길이가 같은 세모를 한 꼭짓점과 마주 보는 변의 가운데를 잇는 선으로 접기","정사각형을 마주 보는 두 꼭짓점을 잇는 선으로 접기","동그라미를 가운데를 지나는 선으로 접기","긴 직사각형을 마주 보는 두 꼭짓점을 잇는 선으로 접기"]
정사각형은 대각선으로, 동그라미는 가운데를 지나는 선으로, 정삼각형은 꼭짓점과 마주 보는 변의 가운데를 잇는 선으로 접으면 꼭 겹쳐요. 긴 직사각형은 대각선으로 접으면 삐져나와서 겹치지 않아요.
큰 정사각형을 그림처럼 작은 정사각형 4개로 나누었어요. 그림에서 찾을 수 있는 크고 작은 정사각형은 모두 몇 개일까요?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 180 180" width="180" height="180"><rect x="10" y="10" width="160" height="160" fill="#fff9c4" stroke="#111111" stroke-width="4"/><line x1="90" y1="10" x2="90" y2="170" stroke="#111111" stroke-width="4"/><line x1="10" y1="90" x2="170" y2="90" stroke="#111111" stroke-width="4"/></svg>
작은 정사각형 4개와 전체 큰 정사각형 1개를 합하면 5개예요.
큰 세모의 꼭대기에서 아래 변까지 곧은 선을 하나 그었어요. 그림에서 찾을 수 있는 크고 작은 세모는 모두 몇 개일까요?

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 220 180" width="220" height="180"><polygon points="110,10 10,170 210,170" fill="#c8e6c9" stroke="#111111" stroke-width="4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="110" y1="10" x2="80" y2="170" stroke="#111111" stroke-width="4"/></svg>
나누어진 작은 세모 2개와 전체 큰 세모 1개를 합하면 3개예요.
칠교판은 큰 세모 2개, 중간 세모 1개, 작은 세모 2개, 정사각형 1개, 평행사변형(기울어진 네모) 1개로 되어 있어요. 세모 조각은 모두 몇 개일까요?
큰 세모 2 + 중간 세모 1 + 작은 세모 2 = 5개예요.
칠교판의 작은 세모 2개를 붙여서 똑같이 만들 수 없는 조각은 무엇일까요?
["평행사변형 조각","정사각형 조각","중간 세모 조각","큰 세모 조각"]
작은 세모 2개로 정사각형, 평행사변형, 중간 세모 조각을 만들 수 있어요. 큰 세모 조각은 작은 세모 4개만큼 커서 2개로는 만들 수 없어요.
앞을 보고 서 있다가 오른쪽으로 한 번 돌고(직각만큼), 또 오른쪽으로 한 번 돌았어요(직각만큼). 지금 바라보는 쪽은 처음의 어느 쪽일까요?
오른쪽으로 한 번 돌면 처음의 오른쪽을 보고, 한 번 더 돌면 처음의 뒤쪽을 보게 돼요.

Nadia had promised herself she would not cry at the regional science fair, but when the judge walked past her table without stopping, her throat tightened anyway.

Her project was a water filter constructed from sand, gravel, and activated charcoal packed into a carefully cut plastic bottle. It was not especially impressive to look at. Across the aisle, a boy named Theo had built a robotic arm that poured lemonade into paper cups, and an enthusiastic crowd of parents had gathered around it, laughing and applauding every time another cup filled.

Nadia looked down at her own table, where two jars sat side by side: one full of cloudy brown pond water, the other nearly transparent. She had spent three entire weekends testing different combinations of layers, recording every result in a notebook whose corners had grown soft from constant handling.

"Is this the one that cleans water?"

She looked up to see a girl of about seven standing at the edge of the table, holding her grandmother's hand and pointing at the clear jar as if it were a magic trick.

"It doesn't make it safe to drink," Nadia explained quickly. "But it removes most of the dirt, because the sand catches the larger particles and the charcoal traps substances you can't even see."

The girl's grandmother leaned closer. "Where we lived before, we had to boil everything, every pot, every single morning," she said quietly. "Does a filter like this cost very much?"

The summer I turned twelve, my father decided I was finally old enough to work in his hardware store on Saturday mornings. I imagined myself operating the cash register with the confidence of a bank teller. Instead, he handed me a broom and pointed toward the storage room, where thirty years of sawdust had settled into every corner and crevice.

For the entire first month, I swept. I sorted loose screws into tiny drawers labeled in my father's cramped handwriting, and I discovered that a wood screw and a machine screw look nearly identical until you examine them side by side. I was thoroughly bored, and I made certain that everyone around me knew it.

Then one Saturday in July, an elderly customer arrived holding a broken faucet handle. Because my father was occupied with a delivery, the man turned hopefully to me. I panicked, since I had no idea what the part was called, let alone where to locate it.

But as I turned the handle over in my hands, something clicked. I had sorted a hundred parts exactly like it. I walked confidently to the third aisle, pulled open the drawer second from the bottom, and found a perfect match. The man tested it right there at the counter, and it fit precisely.

"Your father certainly trained you well," he remarked.

I wanted to explain that my father hadn't trained me at all, that I had only been sweeping and sorting. Then I realized that the sweeping and sorting had been exactly the training. Every tedious drawer had been a lesson I didn't know I was taking.

My father never admitted that he had planned it that way, and I never asked him. But the following Saturday, when he handed me the broom, I accepted it without complaining.
What is the central idea of this memoir?

["Customers trust older workers more than younger ones.","A good store must keep its parts sorted in labeled drawers.","Simple, dull tasks can teach skills we don't notice learning.","Children should not be asked to work in a family business."]
The narrator realizes that the sweeping and sorting "had been exactly the training" and that every tedious drawer "had been a lesson I didn't know I was taking."

Every autumn, forests across much of North America turn from green to brilliant shades of red, orange, and gold. Many people assume the leaves are changing into new colors. In fact, many of those colors were present all along.

During spring and summer, leaves are packed with chlorophyll, a green pigment that plants use to capture energy from sunlight. Chlorophyll is so plentiful that it hides the other pigments in the leaf, much as a bright spotlight can wash out the glow of a candle. Among these hidden pigments are carotenoids, which produce yellow and orange. Carotenoids are the same substances that give carrots and corn their color.

As days grow shorter and nights grow cooler, trees prepare for winter. Many trees cannot keep their broad, thin leaves alive through freezing weather, so they begin to shut down food production. The tree stops making new chlorophyll, and the green pigment that remains breaks down. As the green fades, the yellows and oranges finally show through.

Reds and purples work differently. These colors come from pigments called anthocyanins, which many trees produce only in the fall. Scientists believe anthocyanins may act like a sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree pulls valuable nutrients out of it before it drops. Sunny days and cool nights tend to produce the most anthocyanins, which is why some autumns are far more colorful than others.

Eventually, a layer of cells forms where the leaf stem meets the branch. This layer slowly cuts the leaf off from the tree, and the leaf falls. The tree, now bare, will rest until spring, when the cycle begins again.
What is the main idea of the passage?

["Carrots and corn get their color from the same pigments as fall leaves.","Fall colors appear as leaf pigments change while trees prepare for winter.","Trees lose their leaves because freezing weather damages their branches.","Scientists still do not know why leaves change color in the autumn."]
The passage explains how chlorophyll breaks down to reveal yellows and oranges and how anthocyanins add reds as trees get ready for winter.

In the early 1800s, moving goods across New York State was slow and costly. Roads were rough dirt tracks that turned to mud in the rain, and a wagon loaded with grain might take weeks to travel from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic coast. Farmers in the western part of the state often found it cheaper to send their crops south than to ship them east.

Governor DeWitt Clinton believed the answer was a canal: a human-made waterway stretching more than 360 miles from Albany, on the Hudson River, to Buffalo, on Lake Erie. Many people thought the plan was foolish. Critics mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch," and even President Thomas Jefferson reportedly called it "little short of madness."

Construction began in 1817. Workers, many of them recent immigrants, dug the channel largely by hand, using shovels, horses, and simple machines. Engineers had little formal training, so they learned as they went. To carry boats over hills and valleys, they built a series of locks, which are chambers that raise or lower boats by filling or draining water.

When the canal opened in 1825, the doubters were quickly proven wrong. Mule-drawn boats could now carry goods from Buffalo to New York City in a fraction of the time, and shipping costs dropped dramatically. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew rapidly along the canal's banks. New York City became the busiest port in the nation, and settlers poured into the Midwest, knowing their crops could reach eastern markets.

Within a few decades, railroads began to replace canals as the fastest way to move freight. Yet the Erie Canal had already done its work. It had shown that a bold public project could reshape the economy of an entire region.
Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

["Railroads were a better invention than canals in the 1800s.","Building a canal by hand was dangerous work for immigrants.","DeWitt Clinton was the most popular governor in New York history.","Though many doubted it, the Erie Canal transformed trade and growth."]
The passage describes the doubts about the canal and then shows how it cut shipping costs, grew towns, and made New York City the busiest port.

The house had been sold in October, and by the second week of November only the study remained. Elena had deliberately left it for last, the way a student postpones the most difficult problem on an examination, hoping that by the time she reached it she would somehow have acquired a competence she had lacked at the beginning.

Her father had worked as a land surveyor for forty years, and the room bore abundant evidence of his profession: rolled maps bound with rubber bands gone brittle, a brass compass whose needle still trembled faithfully toward the window, and shelf after shelf of field notebooks, each meticulously labeled with a county and a year. She had expected to feel grief here; what she had not anticipated was irritation. He had preserved everything, from receipts for pencils to weather reports clipped from newspapers that no longer existed, as if the world might someday require him to document precisely where he had been on any particular afternoon.

She opened a notebook at random. Columns of numbers, angles and distances, filled the pages in his small, upright handwriting, and then, in the margin beside a measurement from 1987, appeared a note in the same hand: Lena lost first tooth today; measured the creek bend twice and kept losing count.

Elena sat down slowly on the dusty floor, the notebook open across her knees.

She reached for another. Beside a boundary line in a neighboring county he had written: Lena said "Dad" on the telephone, not "Daddy," noted. Beside a hillside elevation recorded years afterward: Drove Lena to the train station; instruments functioning properly, hands not steady.

For an hour she turned pages, and the precise columns gradually receded until she perceived only the margins, a second survey running alongside the first, charting a territory he had never once described aloud. She had always believed her father was a man who measured things because he was incapable of speaking about them. Now she understood that he had been speaking all along, in the only notation he trusted, to a reader he perhaps never expected to arrive.

When the movers came the following morning, she had already packed the notebooks into her own car. The maps, the compass, and the receipts she allowed them to take.
Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?

["Grief is easier to bear when a person stays busy with practical tasks.","Love may be expressed in quiet ways that others discover only later.","Children rarely appreciate the careers their parents have chosen.","Careful record keeping is the most important part of any profession."]

Elena had deliberately left it for last, the way a student postpones the most difficult problem on an examination, hoping that by the time she reached it she would somehow have acquired a competence she had lacked at the beginning.

Her father had worked as a land surveyor for forty years, and the room bore abundant evidence of his profession: rolled maps bound with rubber bands gone brittle, a brass compass whose needle still trembled faithfully toward the window, and shelf after shelf of field notebooks, each meticulously labeled with a county and a year. She had expected to feel grief here; what she had not anticipated was irritation. He had preserved everything, from receipts for pencils to weather reports clipped from newspapers that no longer existed, as if the world might someday require him to document precisely where he had been on any particular afternoon.

She opened a notebook at random. Columns of numbers, angles and distances, filled the pages in his small, upright handwriting, and then, in the margin beside a measurement from 1987, appeared a note in the same hand: Lena lost first tooth today; measured the creek bend twice and kept losing count.

Elena sat down slowly on the dusty floor, the notebook open across her knees.

She reached for another. Beside a boundary line in a neighboring county he had written: Lena said "Dad" on the telephone, not "Daddy," noted. Beside a hillside elevation recorded years afterward: Drove Lena to the train station; instruments functioning properly, hands not steady.

For an hour she turned pages, and the precise columns gradually receded until she perceived only the margins, a second survey running alongside the first, charting a territory he had never once described aloud. She had always believed her father was a man who measured things because he was incapable of speaking about them. Now she understood that he had been speaking all along, in the only notation he trusted, to a reader he perhaps never expected to arrive.

Winter Orchard

The orchard holds its breath in February,
each branch a dark sentence left unfinished,
written in a hand the frost keeps correcting,
while snow has filed the hills down to a whisper.

My grandfather walked these rows for fifty years,
pruning with the deliberate patience of a man
who trusted what he could not see:
the sap asleep inside the bark like ink
inside a capped pen, waiting.

Now the ladders lean against the empty shed,
their rungs gone silver with disuse,
and crows convene on the fence posts
like a council that has misplaced its agenda.

Still, I have learned to read the bark:
beneath each knot, a bud is clenched
as tightly as a fist around a coin,
and the coin is April.

So I walk the rows the way he walked them,
not to harvest anything,
but to keep the promise the trees are keeping,
to stand in the cold and believe in green.

["Crows and frost slowly destroy an orchard that has been abandoned.","The speaker regrets never learning to prune trees in the old way.","Farming is too difficult to continue in harsh winter climates.","The speaker inherits a patient faith in renewal from a grandfather."]
The speaker walks the rows "the way he walked them" to "believe in green," echoing the grandfather who "trusted what he could not see."

In an age of disposable goods, the ability to fix things has quietly vanished from many households. When a toaster stops working or a chair wobbles, the most common response is not to open it up but to throw it away and order a replacement. Schools, which once routinely offered shop classes and home economics, have largely abandoned instruction in practical repair. This is a mistake, and it is one that schools should correct by making basic repair skills part of the standard curriculum.

The first argument for teaching repair is economic. Replacing an appliance often costs many times more than replacing the small part that failed. A student who can diagnose a broken hinge or a frayed cord gains a skill that will save money for the rest of his or her life, a lesson in financial independence more concrete than any worksheet on budgeting.

The second argument is environmental. Discarded electronics and furniture accumulate in landfills at an alarming rate, and the manufacture of each replacement consumes energy and raw materials. Every object that is repaired rather than replaced represents a small reduction in waste. Multiplied across millions of households, those small reductions become significant.

Critics contend that the school day is already crowded and that time spent on repair would come at the expense of academic subjects. This objection, however, rests on a false distinction. Repairing a device requires reading technical diagrams, forming and testing hypotheses, and applying principles of physics and geometry. Far from distracting students from academic learning, repair puts that learning to work in a setting where mistakes have visible consequences and success is immediately apparent.

Finally, repair cultivates a disposition that extends beyond any single object: the conviction that problems can be understood and solved through patient investigation. Students who learn that a silent radio can be coaxed back to life may approach other challenges, whether in science, in their communities, or in their own lives, with the same confidence.

The objects around us were designed by people, and they can be understood by people. Schools should ensure that every graduate leaves knowing it.

The first paragraph ends by stating schools "should correct" the mistake "by making basic repair skills part of the standard curriculum."

On a summer afternoon, the downtown core of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, and after sunset the difference may grow even larger. Climate scientists call this phenomenon the urban heat island effect, and as cities expand and summers intensify, understanding it has become a matter of public health.

The effect arises primarily from the materials cities are built with. Asphalt, concrete, and dark roofing absorb a large fraction of incoming sunlight and store it as heat. Whereas vegetation releases moisture through its leaves, a process called evapotranspiration that cools the surrounding air much as perspiration cools the skin, paved surfaces offer no such relief. Tall buildings compound the problem by trapping warm air in narrow streets and by blocking breezes that would otherwise disperse it. Heat generated by vehicles, air conditioners, and industry adds still more.

Perhaps counterintuitively, the heat island is often most pronounced at night. Throughout the day, dense urban materials accumulate thermal energy; after dark, they release it slowly, keeping city temperatures elevated long after rural areas have cooled. This nighttime warmth carries real consequences. The human body depends on cooler nighttime temperatures to recover from daytime heat, and during prolonged heat waves, the absence of that relief contributes to heat-related illness, particularly among elderly residents and those without air conditioning.

Fortunately, the factors that create heat islands also suggest remedies. Cities on several continents have experimented with "cool roofs," coated with reflective materials that bounce sunlight back into the sky rather than absorbing it. Others have expanded tree canopies, converted vacant lots into parks, and replaced conventional pavement with lighter or more porous alternatives. Researchers caution that no single strategy is sufficient; the most effective approaches combine several interventions and prioritize the neighborhoods where residents are most vulnerable.

The urban heat island is, in a sense, a problem of design. Because people built the conditions that produce it, people can also rebuild them.

The article explains how urban materials and buildings cause extra heat, describes health risks, and ends by saying people "can also rebuild" these conditions.

The following is a fictional letter in the style of the 1880s, written by a young teacher on the Nebraska prairie to her sister in Ohio.

October 14, 1883

Dearest Margaret,

You asked in your last letter whether I regret coming west, and I confess I have delayed my reply because I wished to answer honestly rather than merely cheerfully. The schoolhouse is constructed of sod, which is to say of the prairie itself, cut into rectangular blocks and stacked like bricks. Whenever it rains, the roof weeps mud upon the readers, and I have learned to arrange the benches according to the leaks rather than the ages of my pupils.

I have nineteen scholars enrolled, though rarely all of them at once. During planting and harvest the older boys are required in the fields, and I cannot in good conscience scold them for their absence, since their families' survival depends upon the crop considerably more than upon the multiplication tables. Several of the children speak German or Norwegian at home and are acquiring English alongside their arithmetic. Last week little Anna Halvorsen read an entire page aloud without assistance, and her mother, who had come to fetch her, wept openly at the door; I own that I did as well.

Loneliness is the most difficult trial of this existence. The nearest neighbor lives two miles distant, and in the evenings the wind across the grass produces a sound so continuous that one ceases to hear it until it stops, whereupon the silence becomes nearly unbearable. I reread your letters until the folds wear through.

And yet, dear Margaret, I do not regret my decision. In Ohio I was merely one teacher among many, and I occasionally wondered whether my absence would be noticed at all. Here, if I do not open the door in the morning, there is simply no school. I have never before been so exhausted, nor so entirely certain that my labor mattered.

Please send more thread and, if you can possibly spare it, a geography book with good maps, for ours ends at the Mississippi.

Your loving sister,
Clara
What is Clara's main message to her sister?

["Despite real hardships, she values the importance of her work.","Her students' families do not support the school or its teacher.","Teaching on the prairie is far easier than teaching in Ohio.","She plans to return to Ohio once the school year has ended."]
Clara describes leaks and loneliness but concludes, "I do not regret my decision," because she has never been "so entirely certain that my labor mattered."

The following is a fictional letter in the style of the 1880s, written by a young teacher on the Nebraska prairie to her sister in Ohio.

October 14, 1883

Dearest Margaret,

You asked in your last letter whether I regret coming west, and I confess I have delayed my reply because I wished to answer honestly rather than merely cheerfully. The schoolhouse is constructed of sod, which is to say of the prairie itself, cut into rectangular blocks and stacked like bricks. Whenever it rains, the roof weeps mud upon the readers, and I have learned to arrange the benches according to the leaks rather than the ages of my pupils.

I have nineteen scholars enrolled, though rarely all of them at once. During planting and harvest the older boys are required in the fields, and I cannot in good conscience scold them for their absence, since their families' survival depends upon the crop considerably more than upon the multiplication tables. Several of the children speak German or Norwegian at home and are acquiring English alongside their arithmetic. Last week little Anna Halvorsen read an entire page aloud without assistance, and her mother, who had come to fetch her, wept openly at the door; I own that I did as well.

Please send more thread and, if you can possibly spare it, a geography book with good maps, for ours ends at the Mississippi.

Your loving sister,
Clara

The shop smelled of oil and old paper, and Mara had stopped noticing either by the third week. Her grandfather worked at the bench beneath the window, a loupe screwed into one eye, his breath slowed to the rhythm of whatever movement lay open before him. He did not speak while he worked, and at first Mara had taken his silence for disapproval. She had arrived in June with a suitcase and a sullen certainty that the summer was a punishment.

On Thursday a woman brought in a mantel clock wrapped in a bath towel. It had belonged to her mother, she said, and it had not run in eleven years. Her grandfather lifted it from the towel the way one might lift a sleeping cat.

"Will it be expensive?" the woman asked.

"It will be slow," he said, which was not an answer, though the woman seemed to accept it as one.

After she left, he slid the clock across the bench toward Mara. She stared at it. In three weeks he had let her sort screws, wind finished pieces, and sweep. He had never let her open anything.

"The case first," he said. "Then you tell me what you see. Not what you think. What you see."

Mara reached for the smallest screwdriver, and her hand, she noticed, was not quite steady.

Every spring, mayors across the country pose with shovels beside freshly planted saplings, announcing goals of ten thousand or a million new trees. The photographs are pleasant, and the ambition is sincere. Yet the obsession with planting obscures a less glamorous truth: a young street tree is a liability before it becomes an asset. In its first three years, it needs regular watering, staking, and protection from mowers and road salt. Without that care, a significant share of newly planted trees in some cities die before they ever cast meaningful shade.

Mature trees, by contrast, deliver benefits that saplings cannot match for decades. A single large oak intercepts far more stormwater, cools far more pavement, and filters far more air than a dozen thin saplings planted in its place. Yet when a sidewalk needs repair or a utility line needs space, the old tree is often the first thing removed, because replacing it with a sapling counts as "no net loss" on a city's spreadsheet.

Cities should therefore measure their urban forests not by how many trees they plant but by how much canopy they sustain. That shift would redirect money toward maintenance crews, watering programs, and engineering solutions that let sidewalks and roots coexist. It would make for duller ribbon cuttings. It would also make for cooler, greener streets.
Which statement best expresses the central claim of the passage?

["Mayors should stop attending tree-planting ceremonies because they waste public money.","Sidewalk repairs are the main reason that urban trees die.","Cities should judge urban forests by the canopy they sustain rather than by the number of trees they plant.","Young street trees are more valuable than mature trees because they live longer."]
The author's concluding paragraph explicitly argues that cities should measure success "not by how many trees they plant but by how much canopy they sustain."

Every spring, mayors across the country pose with shovels beside freshly planted saplings, announcing goals of ten thousand or a million new trees. The photographs are pleasant, and the ambition is sincere. Yet the obsession with planting obscures a less glamorous truth: a young street tree is a liability before it becomes an asset. In its first three years, it needs regular watering, staking, and protection from mowers and road salt. Without that care, a significant share of newly planted trees in some cities die before they ever cast meaningful shade.

Mature trees, by contrast, deliver benefits that saplings cannot match for decades. A single large oak intercepts far more stormwater, cools far more pavement, and filters far more air than a dozen thin saplings planted in its place. Yet when a sidewalk needs repair or a utility line needs space, the old tree is often the first thing removed, because replacing it with a sapling counts as "no net loss" on a city's spreadsheet.

Cities should therefore measure their urban forests not by how many trees they plant but by how much canopy they sustain. That shift would redirect money toward maintenance crews, watering programs, and engineering solutions that let sidewalks and roots coexist. It would make for duller ribbon cuttings. It would also make for cooler, greener streets.

To the Honorable Council of the Town of Ashford Mills,

Gentlemen,—I have this week completed the survey you commissioned regarding the proposed extension of the canal to the northern quarries, and I must, in candor, report that the undertaking is neither so simple nor so cheap as the petition laid before you has represented. The petitioners estimate the cost at eleven thousand dollars. I cannot, in good conscience, place it below nineteen.

The difficulty lies chiefly in the ground itself. Beyond the second mile, the soil gives way to a broken shale which will not hold water without lining, and the lining alone will consume a sum the petitioners have omitted entirely. Moreover, the rise toward the quarries requires not two locks, as they suppose, but four.

I do not write to discourage the enterprise. The quarries are rich, and a waterway would reduce the cost of hauling stone by more than half, to the lasting benefit of every merchant in the town. I write only so that the Council may decide with its eyes open rather than be persuaded by figures that will not survive the first season of digging. An honest estimate disappoints once; a dishonest one disappoints every quarter until the work is abandoned.

I remain, Gentlemen, your obedient servant,
Josiah Whitcombe, Engineer

["to correct an unrealistically low cost estimate while still supporting the project if it is honestly funded","to persuade the Council to reject the canal extension entirely","to request payment for the survey he has completed","to accuse the petitioners of attempting to defraud the town"]
He states that the petitioners' figures are too low but adds, "I do not write to discourage the enterprise," showing he wants an informed decision rather than a rejection.

Lichens look like little more than crusty stains on rocks and bark, but they are among the most sensitive living instruments scientists possess. A lichen is not a single organism but a partnership: a fungus provides structure and shelter, while an alga or cyanobacterium supplies food through photosynthesis. Because lichens have no roots and no waxy outer layer, they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air—and, with them, whatever pollutants the air carries.

This vulnerability makes lichens useful. Species differ sharply in their tolerance for sulfur dioxide and nitrogen compounds. Shrubby, branching lichens tend to vanish first as pollution increases, while flat, crusty species persist in dirtier conditions. By surveying which forms grow on trees in a given area, researchers can estimate air quality without installing expensive monitoring equipment.

The method has limits. Lichens grow slowly, so a survey reflects conditions over years rather than days; a sudden spike in pollution may not register at all. Local factors such as humidity and bark acidity also influence which species thrive, so a sparse lichen community does not automatically indicate dirty air. Researchers therefore treat lichen surveys as a complement to instrument readings, not a replacement—an inexpensive way to map broad patterns and identify places where closer monitoring is warranted.

The passage explains why lichens reveal air quality and then outlines the method's limits, presenting lichens as a valuable but imperfect tool.

Tidewater

Twice a day the river forgets which way it runs.
The salt comes shouldering up from the bay,
patient as a creditor, and the brown water
turns back on itself as if remembering
some errand it left undone upstream.

My grandmother said the marsh keeps two clocks:
one for the sun, one for the moon,
and that a person raised here learns to read both—
when to set the crab pots, when the mud
will hold a boot and when it will keep it.

I have stood on bridges in other cities
and watched the current slide beneath me, sure
and single, carrying its leaves away,
and felt almost sorry for it, never once
asked to turn around.

I live inland now, where rivers know their minds.
They hurry one direction, plain as a sentence.
But some nights, lying awake, I feel it still:
the slow pull backward, the long hesitation,
the water deciding, again, to come home.

["moves quickly and unpredictably through the river","returns steadily and inevitably, as if to collect what it is owed","is weak compared with the force of the river","is generous to the people who live along the marsh"]
A creditor waits calmly but always comes back to collect, which mirrors the tide's slow, certain return twice a day.

Popular history loves a solitary genius. We picture the inventor alone in a workshop at midnight, struck by inspiration that no one else could have summoned. The image flatters our sense of drama, but it distorts how discovery actually happens. Nearly every celebrated breakthrough was preceded by years of incremental work by people whose names have faded, and many were reached almost simultaneously by rivals working independently—a sign that the idea was, in a sense, ready to be found.

This matters for more than historical accuracy. When students absorb the myth of the lone genius, they learn to see talent as a lightning strike that either hits them or does not. Those who struggle conclude that they simply lack the spark, and they quit. Meanwhile, institutions that believe in lone geniuses pour resources into identifying a few stars rather than building the collaborative environments in which most good ideas actually emerge.

None of this means individuals do not matter; some people do see further or work harder than their peers. But we should tell the story of discovery as it usually unfolds: as a relay rather than a sprint, with each runner carrying the baton a little further before handing it on.

For much of the twentieth century, sleep was regarded as a kind of shutdown—a period when the brain, like an idle engine, simply rested. Research over the past several decades has overturned that view. During sleep, and especially during the deep, slow-wave stages that dominate the early part of the night, the brain appears to replay patterns of activity first generated during waking experience.

In studies with rodents, scientists recorded neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, while animals explored a maze. Later, as the animals slept, the same neurons fired in the same sequences, often compressed into a fraction of the original time. Disrupting these replay events tended to impair the animals' performance when they returned to the maze the next day.

Human studies point in a similar direction. Volunteers who learn a list of word pairs and then sleep typically recall more of them than volunteers who spend the same interval awake. Some experiments have even played faint sounds associated with specific learned material during deep sleep and found that the cued items were remembered better.

Researchers caution that much remains uncertain. Replay has been observed most clearly in animals, and the precise mechanisms linking it to human memory are still debated. Still, the evidence has decisively retired the idle-engine metaphor.

["Rodent studies have proved exactly how human memories are stored during sleep.","Once considered a passive state, sleep is now understood to play an active role in memory, though important details remain uncertain.","Playing sounds during sleep is the most effective way for students to learn new material.","Sleep is a period when the brain shuts down so that it can recover energy."]
The passage describes the overturning of the "idle engine" view and presents evidence for memory replay while noting that mechanisms are still debated.

During sleep, and especially during the deep, slow-wave stages that dominate the early part of the night, the brain appears to replay patterns of activity first generated during waking experience.

In studies with rodents, scientists recorded neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, while animals explored a maze. Later, as the animals slept, the same neurons fired in the same sequences, often compressed into a fraction of the original time. Disrupting these replay events tended to impair the animals' performance when they returned to the maze the next day.

Human studies point in a similar direction. Volunteers who learn a list of word pairs and then sleep typically recall more of them than volunteers who spend the same interval awake. Some experiments have even played faint sounds associated with specific learned material during deep sleep and found that the cued items were remembered better.

Researchers caution that much remains uncertain. Replay has been observed most clearly in animals, and the precise mechanisms linking it to human memory are still debated. Still, the evidence has decisively retired the idle-engine metaphor.

["enthusiastic to the point of ignoring the evidence's limitations","dismissive of animal studies as irrelevant to humans","doubtful that sleep has any connection to memory","confident about the overall shift in understanding but careful to note unresolved questions"]
The author says the evidence "decisively retired" the old view while also stating that "much remains uncertain."
