["The ground under big plants is too hard.","Animals eat all the seeds near big plants.","The wind blows those seeds away too quickly.","The parent plant blocks the sun and takes the water."]
The first paragraph says the big plant "blocks the sunlight and drinks up most of the water."

Wilson Bentley grew up on a farm in Vermont in the 1870s, where winters were long and snowy. Most people saw snow as cold, wet stuff to shovel. Wilson saw something different. He believed that every snowflake was a tiny work of art.

When Wilson was fifteen, his mother gave him an old microscope, and he used it to look at snowflakes up close. He tried to draw what he saw, but the flakes melted too quickly. He needed a better way.

Wilson wanted a special camera that could take pictures through a microscope. Such a camera cost a lot of money, but his parents helped him buy one. Then he spent two whole winters failing, because his pictures came out blurry or blank. Still, he did not give up. At last, on a January day in 1885, he took a clear photograph of a single snowflake. It was one of the first ever taken.

For the rest of his life, Wilson took pictures of snowflakes. He caught them on a black tray and moved them with a feather so they would not break. He took more than five thousand pictures, and he never found two flakes that were exactly alike.

Some neighbors laughed at the farmer who spent his days studying snow. Today, people call him "Snowflake Bentley," and scientists still study his photographs.
Why did Wilson want a camera?
["He wanted to sell pictures to his neighbors.","His mother asked him to take photos of the farm.","The snowflakes melted before he could draw them.","His microscope was broken and needed a fix."]
He "tried to draw what he saw, but the flakes melted too quickly," so he "needed a better way."

After the Rain

The rain has gone, the clouds have run,
and a puddle sits beside the sun.
It holds the sky and a tall green tree
and a smiling face that looks like me.

A robin hops down to take a sip,
and a leaf sails by like a tiny ship.
A beetle walking around the rim
stops and wonders if it should swim.

I jump right in, and the pictures shake!
The tree goes wiggly in my wake.
But if I stand still, I will soon see
the sky come back, and the tree, and me.

By noon the sun will drink it dry,
and I will have to find the sky
the old way, high above my head,
and not down at my feet instead.
In the first stanza, when the puddle "holds the sky," it means the puddle
["has caught some falling rain","is hiding under a cloud","shows a reflection of the sky","is as large as the whole sky"]
The puddle also holds "a smiling face that looks like me," which shows it is reflecting what is above it like a mirror.

On the evening of my first piano recital, I wore shoes that pinched and a collar that itched, and I could not stop counting the rows of folding chairs in the auditorium. There were twelve rows, and I counted them four separate times while the younger students performed their short, bouncy songs.

My piece was a slow waltz that I had practiced every afternoon for three months. I had memorized it so completely that I could play it while thinking about something else entirely, which, my teacher warned me, was exactly the problem. "Knowing the notes with your fingers is not the same as knowing them with your head," Mrs. Okafor had told me. I had nodded politely, but I had not really been listening.

When my name was announced, I walked across the stage to the piano and sat down. The first page went smoothly, but halfway through the second page, my mind went completely blank. My fingers continued moving for a moment, the way your feet keep going after you miss a step on the stairs, and then they stopped.

The silence seemed to last for an hour, although it was probably about three seconds. I could hear someone's chair creak in the audience, and I could hear my own heartbeat. Then I remembered another piece of advice Mrs. Okafor used to give us: "If you get lost, don't go back. Find the next place you know and land there."

I skipped ahead to the final section, a passage I had practiced so many times that I could have hummed it in my sleep. My hands located the correct keys, and the waltz returned, a little shaky at first and then steady, and I played it all the way to the end.

Afterward, I expected Mrs. Okafor to be disappointed in me; instead, she shook my hand as if I were a grown-up. "Anyone can play a piece when nothing goes wrong," she said. "Tonight you learned how to keep going when something does."

I still get nervous before every performance, but now, along with the notes, I also practice the landing places.
In the first paragraph, the narrator's repeated counting of the chairs mainly suggests that the narrator
["was in charge of setting up the room","hoped very few people would come","disliked the younger students' songs","felt nervous while waiting to perform"]
Along with pinching shoes and an itchy collar, the narrator "could not stop counting" the chairs, a sign of restless nerves before playing.

Theo had been the strongest chess player in the after-school club for two consecutive years, so when Ms. Varga paired him with a third grader named June for the first match of the season, he almost felt sorry for her.

June was so small that she had to kneel on her chair to reach the far side of the board. She said very little, simply moving her pieces quietly, one after another, and recording each move in a spiral notebook with a purple pencil.

Theo played rapidly, the way he always did. He preferred to attack early, sending his knights and queen forward to put pressure on his opponent before the other player had settled in. Most of his opponents panicked and made careless mistakes, but June did not panic. Every time Theo threatened one of her pieces, she calmly moved it to safety or blocked the attack, and then she returned to strengthening her position, pawn by pawn.

By the twentieth move, Theo realized that his attack had run out of energy. His pieces were scattered across the board, while June's were organized like a sturdy wall. Ten moves later, she quietly announced, "Checkmate."

Theo stared at the board in disbelief, and he felt his face grow hot. For a moment, he wanted to explain that he had not really been trying, or that he was exhausted. Instead, he took a deep breath and asked, "Can you show me what you were doing?"

June's eyes lit up. She flipped open her notebook and walked him through the entire game, move by move, pointing out the exact moment when his queen had wandered too far from home. She explained that her grandfather had taught her to "build the house before you open the door."

That evening, Theo set up the board on his kitchen table and replayed the game twice. He was still the strongest player in the club. But for the first time in a long while, he felt like a beginner again, and to his surprise, he did not mind at all.
At the beginning of the story, Theo most likely expects to
["lose because June is a known champion","be paired with an older player","quit the chess club after this season","win the match against June easily"]
Theo is the club's strongest player and "almost felt sorry" for June, showing he expects an easy win.

If you scoop up a clump of damp moss and look at it under a microscope, you may find one of the toughest animals on the planet. It has eight stubby legs, each tipped with tiny claws, and it moves with a slow, rolling walk. Scientists call it a tardigrade, a name that means "slow stepper." Most people know it by its nickname: the water bear.

Water bears are tiny, usually less than a millimeter long, which is about the size of the period at the end of this sentence. They live almost everywhere: in moss and lichen, in soil, in the deep sea, and even on mountaintops. Yet what makes them remarkable is not where they live but what they can survive.

Like all animals, water bears need water to stay active. When their home dries out, however, they do not simply die. Instead, they pull in their legs, curl into a tight, dry ball called a tun, and let almost all the water leave their bodies. In this state, their metabolism, the set of chemical processes that keeps an animal alive, slows to nearly nothing. A water bear can stay as a tun for years. When water returns, it can swell back up and begin walking again within hours.

As tuns, water bears have survived conditions that would destroy most living things. In laboratory tests, they have lived through temperatures far below freezing, strong doses of radiation, and crushing pressure. Every autumn, the forests of many northern regions seem to catch fire with color. Maples blaze orange and red, birches turn gold, and oaks fade to a deep rusty brown. It might seem as though the trees are painting their leaves for the season. In fact, much of the color was there all along.

During spring and summer, leaves are packed with a green pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs sunlight and helps the tree turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar, the food it needs to grow. Because a leaf contains so much chlorophyll, its green color hides other pigments that are also present. Among these are carotenoids, the same yellow and orange pigments found in carrots and corn.

As the days grow shorter and the nights grow cooler, trees prepare for winter. They begin to seal off the connection between each leaf and its branch. Without fresh supplies, the chlorophyll breaks down and is not replaced. As the green fades, the yellows and oranges that were hidden underneath finally show through.

Reds and purples work differently. These colors come from pigments called anthocyanins, and most of them are not present in summer at all. Some trees make them in autumn, when sugars become trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days followed by cool nights tend to produce the most anthocyanins, which is why some autumns are especially vivid while others look dull.

Eventually, the leaves dry out and drop. This loss may look like a sad ending, but it is actually a clever survival strategy. Without its leaves, a tree loses far less water during the frozen months, when water in the ground is hard to reach. In spring, it will grow a fresh set, and the cycle will begin again.

["colors that trees absorb from sunlight","red pigments that trees store all summer","yellow and orange pigments hidden by green chlorophyll","brown spots that form on leaves in spring"]
The second and third paragraphs explain that carotenoids are present but hidden until "the yellows and oranges that were hidden underneath finally show through."

In the early 1800s, moving goods across the young United States was slow and expensive. Roads were rough dirt tracks that turned to mud in the rain, and wagons pulled by horses could carry only small loads. Shipping a ton of flour from Buffalo, on Lake Erie, to New York City could take weeks and cost far more than the flour itself was worth.

Some leaders proposed a bold solution: a canal, a human-made waterway, stretching more than 350 miles across New York State, from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. Many people thought the idea was foolish. The route crossed forests, swamps, and hills, and the nation had few trained engineers. Critics mockingly called the project "Clinton's Ditch," after the state's governor, who supported it.

Construction began in 1817. Thousands of workers, many of them recent immigrants, dug the channel largely by hand, using shovels, picks, and teams of horses and oxen. Because the land between the Hudson and Lake Erie rises by several hundred feet, the builders constructed locks, chambers with gates at each end that raise or lower boats from one water level to another. Along the way, the workers and their self-taught engineers invented new tools, such as a machine for pulling tree stumps out of the ground.

When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it was an immediate success. Flat-bottomed boats, pulled by mules walking along a path beside the water, carried cargo across the state in a fraction of the old time. The cost of shipping fell by roughly ninety percent. Farmers in the Midwest could now sell their crops in eastern cities, and manufactured goods flowed west in return.

The canal changed the map of the nation. Towns along its route, such as Rochester and Syracuse, grew rapidly. New York City became the busiest port in the country. The "ditch" that critics had laughed at had become one of the most important building projects of its time.

["to explain how a canal lock raises and lowers boats","to tell the life story of the governor of New York","to describe how the Erie Canal was built and how it changed the nation","to argue that canals were better than railroads"]
The passage moves from the problem of shipping, through construction, to the canal's success and how it "changed the map of the nation."

When most people think of a library, they picture shelves of books and a quiet reading room. But a growing number of public libraries now lend out much more: sewing machines, telescopes, cake pans, garden tools, even musical instruments. These collections are sometimes called "libraries of things." I believe every community should have one.

The first reason is simple: many useful objects sit unused most of the time. A family might need a power drill for one afternoon to hang shelves, then leave it in a closet for a year. A ukulele might be played for a week before its owner loses interest. When a library owns these items, dozens of families can share a single one. Each household spends less money, and fewer objects end up in landfills.

Second, a library of things makes it easier to try something new. A child who is curious about the stars may not be able to afford a telescope. A grown-up who wants to learn to bake bread may not want to buy an expensive mixer before knowing whether baking is fun. Borrowing removes the risk. Just as a library book lets a reader explore a subject without buying a whole shelf, a borrowed tool lets a person explore a hobby without a large expense.

Some critics argue that libraries should stick to books and that lending objects is too costly or complicated. It is true that a telescope is harder to repair than a paperback. However, many libraries have found that the items last surprisingly well. Local businesses and volunteers often donate equipment or help with repairs. Besides, libraries have always changed with the times. They once lent only printed books; today they lend movies, audiobooks, and e-books. Lending objects is simply the next step.

At its heart, a library is built on a generous idea: that sharing makes a community richer. A library of things takes that idea and puts it into people's hands, quite literally. I hope that the next time you visit your library, you will be able to check out a book about birds and a pair of binoculars to go with it.
The author's main purpose is to
["argue that every community should have a library of things","compare the costs of books and tools","explain how to repair a borrowed telescope","describe the history of public libraries"]
The first paragraph states, "I believe every community should have one," and the rest gives reasons.

Each household spends less money, and fewer objects end up in landfills.

Second, a library of things makes it easier to try something new. A child who is curious about the stars may not be able to afford a telescope. A grown-up who wants to learn to bake bread may not want to buy an expensive mixer before knowing whether baking is fun. Borrowing removes the risk. Just as a library book lets a reader explore a subject without buying a whole shelf, a borrowed tool lets a person explore a hobby without a large expense.

Some critics argue that libraries should stick to books and that lending objects is too costly or complicated. It is true that a telescope is harder to repair than a paperback. However, many libraries have found that the items last surprisingly well. Local businesses and volunteers often donate equipment or help with repairs. Besides, libraries have always changed with the times. They once lent only printed books; today they lend movies, audiobooks, and e-books. Lending objects is simply the next step.

At its heart, a library is built on a generous idea: that sharing makes a community richer. A library of things takes that idea and puts it into people's hands, quite literally. The violin arrived in a cardboard box lined with crumpled newspaper, its neck snapped cleanly from the body and its delicate top split along the grain like a dry riverbed. Ines lifted it out with both hands, as if it might still feel pain, and laid it on the felt-covered bench where Mr. Halloran performed his most meticulous restorations.

In the eleven months she had served as his apprentice, she had learned to sharpen chisels until they could shave a translucent curl from the end grain of spruce, to warm animal glue in a double boiler that smelled faintly of a barn, and, above all, to wait. Mr. Halloran did nothing hurriedly: he would examine a single crack for an entire morning before touching it, rotating the instrument beneath the lamp and running a fingertip along its edge as though deciphering a sentence written in a language only he understood.

When she finally asked whether it could be saved, he did not answer immediately; instead, he held the violin up to the window, and the afternoon light passed through the thin wood of the top, revealing a faint amber map of earlier repairs: a reinforcing cleat here, a patch there, the ghostly outline of a crack mended long before either of them was born.

"Look," he said, tracing the oldest of the patches with his finger. "Someone has already rescued it, three times, perhaps four. Whoever did this was not as careful as he might have been, but he was careful enough, and the violin kept singing."

Ines had expected him to criticize the earlier workmanship, as he frequently criticized hers. Instead, his voice contained something remarkably close to gratitude. It occurred to her that he was speaking not only of the violin's previous menders but also of himself, and perhaps of her as well: of all the imperfect hands an instrument passes through on its long journey from one century to the next.

They labored over the violin for six weeks, and Mr. Halloran permitted her to fit the new cleats along the split, small diamonds of spruce positioned crosswise to the grain, and he did not correct her once, although she noticed him look twice at the third one. When at last the strings were tuned and he drew the bow across them, the sound that emerged was not flawless; it possessed a slight roughness in the lower register, like a voice that has lingered too long in the cold.

"There," he said, handing the instrument to her with unexpected ceremony. "Now you are part of its history too."

That night, walking home through the darkening streets, Ines discovered that she was not thinking about the roughness at all. She was imagining some future apprentice, decades from now, holding the violin up to a window and discovering her small diamonds glowing in the light.
The detail that Ines lifts the violin "as if it might still feel pain" primarily conveys her
["fear that she will be blamed for the damage","impatience to begin working on it","tender respect for the damaged instrument","doubt that the violin can be repaired"]
Treating the broken violin as though it were a living, injured thing shows gentleness and reverence, consistent with her careful placement of it on the felt bench.

The Cartographer's Daughter

My father drew the coastlines of the world
from other people's journeys, never his:
the jagged inlets sailors had reported,
the islands rumored, half-imagined, named
for patrons who would never see them either.
He worked by lamplight, patient as the tide,
correcting capes by fractions of a degree.

I asked him once if it unsettled him
to chart a shoreline he could never verify.
He smiled and lifted up his finest pen.
"Each map," he said, "is someone's best belief,
recorded honestly, and then revised.
The world is always larger than the paper;
the error is in thinking we are finished."

Now, decades later, holding the exacting
photograph a satellite has taken,
I find his careful coastline wandering
a mile too far into the open water.
I do not mark it wrong; I trace it slowly,
the way one reads a treasured, faded letter,
and recognize the honesty of distance,
the faith of someone drawing what he was told
who left a margin for the truth to enter.
According to the first stanza, the father's maps were based mainly on
["guesses he made without any information","reports from other people's travels","photographs taken from above","his own voyages along the coasts"]
He drew coastlines "from other people's journeys, never his," using inlets "sailors had reported."

Every autumn, a small songbird called the European robin leaves its breeding grounds in Scandinavia and flies south toward the Mediterranean, often traveling at night and across unfamiliar terrain. Young birds making the journey for the first time have no experienced companions to follow. Yet they reliably head in the right direction. How they do this has puzzled biologists for more than a century.

Part of the answer, researchers now agree, is that many migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s, German scientists placed robins in cages surrounded by electric coils that could alter the direction of the magnetic field. During the migratory season, the restless birds tended to hop toward one side of the cage. When the researchers rotated the magnetic field, the birds shifted their preferred direction accordingly. Intriguingly, the birds did not seem to respond to the field's polarity—whether it pointed north or south—but rather to its angle relative to the ground. In effect, they could tell "toward the pole" from "toward the equator." Scientists call this ability an inclination compass.

Detecting the field is one thing. Explaining how a living body does it is another. One leading hypothesis focuses on proteins called cryptochromes, located in the retina of the eye. According to this idea, when light strikes a cryptochrome molecule, it produces a pair of chemically reactive particles whose behavior is subtly influenced by the magnetic field. If this is correct, birds may literally see the field, perhaps as a faint pattern of light or shade overlaid on their ordinary vision. Supporting this view, experiments have shown that robins' magnetic sense is disrupted under certain colors of light and by weak radio-frequency noise, effects that would be difficult to explain if the sense depended solely on a magnetic mineral.

Still, the question is far from settled. Some birds appear to have tiny deposits of iron-containing minerals in their beaks or inner ears, and certain researchers suspect that these play a role as well, perhaps in measuring the strength of the field rather than its direction. It is entirely possible that birds use more than one magnetic mechanism, in addition to cues from the sun, the stars, and familiar landmarks.

What makes the subject especially compelling is that it lies at the boundary between biology and physics. If the cryptochrome hypothesis holds, it would mean that a phenomenon from quantum physics, usually observed only in carefully controlled laboratory conditions, is quietly operating inside a bird's eye, guiding it across a continent in darkness.
The primary purpose of the passage is to

["argue that birds rely only on the stars to navigate","describe the migration route of the European robin in detail","present evidence that birds sense magnetic fields and discuss how they might do so","explain why quantum physics is difficult to study in laboratories"]
The passage first shows that birds detect the field (the cage experiments) and then examines competing explanations: cryptochromes and iron minerals.

Every autumn, a small songbird called the European robin leaves its breeding grounds in Scandinavia and flies south toward the Mediterranean, often traveling at night and across unfamiliar terrain. Young birds making the journey for the first time have no experienced companions to follow. Yet they reliably head in the right direction. How they do this has puzzled biologists for more than a century.

Part of the answer, researchers now agree, is that many migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s, German scientists placed robins in cages surrounded by electric coils that could alter the direction of the magnetic field. During the migratory season, the restless birds tended to hop toward one side of the cage. When the researchers rotated the magnetic field, the birds shifted their preferred direction accordingly. Intriguingly, the birds did not seem to respond to the field's polarity—whether it pointed north or south—but rather to its angle relative to the ground. In effect, they could tell "toward the pole" from "toward the equator." Scientists call this ability an inclination compass.

Detecting the field is one thing. Explaining how a living body does it is another. One leading hypothesis focuses on proteins called cryptochromes, located in the retina of the eye. According to this idea, when light strikes a cryptochrome molecule, it produces a pair of chemically reactive particles whose behavior is subtly influenced by the magnetic field. If this is correct, birds may literally see the field, perhaps as a faint pattern of light or shade overlaid on their ordinary vision. Supporting this view, experiments have shown that robins' magnetic sense is disrupted under certain colors of light and by weak radio-frequency noise, effects that would be difficult to explain if the sense depended solely on a magnetic mineral.

Still, the question is far from settled. Some birds appear to have tiny deposits of iron-containing minerals in their beaks or inner ears, and certain researchers suspect that these play a role as well, perhaps in measuring the strength of the field rather than its direction. It is entirely possible that birds use more than one magnetic mechanism, in addition to cues from the sun, the stars, and familiar landmarks.

What makes the subject especially compelling is that it lies at the boundary between biology and physics. If the cryptochrome hypothesis holds, it would mean that a phenomenon from quantum physics, usually observed only in carefully controlled laboratory conditions, is quietly operating inside a bird's eye, guiding it across a continent in darkness.

Most of us assume that more options are better. If a store offers twenty kinds of cereal rather than five, surely shoppers are more likely to find exactly what they want. Yet a well-known study published in 2000 suggested that, under some circumstances, abundance can be paralyzing.

In the study, psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting table at an upscale grocery store. On some days, the table displayed twenty-four varieties of gourmet jam; on other days, it displayed only six. Shoppers who stopped at the table received a coupon toward a purchase. The larger display attracted more visitors—about sixty percent of passersby stopped, compared with forty percent for the smaller one. But when the researchers tracked the coupons, the pattern reversed dramatically. Roughly thirty percent of the shoppers who saw six jams went on to buy one, while only about three percent of those who saw twenty-four did so.

The researchers proposed that a large set of options can create what came to be called "choice overload." Comparing many alternatives requires mental effort, and the more options there are, the more likely a person is to worry that a better choice was overlooked. Faced with this burden, some people simply decline to choose at all.

The jam study became famous, and the idea spread quickly into business books and popular articles. Later research, however, complicated the picture. When other scientists attempted to repeat similar experiments, they sometimes found the effect, sometimes found no effect, and occasionally found the opposite: larger assortments leading to more purchases. A broad review of dozens of studies concluded that the average effect of assortment size was close to zero.

This does not mean the original finding was mistaken. Instead, researchers have begun to identify the conditions under which choice overload is most likely to appear. It seems strongest when people do not already know what they prefer, when the options are difficult to compare, and when they feel pressure to make the best possible decision. A shopper who always buys strawberry jam will hardly be troubled by a shelf of two dozen flavors; a first-time buyer trying to select the perfect gift may be overwhelmed.

The history of the jam study offers a lesson that extends beyond psychology. A single striking result can capture the public imagination, but science advances by testing, questioning, and refining such results. The most useful conclusion is often not a simple rule—"more choice is bad"—but a more careful account of when, and for whom, a pattern holds.

The following letter is an imagined account, written in the style of the period, of a young woman's first railway journey in the early 1840s.

My dear Margaret,

You made me promise to write the moment I arrived, and so I sit, still in my traveling cloak, at Aunt Harriet's writing desk, my hand not altogether steady—though whether from the motion of the carriage or from sheer astonishment I cannot say.

I confess I approached the station this morning in a state of considerable dread. You will recall that Mr. Pell assured us at dinner last month that the human frame was never designed to travel at more than twenty miles in the hour, and that the rush of air at such velocities would certainly stop the breath. I half believed him, and when the engine came hissing alongside the platform, enormous and black and exhaling steam like some creature in a fable, I very nearly retreated to the coach office.

I did not retreat, and I am exceedingly glad of it. For the first few minutes I gripped the edge of the seat and kept my eyes fixed upon my gloves; but curiosity is a more powerful force than fear, at least in my temperament, and presently I looked out. Margaret, the fields went by as if someone were drawing a painted ribbon past the window. Hedges, cottages, a church tower, a boy waving from a gate—each appeared and vanished before I could properly take it in. My breath, I assure you, continued perfectly well, whatever Mr. Pell's predictions.

What struck me most was not the speed itself but what it does to distance. The journey that once cost Father two full days by coach, with a night at that miserable inn, I completed between breakfast and a late luncheon. It seems to me that the entire country has grown smaller since Tuesday. Aunt Harriet, who has lived her whole life in this town, says that the railway will bring London newspapers here on the very day they are printed, and that she hardly knows whether to be pleased or alarmed.

I confess I share something of her uncertainty. There is a great deal of soot, and the noise is beyond description, and I could not help but feel for the coachmen standing idle in the yard as we passed. Yet I cannot wish the thing undone, for I have seen the future arriving, and it came in at forty miles an hour.

Do tell Mother that I am entirely well, and that I wore my scarf exactly as she instructed; I shall write again on Sunday.

Your affectionate sister,
Eleanor
Eleanor's account of Mr. Pell's warning at dinner mainly serves to

["explain the source of a fear that the journey later proves unfounded","introduce a dinner guest who will join her on the train","criticize her family for inviting Mr. Pell to dinner","show that Eleanor trusts Mr. Pell's scientific knowledge"]
Mr. Pell claimed high speed "would certainly stop the breath," and Eleanor half believed him; later she notes, "My breath, I assure you, continued perfectly well."

Your affectionate sister,

In recent years, boredom has become something most of us work hard to avoid. A few seconds of waiting—in line, at a bus stop, between classes—are enough to send many people reaching for a screen. The impulse is understandable: boredom is uncomfortable, and relief is always within reach. But I want to suggest that in eliminating boredom so efficiently, we may be surrendering something valuable.

Consider what boredom actually is. Psychologists often describe it as a signal: an unpleasant feeling that arises when our current activity fails to engage us. Like hunger, it is not pleasant, but it is useful. Hunger tells us to look for food; boredom tells us to look for something more meaningful to do. When we silence that signal the moment it appears, we lose its message. We trade the restless search for a new pursuit for a stream of small distractions that occupy our attention without ever satisfying it.

There is also evidence that boredom can nourish creativity. In one frequently cited experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately dull task—copying numbers from a telephone directory—later came up with more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than participants who skipped the tedious task. The researchers suggested that boredom prompts the mind to wander, and that a wandering mind is more likely to make unexpected connections. A single study cannot prove a general rule, of course, but the finding is consistent with the experience of many writers, scientists, and artists who report that their best ideas arrived during idle moments: on long walks, in the shower, while staring out a window.

Some will object that this argument romanticizes a feeling that, for many people, is simply miserable, and that chronic boredom is associated with poor concentration and unhappiness. This is a fair point. I am not arguing that boredom is pleasant or that it should be imposed on anyone as a kind of discipline. Prolonged, inescapable boredom—the kind experienced by someone trapped in meaningless work—is genuinely harmful. My claim is narrower: that brief, ordinary boredom, the kind we now dispel by reflex, deserves a little more tolerance.

What might that look like in practice? Perhaps it means leaving the phone in a pocket during a ten-minute wait, or allowing a free afternoon to remain unscheduled. It means treating the first flicker of restlessness not as a problem to be solved instantly but as an invitation. The mind, given a little empty space, has a way of filling it with something of its own making. We should be willing, now and then, to find out what.

Mangrove forests grow where few other trees can survive: in salty mud that is flooded twice a day by the tide. Their tangled roots rise above the waterline like stilts, allowing the trees to take in air even when the soil beneath them contains almost none. Some species also pump excess salt out through their leaves, which can be seen as white crystals on sunny afternoons. These adaptations are only part of the story. The roots slow incoming waves, so sediment settles and builds up new land over time, and the sheltered water among them serves as a nursery for young fish. When coastal communities clear mangroves for shrimp farms, they often discover too late that storms hit harder and local fish catches shrink.

Some species also pump excess salt out through their leaves, which can be seen as white crystals on sunny afternoons. These adaptations are only part of the story. The roots slow incoming waves, so sediment settles and builds up new land over time, and the sheltered water among them serves as a nursery for young fish. When coastal communities clear mangroves for shrimp farms, they often discover too late that storms hit harder and local fish catches shrink.

["They always earn more money from shrimp.","They may later suffer worse storm damage and smaller fish catches.","They no longer need protection from waves.","They quickly replant the trees."]

Sociologists use the term "third place" for spots that are neither home nor workplace, such as barbershops, community gardens, and public libraries. In a third place, status matters little: a retired electrician and a college student may end up chatting over the same chessboard. Researchers who studied a town after its only cafe closed found that residents reported feeling less connected to neighbors, even though most had plenty of online contacts. The finding does not prove that screens are to blame. It suggests instead that casual, repeated, face-to-face encounters build a sense of belonging that is hard to replace. Planners who treat such places as luxuries, the researchers argue, may be overlooking the quiet work they do holding a community together.

Railways could carry coal faster, and by 1850 the barge traffic had dwindled to a trickle. Yet the canal did not disappear. Scientists once assumed that the sleeping brain simply rests. Experiments with volunteers have since overturned that view. In one study, participants learned a list of word pairs and were then divided into two groups: one slept for eight hours, the other stayed awake. When tested the next day, the sleepers recalled roughly 20 percent more pairs. Brain scans suggest why: during deep sleep, patterns of activity from the day are replayed, apparently strengthening the connections that store new information. Researchers caution that sleep is not a substitute for study; a student who never reviews material has nothing for the brain to replay. Still, the results make all-night cramming look like a poor bargain.
What is the main idea of the passage?
["Volunteers dislike memory experiments.","The brain rests completely during sleep.","Sleep helps the brain strengthen new memories.","Students should avoid studying."]
The passage reports that sleep boosted recall by strengthening connections.

An octopus has no shell and no bones, yet it survives in waters full of hungry predators. Its best defense is camouflage. Special cells in its skin, called chromatophores, can expand or shrink in a fraction of a second. Each cell holds a tiny sac of color, so the octopus can turn from red to brown to nearly white as it moves across a reef. Some octopuses also change the texture of their skin, raising small bumps to look like rough rocks or seaweed. Scientists once believed the animal relied on its eyes to match its surroundings. However, recent studies suggest that the skin itself may sense light, helping the octopus blend in even when parts of its body are hidden from view. If camouflage fails, the octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and escape.

["The octopus can only live near a reef.","The octopus builds shells from rocks.","The octopus is the fastest animal in the sea.","The octopus uses color and texture changes to protect itself."]

Beginning more than two thousand years ago, a network of trade routes known as the Silk Road linked China with the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Few merchants traveled the entire distance. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and each handoff raised the price. Silk, spices, and paper moved westward, while glass, gold, and horses traveled east. Yet merchandise was not the only thing that crossed these deserts and mountains. Ideas, religions, and even diseases moved along the same paths. Buddhism, for instance, spread from India into East Asia largely through travelers on these roads. Towns along the way, such as Samarkand, grew wealthy by providing food, water, and shelter to caravans. Historians therefore describe the Silk Road not merely as a place for buying and selling but as a meeting point of cultures.

Every spring, Grandfather Chen knelt in the same corner of the yard and pressed a handful of seeds into the soil as gently as if he were tucking in a baby. Lian, who was nine, thought it was a strange habit, since the store sold tomatoes all year. "Those are not the same tomatoes," he told her one morning, wiping his hands on his old gray apron. When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a figure-eight dance on the honeycomb. The straight middle part of the dance, called the waggle run, carries the message. The angle of the run, measured against gravity, tells the other bees which direction to fly relative to the sun. The length of the run indicates distance: the longer the waggle, the farther the flowers. Researchers who first decoded the dance in the 1940s were astonished, because it suggested that insects could share precise information symbolically. Later experiments strengthened that view. When scientists moved a food source while a hive's dancers were advertising its old location, bees that followed the dance arrived at the empty spot and searched there, which showed that they were relying on the dancers' directions rather than simply smelling the food.
What does the length of the waggle run tell other bees?
["Which flower is the largest","How many bees should go","How sweet the nectar is","How far away the flowers are"]
The passage says a longer waggle means farther flowers.

Before canals, farmers in inland regions often struggled to sell their crops. Wagons were slow, roads turned to mud in the rain, and a heavy load of grain could cost nearly as much to haul as it was worth. Then a canal was dug linking the interior to the coast. Towns along the waterway grew into busy markets, and farmers began planting crops specifically to sell rather than only to feed their families. Leaves look green in summer because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that captures sunlight for making food. As days grow shorter in autumn, trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the green fades. The yellow and orange colors that remain were present all along; they were simply hidden. Red leaves are different. Their color comes from anthocyanins, pigments that many trees manufacture only in autumn, from sugars trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days and cool nights produce the richest reds, because sunshine builds up sugar while cold prevents it from leaving the leaf. In a cloudy, warm autumn, the display is usually duller. Brown leaves, finally, result from waste products left behind after the other pigments are gone.
Why do yellow and orange colors appear in autumn?

Those colors were present all along but hidden by chlorophyll.

This summer, the Maple Street Library invites students ages 11 to 15 to participate in our Summer Reading Challenge, which begins on June 20 and ends on August 15.

Sign up at the front desk or on our website, and you will receive a reading log. Each time you finish a book, write its title in your log and ask a librarian to stamp it. Books that are assigned for school do not count, but comic books and audiobooks do.

Many animals locate food by looking for it. Bats that hunt at night, however, face a serious problem, because it is often too dark to see insects flying through the air. To solve this problem, most of these bats rely on an ability called echolocation.

Echolocation works by using sound. As a bat flies, it produces a series of extremely high-pitched calls, most of which are too high for human ears to detect. When the sound waves hit an object, such as a moth or a tree branch, they bounce back toward the bat. These returning sounds are called echoes. The bat's large ears collect the echoes, and its brain uses them to create a detailed picture of its surroundings.

The echoes provide the bat with a surprising amount of information. The time it takes for an echo to return tells the bat how far away an object is: a quick echo means that the object is close, while a slow echo means that it is farther away. Changes in the echo can also indicate whether an insect is moving toward the bat or away from it, and even how large the insect is.

As a bat approaches its prey, it calls faster and faster. At the beginning of a hunt, a bat might produce about ten calls per second, but in the final moment before it captures an insect, it may produce nearly two hundred. This rapid series of calls, sometimes called a "feeding buzz," allows the bat to follow every sudden turn its prey makes.

Bats are not the only animals that use echolocation. Dolphins and some whales use it underwater, where light does not travel far. Scientists have also studied echolocation in order to design useful tools for people. For example, ships use a system called sonar to measure the depth of the ocean and to locate objects beneath the surface. In this way, an ability that helps a small animal catch its dinner has also helped humans explore the sea.
What is the passage mainly about?

["Why humans cannot hear the calls of most bats","Why bats are more active at night than during the day","How ships measure the depth of the ocean","How some animals use sound to find objects and food"]
The passage explains how echolocation works for bats and notes that dolphins, whales, and even ships use similar methods.

Many animals locate food by looking for it. Bats that hunt at night, however, face a serious problem, because it is often too dark to see insects flying through the air. To solve this problem, most of these bats rely on an ability called echolocation.

Echolocation works by using sound. As a bat flies, it produces a series of extremely high-pitched calls, most of which are too high for human ears to detect. When the sound waves hit an object, such as a moth or a tree branch, they bounce back toward the bat. These returning sounds are called echoes. The bat's large ears collect the echoes, and its brain uses them to create a detailed picture of its surroundings.

The echoes provide the bat with a surprising amount of information. The time it takes for an echo to return tells the bat how far away an object is: a quick echo means that the object is close, while a slow echo means that it is farther away. Changes in the echo can also indicate whether an insect is moving toward the bat or away from it, and even how large the insect is.

As a bat approaches its prey, it calls faster and faster. At the beginning of a hunt, a bat might produce about ten calls per second, but in the final moment before it captures an insect, it may produce nearly two hundred. This rapid series of calls, sometimes called a "feeding buzz," allows the bat to follow every sudden turn its prey makes.

Bats are not the only animals that use echolocation. Dolphins and some whales use it underwater, where light does not travel far. Scientists have also studied echolocation in order to design useful tools for people. For example, ships use a system called sonar to measure the depth of the ocean and to locate objects beneath the surface. In this way, an ability that helps a small animal catch its dinner has also helped humans explore the sea.

Today, most people pay for goods with coins, paper bills, or electronic cards. However, money as we know it has not always existed. For thousands of years, people obtained what they needed through a system called barter.

In a barter system, people exchange goods or services directly. A farmer with extra wheat, for instance, might trade some of it to a potter for a clay pot. This arrangement works well when each person has something the other one wants. But barter has a serious weakness. Imagine that the potter does not need any wheat. The farmer would then have to find someone who wants wheat and who also has something the potter wants, and finding such a match could take days.

To make trading easier, many societies began using particular objects as an early form of money. These objects had to be valued by almost everyone in the community. In different regions of the world, people used shells, salt, cattle, and even enormous stones. Because everyone accepted these items, a farmer could sell wheat for shells and later use the shells to purchase a pot.

Eventually, metal became a popular choice. Metals such as gold, silver, and copper were durable, which meant that they did not rot or break easily, and they could also be divided into smaller pieces for inexpensive purchases. Still, traders had to weigh the metal every time they used it, which was a slow process.

About 2,600 years ago, rulers in the kingdom of Lydia, located in what is now Turkey, solved this problem. They began producing coins that had a standard weight and an official stamp on each one. The stamp showed that the ruler guaranteed the coin's value, so people no longer needed to weigh it. The idea spread quickly to other lands, and coins soon became an ordinary part of daily life.

Before electric refrigerators were invented, keeping food cold was a genuine challenge. In many places, people depended on natural ice, which was cut from frozen lakes and ponds during the winter months. For a period in the 1800s, this ice became a valuable product that was shipped around the world.

The ice trade began with a Boston businessman named Frederic Tudor. In 1806, he filled a ship with ice and sent it to the Caribbean island of Martinique, where the weather is hot throughout the year. Many people laughed at the plan, because they believed that the ice would simply melt during the long voyage. In fact, much of it did, and Tudor lost money on his first attempts.

However, Tudor did not give up. He experimented with various methods to keep ice from melting, and he discovered that packing the blocks tightly together and surrounding them with sawdust slowed melting considerably. Sawdust, a waste product from lumber mills, was inexpensive and easy to find. It acted as insulation, a material that prevents heat from passing through.

The method of cutting ice also improved. Workers originally used axes and hand saws, which was slow and produced uneven pieces. Later, a horse-drawn tool was invented that cut deep lines across the ice in a grid pattern. This allowed workers to divide the ice into neat blocks of identical size, which were easier to stack and store.

By the middle of the 1800s, ice from New England was traveling as far as India. Cold drinks, fresh fish, and ice cream became possible in places that had never seen frozen water. The trade gradually ended in the early 1900s, when machines that could manufacture ice became common. Nevertheless, the ice trade demonstrated how a creative idea and patient testing could transform a winter resource into a global business.

["How natural ice became a product shipped around the world","How electric refrigerators were invented","How lumber mills produced sawdust in the 1800s","Why the weather in the Caribbean is hot all year"]
The passage describes the ice trade, from Tudor's first shipment to ice traveling as far as India.

Deep underground, some of the most remarkable landscapes on Earth are hidden in complete darkness. Limestone caves, with their long tunnels and enormous chambers, can stretch for many kilometers. Although caves may look as if they were carved by powerful tools, most of them were shaped gradually by something much gentler: water.

The process begins with rain. As rainwater falls through the atmosphere, it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide gas, and when the water soaks into the soil, it picks up even more carbon dioxide from decaying plants. The carbon dioxide combines with the water to form a weak acid called carbonic acid. This acid is far too mild to harm a person, but it has an important effect on one particular kind of rock.

Limestone is composed mostly of a mineral called calcite, which slowly dissolves in carbonic acid. As acidic water moves downward through small cracks in limestone, it dissolves a thin layer of rock along the way. Over thousands of years, the cracks widen into narrow passages, and eventually some passages become large enough for a person to walk through. The largest caves may require millions of years to develop.

Once a cave has formed, water continues to change it, but in a different way. When water drips from the ceiling of a cave, it carries dissolved calcite with it. Inside the cave, some of the carbon dioxide escapes from the water into the air. As a result, the water can no longer hold all of its calcite, and a tiny amount of the mineral is left behind. Drop by drop, these deposits accumulate. Formations that hang from the ceiling like icicles are called stalactites, while those that rise from the floor, where the drops land, are called stalagmites. When a stalactite and a stalagmite finally meet, they form a column.

These formations grow extremely slowly; in many caves, a stalactite may gain only a centimeter or so in a hundred years. For this reason, scientists can examine cave formations to learn about the past. Layers inside a stalagmite, much like the rings of a tree, can reveal how much rain fell in the surrounding area long ago.

Because they take so long to form, cave formations are easily damaged and nearly impossible to replace. Even the natural oils from a single human hand can prevent a formation from growing in the location where it was touched. Consequently, many caves that are open to visitors have designated paths and railings, and guests are instructed never to touch the walls or formations. By following these regulations, visitors help protect features that nature required thousands of years to create.

The passage explains how acidic water dissolves limestone to form caves and then builds formations inside them.

Drop by drop, these deposits accumulate. Formations that hang from the ceiling like icicles are called stalactites, while those that rise from the floor, where the drops land, are called stalagmites. When a stalactite and a stalagmite finally meet, they form a column.

These formations grow extremely slowly; in many caves, a stalactite may gain only a centimeter or so in a hundred years. For this reason, scientists can examine cave formations to learn about the past. Layers inside a stalagmite, much like the rings of a tree, can reveal how much rain fell in the surrounding area long ago.

Because they take so long to form, cave formations are easily damaged and nearly impossible to replace. Even the natural oils from a single human hand can prevent a formation from growing in the location where it was touched. Consequently, many caves that are open to visitors have designated paths and railings, and guests are instructed never to touch the walls or formations. By following these regulations, visitors help protect features that nature required thousands of years to create.

The comparison appears in a sentence about learning "about the past"; like tree rings, the layers record how much rain fell long ago.

Today, it seems natural that everyone in the same region sets their clocks to the same time. Yet for most of history, this was not the case. Until the late 1800s, nearly every community kept its own time, and this system functioned reasonably well until a new form of transportation made it confusing.

In the past, people set their clocks according to the sun. When the sun reached its highest point in the sky, it was noon. Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the sun reaches this position slightly earlier in towns to the east and slightly later in towns to the west. As a result, when it was noon in one city, it might be 12:10 in a city to the east and 11:50 in a city to the west. This method, known as local solar time, caused few difficulties when most people traveled by horse or on foot, because a journey between two towns took so long that a difference of a few minutes hardly mattered.

The railroads transformed this situation. By the middle of the 1800s, trains could carry passengers hundreds of kilometers in a single day. Each railroad company usually established its schedules according to the time in its home city, so travelers had to deal with numerous different times at once. In the United States alone, there were more than fifty different railroad times. A train station might display several clocks on the same wall, each showing a different hour. Passengers frequently missed connections, and in the worst cases, confusion about schedules contributed to accidents when two trains used the same track.

To solve the problem, railroad leaders in the United States and Canada agreed on a new plan. On November 18, 1883, they divided the continent into a small number of time zones. Within each zone, every clock would display the same time, and neighboring zones would differ by exactly one hour. Some people called the event "the day of two noons," because many towns had to set their clocks back, and in those places the clocks struck noon a second time that day.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Some people complained that the railroads had no right to control time, which they believed belonged to the sun, and a few cities refused to adopt standard time for years. Nevertheless, the system proved so useful that it spread. In 1884, representatives from many nations met in Washington, D.C., and selected a line passing through Greenwich, England, as the official starting point for measuring longitude. This decision helped establish the worldwide system of time zones that people rely on today.
What is the passage mainly about?
["Why trains became faster during the 1800s","How the city of Greenwich became famous","Why and how standard time zones were created","How people measured the position of the sun"]
The passage explains the problems caused by local solar time and railroads, the creation of time zones in 1883, and their spread.

Lab: Which Solids Dissolve in Water?

Goal: In this investigation, you will find out which of three common solids dissolve in water.

Materials: three clear plastic cups, warm water, a measuring cup, a metal spoon, salt, sand, sugar, labels, and a marker

Procedure:
Step 1: Use the marker to label the three cups "Salt," "Sand," and "Sugar."
Step 2: Carefully pour 200 milliliters of warm water into each of the cups.
Step 3: Add one spoonful of salt to the cup that is labeled "Salt."
Step 4: Stir the water for 30 seconds. Then wait one minute and carefully observe what happens in the cup.
Step 5: Clean the spoon. Then repeat Steps 3 and 4 with the sand and then the sugar.
Step 6: Record all of your observations in the data table.

Safety: Wear safety goggles during the entire investigation. Do not taste any of the materials, even if you think you already know what they are.

Hint: A solid has dissolved if you can no longer see it in the water. However, if you can still see pieces at the bottom of the cup after waiting, the solid did not dissolve.

["To find out which solids dissolve in water","To measure how warm the water is","To learn how to label cups correctly","To compare the taste of salt and sugar"]
The lab states its goal: "you will find out which of three common solids dissolve in water."

Many of the world's first cities developed beside rivers. In ancient Egypt, people built towns along the Nile River, and in Mesopotamia, cities formed between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers. Why did early people choose these locations?

First, rivers provided fresh water for drinking, cooking, and washing. Second, rivers helped farmers. Each year, many rivers flooded, and when the water went down, it left behind a layer of rich, dark soil called silt. Crops grew well in this soil, so farmers could produce more food than their families needed. Extra food meant that not everyone had to farm, so some people could become builders, traders, or teachers.

Rivers also functioned like highways. Boats could transport heavy goods, such as grain and stone, much faster than people could carry them over land, which made trade between towns easier.

Of course, living near a river also had risks, since a flood that was too large could destroy homes and fields. Still, for early people, the benefits were greater than the dangers.

["A crop grown along the Nile River","A wall built to stop floods","Rich soil left behind after a flood","A kind of boat used for trade"]
The passage says floods "left behind a layer of rich, dark soil called silt."

Along the Pacific coast of North America, underwater forests of kelp, a type of large brown seaweed, provide food and shelter for many species of fish, snails, and other organisms. The health of these kelp forests depends heavily on a small, furry mammal: the sea otter.

Sea otters consume large numbers of sea urchins, spiny animals that feed on kelp. When otters are present, they keep the urchin population under control, and the kelp can grow tall and dense. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, however, hunters killed sea otters in enormous numbers for their valuable fur. In many areas, otters disappeared completely. Without their main predator, sea urchins multiplied rapidly and devoured huge areas of kelp. Locations that had once been rich forests became "urchin barrens," rocky sea floors with little life.

After laws began protecting sea otters in the twentieth century, otters gradually returned to parts of their former range. Where they recovered, urchin populations declined and kelp forests began to regrow, bringing back many of the fish and other animals that depend on them.

Scientists describe the sea otter as a keystone species. Like the keystone at the top of a stone arch, which holds the other stones in place, a keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem that is much larger than its numbers would suggest. Removing it can cause the entire system to change.
What is the main idea of the passage?

["Sea otters play a key role in keeping kelp forests healthy.","Hunting laws have failed to protect sea otters.","Sea urchins are the most important animals in kelp forests.","Kelp is the largest type of seaweed in the Pacific Ocean."]
The passage says kelp forests depend "heavily" on sea otters and shows how forests disappeared without otters and regrew when otters returned.

During the 1930s, a series of severe dust storms struck the southern Great Plains of the United States, a region that included parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico. This area became known as the Dust Bowl.

The disaster had both natural and human causes. In the early 1900s, high wheat prices and new machines such as gasoline-powered tractors encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of grassland. The deep roots of native prairie grasses had held the soil in place for thousands of years. Once the grass was removed, the soil was exposed. Then, beginning in 1931, a long drought struck the region. Crops failed, and with nothing to anchor it, the dry topsoil was easily lifted by strong winds.

Some storms carried dust hundreds of miles, darkening skies as far away as the East Coast. Many families lost their farms, and hundreds of thousands of people migrated west in search of work.

In response, the federal government created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935. Its experts taught farmers methods such as planting rows of trees as windbreaks and plowing along the natural curves of the land. These practices reduced erosion, and when rain finally returned near the end of the decade, the land gradually began to recover.
What is the passage mainly about?
["The invention of the gasoline-powered tractor","The causes, effects, and response to the Dust Bowl","The history of wheat farming in Oklahoma","The reasons families moved to the East Coast"]
The passage explains the human and natural causes of the Dust Bowl, the damage it did, and how the government responded.

Statistics appear constantly in everyday life, from news reports about home prices to announcements about average test scores. Two of the most common statistics are the mean and the median. Understanding the difference between them can help people interpret information more accurately.

The mean, often called the average, is calculated by adding all the values in a data set and dividing by the number of values. The median is the middle value when all the values are arranged in order from smallest to largest. In many data sets, these two numbers are fairly similar. However, they can differ significantly when a data set contains outliers, values that are much larger or smaller than the rest.

Consider a small company with five employees. Four of them earn $40,000 per year, and the owner earns $240,000. The mean salary is $80,000, which is twice what most employees actually earn. The median salary, however, is $40,000, which describes the typical worker much more accurately. A single high salary pulled the mean upward but had no effect on the median.

For this reason, economists usually report the median when describing incomes or home prices. Otherwise, a few extremely expensive houses or very high salaries could make an area appear wealthier than it actually is. Before drawing conclusions from a statistic, a careful reader should ask which measure is being used and whether outliers might be influencing it.

["To explain the difference between the mean and the median and why it matters","To argue that the mean should never be used","To show why home prices have increased","To explain how to calculate a company's profits"]

The vertex moves from (0, −2) to (2, 0): 2 unit(s) right and 2 unit(s) up, so g(x) = f(x − 2) + 2.

The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3), and rises -0.5 unit(s) for each unit to the right, so the slope is -0.5 and the equation is y = −(1/2)x + 3.

The lines intersect at (1, 2), so x + y = 3.

The vertex of the parabola is (-1, -2); its y-coordinate -2 is the minimum value of f.
The graph of y = f(x) is shown, where f is a quadratic function. Which of the following could define f?
The graph crosses the x-axis at x = -1 and x = 4, so (x + 1) and (x − 4) are factors of f(x); the graph opens upward.
The graph of the exponential function f is shown. Which equation could define f?
f(0) = 3 gives the initial value, and f(1)/f(0) = 3 gives the growth factor: f(x) = 3·3^x.
